papers.abstract: Models read a book, an hour of video, or an image in one forward pass. As the context grows, this pass slows down, loses accuracy, and stops at the context window. Sparse attention is efficient, but keeps the other two limitations. Grid probing, a recent training-free method, recovers the accuracy and extends the reach by asking a frozen model the same question about short local and strided spans of the input, but every question repeats the whole computation, since each span is encoded again. Our insight is that grid probing is emulated attention, an attention pattern reproduced from outside the model through prompts, since each probe only restricts which part of the input the question can see. We introduce Factorized Context Attention (FCA), a training-free block-sparse attention that runs the same pattern natively, as the attention of the model itself. FCA encodes the input once into a KV cache, reads all spans as masked sequences in one batched forward, and uses a stair position schedule to keep every span inside the trained position range. Across long video understanding, long-context text inference and image grounding, FCA matches the accuracy and the reach of grid probing at a fraction of its cost. It gains about 10 points over the single pass on long video and 9 to 14 points on long novels, finds needles in videos of over a thousand frames and in texts four times the length of the window, and answers a later question about the same input in as little as a tenth of the time of grid probing. Native attention thus keeps what emulated attention gains without its cost, all with existing frozen language and vision-language models.
authors: Mohamed Eltahir, Manar Eyad, Yara Alzahrani, Fatimah Albesher, Duaa M. Tahir, Tanveer Hussain, Naeemullah Khan
bullets: Addresses the slowdown, accuracy loss, and context-window limits of one-pass long-context inference.
Uses training-free block-sparse attention to read local and strided spans from a single KV cache in one batched forward pass.
Employs a stair position schedule to keep spans within the model’s trained position range.
Matches grid probing’s accuracy and reach across long video, long-text inference, and image grounding while using a fraction of its cost.
Reports up to roughly 10-point gains over single-pass inference, finds information beyond the context window, and can be as fast as one-tenth of grid probing.

papers.selection_reason: Training-free block-sparse attention for native grid probing over long contexts; fits efficient attention and long-context models.
papers.title: Factorized Context Attention: From Emulated to Native Grid Probing
papers.tldr: Factorized Context Attention natively reproduces grid probing’s long-context benefits with much lower inference cost in frozen language and vision-language models.

papers.abstract: Linear attention replaces softmax attention with a linear formulation, enabling linear-time computation with a fixed-size recurrent state instead of a growing key-value cache. These computational and memory advantages have attracted growing interest in linear attention for long-context language modeling. However, compressing past information into a fixed-size state causes memory collisions that hinder long-context understanding. Although DeltaNet mitigates memory collisions through delta-rule updates and Gated DeltaNet extends this approach with gating, these mechanisms may also discard information relevant to future predictions. To address this limitation, we introduce Integral DeltaNet, which maintains two complementary recurrent states: a fast-updating delta state that captures current key-value associations and an integral state that preserves a weighted history of the delta state. At readout, the model adaptively combines these states to access information across different timescales. We further derive a chunkwise parallel formulation that enables hardware-efficient training. We evaluate Integral DeltaNet using 340M and 1.3B parameter models trained from scratch on 15B and 100B FineWeb-Edu tokens, respectively. Comparisons with strong recurrent baselines show improved overall performance in language modeling, commonsense reasoning, real-world and synthetic retrieval, long-context understanding, and length extrapolation. We also compare training throughput and activation memory, as well as decoding latency and memory.
authors: Junsoo Oh, Jihun Yun, Junhyuck Kim, Hanbaek Lyu
bullets: Linear attention avoids growing key-value caches but can lose information through fixed-size memory collisions.
The method uses a delta state for current key-value associations and an integral state that preserves a weighted history of past delta states.
An adaptive readout combines both states to retrieve information across multiple timescales.
A chunkwise parallel formulation supports hardware-efficient training.
Experiments report improved performance across language modeling, reasoning, retrieval, long-context understanding, and length extrapolation, alongside evaluations of efficiency and memory use.

papers.title: Integral DeltaNet: Improved Linear Attention with Adaptive Memory Integration
papers.tldr: Integral DeltaNet improves linear attention by combining fast-changing and long-term recurrent memories for better long-context information retention.

papers.abstract: Gated DeltaNet (GDN) achieves linear computational complexity through recurrent state updates, but sequential dependencies between chunks limit parallelism, particularly for long-context workloads with small batch sizes or limited head-level parallelism per GPU. We present FlashQLA, a context-parallel execution framework for GDN that exposes additional sequence-level parallelism while reducing boundary-state preprocessing overhead. FlashQLA reduces boundary-state preprocessing overhead through decay-aware preparation and extends sequence parallelism across GPUs with Dual CP, which shares summary computation across parallelism levels. Workload-adaptive Auto CP and CP-aware kernel co-design further improve execution efficiency. FlashQLA achieves $1.7\times$-$3.1\times$ forward speedup and up to $4.4\times$ backward speedup over Flash Linear Attention (FLA) on a single GPU. On eight GPUs with context lengths up to 1M tokens, Dual CP achieves up to $4.8\times$ forward speedup and $4.4\times$ speedup for combined forward and backward execution over FLA KCP.
authors: Xi Lin, Chengruidong Zhang, Huiqiang Jiang, Xiao Li, Zekun Wang, Junda Feng, Yunfei Mao, Siqi Zhang, Siyu Wang, Man Yuan, Rui Men, Bo Zheng, Dayiheng Liu, Bohan Zhuang, Jianwei Zhang
bullets: Addresses limited parallelism from GDN’s sequential chunk dependencies, especially for long contexts and small batch sizes.
Uses decay-aware boundary preparation and Dual CP to share summary computation across parallelism levels.
Adds workload-adaptive Auto CP and context-parallel-aware kernel co-design for improved efficiency.
Reports 1.7×–3.1× forward and up to 4.4× backward speedup over FLA on one GPU.
Across eight GPUs and up to 1M-token contexts, Dual CP reaches up to 4.8× forward speedup and 4.4× combined forward/backward speedup over FLA KCP.

papers.abstract: Reasoning models degrade as their context grows, so longer reasoning traces do not by themselves give longer effective horizons. One way to extend the horizon is to compress the reasoning history into a compact state from time to time and continue from the state. Existing methods train the state with the final-answer reward or distill it from a stronger model. Neither signal is tailored to measure the contribution of the state alone. We observe that a reasoning model that degrades over long trajectories still behaves reliably in short contexts. We aim to preserve this short-context behavior when compressing the reasoning history. Motivated by this, we train a separate summarizer with Delta-KL, a reward computed from the frozen reasoning model's token-level predictions on sampled continuations, and run inference by truncating the trace, summarizing it, and continuing from the summary (TruSuCo). Training uses a few thousand questions with 4k-token reasoning prefixes and does not need answers or external teachers. Under a fixed 32k-token budget, the trained summarizer improves on vanilla reasoning and on an untrained summarizer in all nine settings across mathematical benchmarks and Reasoning Gym puzzles, by up to 7.7 points and 12 points, respectively. The improvement over vanilla reasoning grows with the budget. At 128k tokens, our method outperforms it by 10 points on AIME 2024--2026. Analyses show that truncation prevents the collapse of vanilla reasoning and that the trained summaries retain more of the reasoning history.
bullets: Long reasoning traces degrade as context grows, limiting effective reasoning horizons.
A separate summarizer is trained with Delta-KL from token-level predictions on sampled local continuations.
Inference repeatedly truncates the trace, summarizes the history, and continues reasoning from the summary.
Using a few thousand questions and no answers or external teacher, TruSuCo improves over vanilla reasoning across nine settings.
Under fixed token budgets, gains reach 7.7 points and 12 points over vanilla and an untrained summarizer; at 128k tokens, it gains 10 points on AIME 2024–2026.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses long-context reasoning degradation via learned summaries, directly relevant to long-context LLM methods.

papers.abstract: A training-time attention change is usually judged for zero-shot context extension against a dense baseline beyond the training length at the default temperature, $\tau = 1$. The outcome depends on how miscalibrated the baseline is there: the share of perplexity it recovers when its logits are sharpened by one scalar. Under the standard recipe (fp32 master weights), an 8k-trained baseline is 8-15% miscalibrated at 30k in three seed-paired 365M twins; in one of them this makes the block-sparse-trained twin look 7% better, which calibration removes. In pure-bf16 training without master weights the miscalibration is several times larger: an AdamW step ($\beta_2 = 0.95$) on a gain initialised at 1.0 is below half the bf16 spacing at peak learning rates under $1.7\times10^{-3}$, so gains never move (22 checkpoints), the baseline is 37-58% miscalibrated, and block-sparse pretraining, attention dropout and ALiBi look 6-35% better. Calibrating one temperature per model and length removes all three advantages, leaves ALiBi 5% behind RoPE and keeps part of the gain of a positive control, NTK-aware scaling. Unfreezing the gains reverses the block-sparse advantage at 365M and removes 71-89% of it at 1.2B. We recommend reporting extension results at calibrated temperatures and checking that normalisation gains moved.
bullets: At the default temperature, baseline miscalibration beyond training length can make alternative attention methods appear better than they are.
In fp32-master-weight 365M twins, calibration removed a reported 7% block-sparse advantage; in pure-bf16 training, larger miscalibration produced apparent 6–35% advantages for several methods.
Per-model, per-length temperature calibration removed the apparent gains of block-sparse attention, attention dropout, and ALiBi, while retaining part of NTK-aware scaling’s gain.
Unfreezing attention gains reversed the block-sparse advantage at 365M and removed 71–89% of it at 1.2B.
The authors recommend calibrated-temperature reporting and checking that normalization gains actually update.

Curves: the 13-point sweep on the calibration windows, on which each arm’s τ∗ is selected (filled marker; open marker τ = 1; thin lines single pairs, thick their mean); these windows are easier than the held-out windows quoted in the text, so the curves sit lower than those numbers. Boxes: the held-out ∆ = log PPL(Mixed) − log PPL(Dense) at τ = 1 and at τ∗, seed-averaged (Table 1 for (a); Table 3 for (b)–(d)). With frozen gains (a) the baseline sits far up the right-hand branch at τ = 1 while Mixed’s curve is flatter there; the later recipes shrink that climb without removing it.

papers.selection_reason: Directly studies zero-shot context extension, calibration, RoPE/ALiBi scaling, and long-context evaluation for language models.
papers.title: Attention Temperature Confounds Zero-Shot Context Extension
papers.tldr: Zero-shot context-extension gains can be artifacts of baseline logit miscalibration, so evaluations should calibrate temperature and verify normalization parameters moved.

papers.abstract: The search for computationally efficient alternatives to the Transformer has yielded numerous architectures in recent years; however, most exhibit severe weaknesses in associative recall-such as key-value (KV) retrieval-and length extrapolation, where even standard Transformers struggle. This paper introduces LimeTree, a linear-complexity architecture in both memory and compute for sequence modeling. By integrating synthetic KV retrieval tasks directly into standard language modeling training, LimeTree achieves strong perplexity alongside reliable recall. Two variants were evaluated on WikiText-103 and PG-19 under strict compute constraints. On WikiText-103, LimeTree reaches a token-level perplexity of 19 in just 6 hours on four Quadro RTX 8000 GPUs, while maintaining 100\% KV retrieval accuracy even when extrapolating from a training context length of 512 to an evaluation length of 16,384. On PG-19, the model achieves a token-level perplexity of 13 in 35 hours on a single RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU with minimal hyperparameter tuning. These results position LimeTree as a competitive linear-complexity alternative to Transformers, combining superior perplexity and training throughput with robust in-context retrieval and length extrapolation.
bullets: Targets Transformer inefficiencies, especially associative recall and context-length extrapolation.
Uses a tree-graph architecture and incorporates synthetic key-value retrieval tasks into language-model training.
Evaluated on WikiText-103 and PG-19 under strict compute constraints.
On WikiText-103, achieves perplexity 19 and 100% KV retrieval accuracy when extrapolating from context length 512 to 16,384.
Reports perplexity 13 on PG-19 with minimal hyperparameter tuning.

(b) During the top-down pass, the global root hroot modulates mid-level subtree slots Hmid through a multiplicative bilinear gate before a secondary convex tree sweep produces the global summary htd.

papers.abstract: Sparse attention reduces the cost of long-context decoding, but token selection introduces additional scoring and ranking overhead. Moreover, uniform page scoring overlooks differences in relevance between near and far context. We propose Near-Far Attention (NFA), which adapts retrieval to regional attention patterns while keeping candidate scoring lightweight. During prefill, the Lightweight Gate Estimator identifies regions that can be skipped during decoding, adding less than 1% to dense-prefill time. For the remaining regions, the Calibration-Free Subspace Extractor supplies compact features shared by page-level and token-level scoring without offline calibration. The Distance-Aware Two-Level Selector then scores near and far pages differently and jointly ranks candidate tokens under a shared budget. Evaluations across model families, parameter scales, and GQA/MLA architectures show aggregate task quality comparable to full attention. On Qwen3-8B at 512K context length, NFA achieves up to $5.49\times$ operator speedup and $2.97\times$ whole-model decoding speedup over FlashInfer, including selection overhead.
authors: YuanShuo Wang, Jianchao Tan, Lei Gong, Teng Wang, Wenqi Lou, Xuehai Zhou
bullets: Addresses retrieval overhead and the limits of uniform page scoring in sparse attention.
Uses a Lightweight Gate Estimator during prefill to skip low-value regions with under 1% added dense-prefill time.
Extracts compact, calibration-free features for both page- and token-level scoring.
A distance-aware two-level selector ranks near and far pages and candidate tokens under a shared budget.
On Qwen3-8B at 512K context, achieves up to 5.49× operator and 2.97× whole-model decoding speedup over FlashInfer, including selection overhead.

papers.selection_reason: Sparse region-aware attention for long-context LLM decoding with lightweight page/token selection and retrieval.
papers.title: Near-Far Attention: Region-Aware Sparse Retrieval for Long-Context LLM Decoding
papers.tldr: Near-Far Attention accelerates long-context LLM decoding by sparsely retrieving tokens with region-aware scoring while preserving task quality comparable to full attention.

papers.abstract: Professional documents are a long-context workload that retrieval-style benchmarks do not capture. In a ten-domain enterprise collection, a task's evidence is spread across a source document of median length 27 pages (mean 48.8, maximum 873); a third of tasks rest mainly on charts, drawings, and maps; and 70.9% require two or more reasoning hops. We post-train Kimi-K2.7, an open-weight foundation model, at its full context window on 1,465 expert-authored tasks with atomic rubrics from that collection, training rank-32 adapters with one round of privileged-context on-policy self-distillation followed by two rounds of rubric-reward reinforcement learning. We render each PDF as text for training and as extracted text plus selected page images at evaluation. The smoothed RL training reward rises from 0.37 in the first tenth of the run to 0.67 in the last. On the 100-task GDP.pdf holdout, served in a 262,144-token window, strict pass (all rubric criteria met) more than doubles after the second round, from 11.0% to 24.5%, with gains across input lengths up to 240K tokens. Mean tokens generated stay flat (9,803 to 9,733), so the gain does not come from longer outputs. GPT-5.6 Sol's leaderboard strict pass is 30.7% at a measured 3,422 tokens. On 220 out-of-domain GDPval tasks, where the model runs as a long-horizon tool-using agent, mean rubric reward rises from 0.571 to 0.746 after the third round and zero-credit tasks fall from 54 to 10, while messages per task fall 18%, from 70.9 to 58.2. In paired trajectories, the third round replaces a context-thrashing retry loop with one up-front check of all sources, and verification extends from checking that files exist to checking what they contain. We argue that long-context evaluation of agents should report accuracy jointly with tokens and turns, and that datasets of long documents should ship text and image renderings alongside each PDF.
authors: Sushant Mehta, Logan Ritchie, Edwin Chen
bullets: Evaluates professional-document tasks involving very long sources, visual evidence, and multi-hop reasoning across ten enterprise domains.
Post-trains Kimi-K2.7 using rank-32 adapters, one self-distillation round, and two rubric-reward RL rounds over 1,465 expert-authored tasks.
On a 100-task GDP.pdf holdout, strict pass rises from 11.0% to 24.5%, with gains up to 240K-token inputs while generated tokens remain nearly unchanged.
On 220 out-of-domain GDPval tasks, mean rubric reward increases from 0.571 to 0.746, zero-credit tasks decrease from 54 to 10, and messages per task fall 18%.
Argues that long-context agent evaluation should jointly report accuracy, tokens, and turns, and that document datasets should include both text and image renderings.

papers.selection_reason: Post-training agents for long-document reasoning, directly relevant to long-context and LLM post-training.
papers.title: Post-Training Agents for Long-Document Reasoning
papers.tldr: Post-training with privileged-context self-distillation and rubric-based reinforcement learning substantially improves long-document reasoning and tool-use efficiency without requiring longer answers.

papers.abstract: Top-k sparse attention relies on an indexer, a lightweight per-layer module that ranks cached tokens so attention covers only the k highest-scoring ones. Indexers are usually distilled from dense attention at the full serving length, so every training step pays for long-context dense attention. We show that when an indexer is distilled on short sequences, its failure to generalise to longer contexts is driven mainly by rotary positional encoding (RoPE), not by degraded content matching. We propose position-skipped distillation: the indexer and the frozen teacher see short sequences whose position IDs contain a randomly placed gap, so neither ever processes more than the short training length. On DeepSeek-V2-Lite and Qwen3-30B-A3B, an indexer distilled on 8K tokens this way matches a 32K-distilled indexer to within about 0.5 perplexity up to 32K, and on DeepSeek-V2-Lite matches a 64K-distilled indexer at 64K with roughly 6x less training compute per token. On Llama-3.1-8B it trails the stronger 32K run by 0.6 perplexity, and at 64K simple position compression is often as good, so the main gain is training cost rather than quality. We also quantise indexer keys to 3-4 bits without retraining and score them with a fused integer kernel: at 4 bits, perplexity changes by at most 0.05 and the scan is 1.6-2.2x faster than half precision. In a current serving engine, the indexer speeds up decoding only for long contexts with multiple concurrent streams.
authors: Fu Dai, Haodi Quan, Kamal Taha
bullets: Short-sequence failures are mainly attributed to rotary positional encoding rather than content matching.
Random gaps in position IDs let the indexer and frozen teacher learn long-range positions without processing long sequences.
An 8K-distilled indexer nearly matches 32K- and, on one model, 64K-distilled quality; the reported training-cost reduction is about 6× per token.
3–4-bit key quantization requires no retraining; 4-bit keys change perplexity by at most 0.05 and yield 1.6–2.2× faster scans.
Benefits vary by model and serving setting: position compression can be competitive, and decoding speedups appear mainly for long contexts with multiple streams.

(2) The frozen model computes dense attention under the same ids, and each layer’s indexer matches its head-summed attention pt,s with a KL loss; only the indexer receives gradients. papers.selection_reason: Improves sparse-attention indexer distillation for long-context serving with position-skipped training and quantization, relevant to efficient long-context LLMs.
papers.title: Position-Skipped Distillation of Sparse-Attention Indexers: Train Short, Serve Long
papers.tldr: Position-skipped distillation trains sparse-attention indexers on short sequences that generalize to long contexts, substantially reducing training cost while preserving quality in several models.

papers.abstract: Modern language models (LMs) are post-trained and deployed as agents inside a "harness", but standard harness designs accumulate context that the neural network is forced to generalize to, making training for long-horizon tasks expensive and time-consuming. We study an alternative emerging path: training inherently neurosymbolic LM harnesses, which externalize and manage context programmatically to compose existing LM capabilities. We hypothesize that training around these harnesses can offer a better return on compute by enabling compositional generalization, as they can learn to decompose complex problems so that every observation their neural LM receives is locally in-distribution, even when the full task is novel. We find that harnesses like the Recursive Language Model (RLM) learn such decompositions readily under reinforcement learning post-training: (1) we demonstrate that training only on short tasks can generalize to tasks 2-64$\times$ longer while the base neural LM improves less, and (2) training on one domain transfers to novel domains that share latent structure. On messier, complex tasks, we find that we can target individual LLM calls within a harness by generating and training on easier, synthetically generated surrogate environments with fake tool / sub-calls, a technique we call surrogate harness training. From this finding, we train RLM-27B on synthetic data, and show it improves Qwen3.8-27B in the same RLM harness on a hard suite of long-context tasks like CTC-Bench and ExpertLongBench by 26.9% on average while using $\sim$2$\times$ fewer tokens at inference time. Finally, we show that harnesses can compose over these newly learned decompositions using recursive sub-harness calls.
authors: Alex L. Zhang, Souradip Chakraborty, Omar Khattab
bullets: Standard harnesses accumulate context, making long-horizon training costly because the LM must generalize over increasingly complex inputs.
Recursive Language Model (RLM) harnesses trained on short tasks generalize to tasks 2–64× longer, while the base LM improves less.
Decompositions learned in one domain transfer to novel domains with shared latent structure.
Surrogate harness training uses easier synthetic environments to target individual LM calls within complex harnesses.
RLM-27B trained on synthetic data improves Qwen3.8-27B by 26.9% on average on CTC-Bench and ExpertLongBench while using about 2× fewer inference tokens.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Harnesses like Recursive Language Models (RLM) can enable compositional generalization on unseen tasks by shaping prompts for each individual language model call to be indistribution, a property we call locally-in-distribution (LID). “Trajectory-as-a-prompt” harnesses like ReAct rely on a root language model to generalize its policy to a growing trajectory as incontext prompts, frequently leading to erroneous behavior on out-of-distribution (OOD) prompts.

Figure 3: On six environments with controlled context lengths, we train several harnesses and the base Transformer on short tasks, and evaluate on longer variants. We plot their train reward (smoothing window=3) and evaluation reward (smoothing window=11) over training, and include a frontier model, GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI, 2026b), using the RLM as a reference. The evaluation reward of the RLM closely follows the trend of the training reward, while for the base Transformer it does not.

Figure 4: We choose three environments with splits that are completely disjoint in domain (e.g. math vs. essay writing questions), but share a similar decomposition structure (e.g. ranking). We train several harnesses and the base Transformer (Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507) on one domain, and evaluate on the other, where the RLM generalizes the strongest among other harness abstractions and the base model.

Figure 5: For several harnesses, we train on short tasks and evaluate on their long-context variants. For each setting, we track the nearest three training trajectories by Weighted Jaccard Similarity to each long evaluation trajectory, and average their rewards. We find that context-offloading harnesses learn root-level trajectories that are re-used in longer tasks compared to “trajectory-as-a-prompt”, but training performance does not necessarily transfer for all harnesses, like Pi on OOLONG.

Figure 6: Harnesses that decompose tasks to be locally in-distribution (LID) are composed of individual LLM trajectories. (a) On the left, we describe surrogate harness training, a strategy for training on synthetic environments to target individual LLM behavior within a harness, using a surrogate synthetic environment that transfers behavior to the real environment when tools and sub-calls are real. (b) On the right, we describe how learned decomposition strategies invoked by the harness can be composed to be LID, by enabling the harness to invoke sub-harness calls recursively.

Figure 7: We reproduced Figure 3 but swapped out the RLM implementation with a version that does not use the orchestration hint. The model roughly follows the same trends, except on MRCRv2, where it learns a non-generalizable solution that has context window issues.

Figure 2: Several popular harness abstractions are useful for controlling what individual LM calls observe. (a) Context offloading keeps the full context in the environment and only allows the model to see slices. (b) Programmatic tool calling treats tools (e.g. sub-agents) as functions in code, which can manipulate intermediate state without the model needing to see it. (c) Sub-agent calling allows the model to explicitly fan out to other LMs, each with their own fresh context. These abstractions can be composed, yielding stronger task generalization effects.

Figure 11: Cross-task harness trajectory similarity. For each evaluation environment in the length generalization experiments in Figure 3, we also check how similar RLM trajectories on evaluation tasks are to unrelated tasks. We look at cross-task trajectory similarity: we plot the mean maximum similarity of trajectories in each long evaluation setting, to its closest training trajectory in each training environment, even those unrelated to the target evaluation task. Across all tasks, there is a higher similarity for harness trajectories transferring from a shorter variant to the longer variant of the same environment versus shorter variants of different tasks.

Figure 10: For each evaluation environment in the length and strategy generalization experiments in Figures 3, 4, we plot the mean maximum similarity to a successful training trajectory under each metric. Higher values indicate higher similarity.

Figure 9: We evaluate 2000 meta-tasks, each sampling (without replacement) four tasks that must be solved in order. Left: The selected tasks are drawn from a pool of tasks that the RLM-27B was trained to solve, whose root LM learned in post-training how to decompose the task over existing tools and sub-calls. Right: a chain is any four pool tasks in any order. Only the first task is visible, and must be solved. The unlock tool reveals the next task after a correct answer and handoff starts a fresh RLM call on it, so solving a chain composes the learned compositions by recursion.

Figure 8: We report the average training reward in gray and the held-out reward (red) for Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 on the broader training mixture in Table 9. The dotted line is the checkpoint selected for evaluation.

papers.selection_reason: Shows neurosymbolic LM harnesses improve compositional generalization and long-context task performance with fewer inference tokens.
papers.title: Language Model Harnesses can be Compositional Generalizers
papers.tldr: Programmatically managed LM harnesses can learn reusable task decompositions, enabling stronger compositional generalization to longer and new-domain tasks with fewer inference tokens.

papers.abstract: Deploying large language models (LLMs) in long-horizon and continual interactions requires maintaining reusable memory states for future inference, posing challenges for existing architectures. Standard Transformers accumulate layer-wise, token-level KV caches, incurring linear GPU memory growth and quadratic computational complexity as the context expands. In contrast, linear-time architectures compress history into fixed-size states, but struggle to retain fine-grained details. We introduce MemOnce, a foundation architecture that learns scalable memory states for language models. MemOnce is based on two core designs: (a) Memory encoder-decoder: it caches only a small subset of final-layer hidden states as compact memory representations and dynamically decodes them back into KV caches for attention layers; (b) Memory sparse attention: for each continual input, MemOnce adaptively retrieves relevant memory representations, with the sparse indices computed only once across layers. Coupling these two designs enables efficient on-the-fly memory loading and KV cache decoding, drastically reducing the GPU memory footprint and achieving linear-time complexity. We conduct extensive experiments to show that MemOnce outperforms Transformers and other architectures across varying model sizes, context lengths, and training paradigms (pretraining and post-training adaptation). In particular, adapting Qwen3.5-4B with MemOnce reduces memory state cache by 1313$\times$ and prefill latency by 6.9$\times$ at 1M context, and improves throughput by 3.5$\times$ and overall memory performance by +5.77%. Finally, MemOnce generalizes zero-shot to downstream representation tasks, achieving competitive results against specialized models.
authors: Chang Nie, Chaoyou Fu, Songlin Liu, Yiqing Hu, Caifeng Shan
bullets: Addresses the linear GPU-memory growth and quadratic computation of Transformer KV caches, while preserving more detail than fixed-size state compression.
Uses a memory encoder-decoder to store selected final-layer hidden states and dynamically reconstruct attention KV caches.
Applies sparse attention that retrieves relevant memories once per input and shares the sparse indices across layers.
Reports substantial efficiency gains, including 1313× lower memory-state cache, 6.9× lower prefill latency, and 3.5× higher throughput at 1M context in one adaptation setting.
Generalizes zero-shot to downstream representation tasks with competitive performance against specialized models.

figures.caption: Figure 2 Overview of theMemOnce architecture. (Left) The Hybrid Backbone stacks linear blocks with memory sparse attention across L stages. (Right) The Memory Encoder-Decoder caches a trailing subset (1/r) of final-layer states into a persistent memory bank, partitioned into a local short-term window and a sparse long-term pool. For each incoming input, relevant memory states are retrieved only once and dynamically decoded into KV caches for attention layers. This enables a constant active memory state for continual inference, alongside an Lr× cache compression across both depth and time dimensions.

Figure 3 Training and scaling curves of MemOnce as a foundation architecture. (Left) Validation perplexity vs. training tokens under different compression ratios. Even at r = 8, MemOnce remains competitive with the Transformer and strong baselines. (Right) Validation perplexity vs. model scale (0.15B to 1.0B), where MemOnce delivers the best scaling performance.

Figure 1 Comparison between MemOnce and advanced architectures. (Left) Memory state cache vs. context length. MemOnce activates minimal memory states during continual inference, reducing the cache footprint by orders of magnitude compared to attention-based baselines. (Right) Overall performance vs. prefill latency and decoding throughput. Compared to existing native memory models, MemOnce significantly advances the Pareto frontier, marking the first native memory approach to surpass the full-context baseline. Performance is averaged across five memory benchmarks, while prefill time and throughput are measured at a 1M context length.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces scalable memory architecture for LLMs with KV-cache reduction and long-context efficiency.
papers.title: MemOnce: A Scalable Memory Architecture for Large Language Models
papers.tldr: MemOnce enables LLMs to retain long-term, fine-grained memories with compact states, reducing memory and computation costs for long-context continual inference.

papers.abstract: Long-context models use sparse or structured attention to avoid quadratic cost, yet retrieving a small set of relevant facts embedded among hundreds of thousands of distractors degrades as normalization mass disperses with length. Hub-and-spoke optimal transport (OT) replaces the dense $L \times L$ matrix with a linear-size graph over local windows and $K$ shared hubs balanced by Sinkhorn scaling. Building on block-wise tail refinement and fixed-support transport topology (arXiv:2605.08123, arXiv:2609.07954), we introduce Topology Hub Optimal Transport (THOT): (1) bounded-support capacity gating via simplex sparsemax ($O(L\log L)$) or sorting-free token-local thresholded ReLU ($O(L)$), driving excess distractor mass to zero; (2) a three-sweep $1+2$ annealed row-closed Sinkhorn schedule that damps bipartite residuals; (3) an exact rank-$(D+2R+1)$ One-Reference-Tile adjoint in batched split-factor Triton kernels (BF16 Tensor Cores, FP32 potentials); and (4) a chunked exclusive-prefix causal variant with verified zero future leakage. On NVIDIA L4, sparsemax THOT trained at $L=128$ reaches 97.40% zero-shot recall of fixed bindings at $L=262{,}144$ under pure task loss ($\alpha=0$) and 98.83% at $\alpha=0.05$ (matched by $O(L)$ thresholded ReLU at $\alpha=0.05$, vs. 80.60% at $\alpha=0$), while softmax-gated hub OT drops to 3.52%. In bidirectional operator microbenchmarks, our kernel runs forward+VJP in 100.1 ms at $H=8, D=64, L=262\mathrm{K}$ (2.2x faster with 4.0x smaller compiler temporaries than latent softmax) and 1.34 ms vs. 4.37 ms for cuDNN FlashAttention at $L=4{,}096$; multi-layer LM runs use the unfused path. Zero-shot WikiText-103 multi-needle retrieval hits 100.00% (128/128 queries at $L=65\mathrm{K}$) vs. 0.78% for short-trained RoPE FlashAttention, and compact 4-layer WikiText-4K runs show modest causal and masked LM gains.
bullets: Addresses long-context retrieval degradation caused by attention normalization mass spreading across distractors.
Builds a linear-size local-window-plus-hub transport graph with sparsemax or thresholded-ReLU gating to eliminate excess distractor mass.
Adds annealed Sinkhorn updates, an exact low-rank adjoint, fused Triton kernels, and a causal chunked variant with zero future leakage.
At 262K tokens, sparsemax THOT achieves 97.40% or 98.83% fixed-binding recall depending on loss regularization, while softmax-gated hub OT reaches 3.52%.
Reports 100% multi-needle retrieval on 65K-token WikiText-103 queries and faster operator benchmarks than the compared baselines; broader multi-layer LM runs use an unfused path.

(a) Under verified 0.0 future leakage (annealed gate warmup over steps 1–256), Causal THOT sustains 90.10% zero-shot recall at L = 262K (0.00% excess filler share), outperforming Causal Latent Softmax (81.77%) and Causal Hub OT (Softmax Gate) (32.81%). (b) On compact 4-layer Causal Next-Token LM (512 steps) and Deep 4-Layer MLM (640 steps) over WikiText-103 4K documents, THOT achieves the lowest held-out NLL, with modest margins (0.015–0.016 nats) over the strongest nearby structured baselines.

(a) On synthetic associative recall (R = 8 fixed bindings, trained at L = 128), softmax-gated Hub OT (Hub OT (Softmax Gate), dashed crimson) collapses from 98.31% to 3.52% at L = 262K as distractors absorb 93.4% of excess source capacity. Sparsemax gating with our 1+2 annealed row-closed schedule (THOT) holds 98.83% with light gate supervision (α = 0.05) and 97.40% under pure cross-entropy training (α = 0). (b) On zero-shot multi-needle retrieval embedded in WikiText-103 prose (pure cross-entropy, trained at L = 512), the short-trained RoPE FlashAttention baseline drops from 99.22% to 0.78% beyond its training window, while sparsemax THOT reaches 100.00% (128/128 queries, 0.0514 NLL) at L = 65,536.

Figure 2: Bidirectional GPU operator latency and static XLA compiler temporary memory on NVIDIA L4. (a) At multi-head transformer geometry (H = 8, D = 64, L = 262,144), our batched split-factor BF16 Tensor-Core kernel completes forward+VJP in 100.1ms (1,132MiB static compiler temp), outperforming Unfused Hub OT by 4.8×, Latent Softmax by 2.2× (4.0× smaller compiler temporaries than Latent Softmax), and dense cuDNN FlashAttention by 92×. (b) On a bidirectional WikiText-4K layer geometry (B = 2, L = 4,096, H = 8, D = 32, r = 32), THOT (BF16 TC) runs forward+VJP 3.3× faster than cuDNN FlashAttention (1.34ms vs. 4.37ms).

papers.selection_reason: Introduces hub optimal transport with sparse gating for long-context attention, directly targeting long-context models and efficient attention.
papers.title: Topology Hub Optimal Transport: Eliminating Long Context Dilution at Flash Speed
papers.tldr: THOT uses sparse capacity-gated hub optimal transport and optimized kernels to preserve relevant facts in extremely long contexts while reducing attention overhead.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-based sparse attention, exemplified by DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA), reduces attention computation by selecting a small subset of key-value entries. However, selecting these entries can still require searching the entire visible history. For long sequences, retrieval becomes a major bottleneck, limiting the efficiency gains from sparse attention. To address this problem, we propose LongCat Recall Sparse Attention (LRSA), which combines fine-grained representatives with paged retrieval in an incrementally maintained index. LRSA partitions the sequence into time buckets that can be indexed independently as new keys arrive, without regrouping existing history. Within each bucket, it organizes indexing keys into capacity-balanced directional groups and packs a fixed number of complete groups into each page, retaining a separate center for every group. These centers provide fine-grained representatives for page selection, after which refinement scores members of the selected pages together with sink, sliding-window, and visible unindexed candidates to select the final Top-$K$ logical positions. To execute this retrieval process efficiently, we store members in reordered pages, fuse construction stages according to group size, and share storage for overlapping fixed candidates across queries during chunked prefill. These choices support regular member access while reducing kernel launches during construction and repeated candidate transfers. Moreover, we integrate LRSA into SGLang to maintain the index during inference, overlapping asynchronous index construction for new buckets with subsequent computation and reusing compatible bucket indices and member pages after a prefix match in the original key-value pool. With a 1024K-token context, LRSA accelerates key selection by 4.70$\times$ over DSA and combined selection and attention by 35.60$\times$ over full attention.
authors: Hao Zhang, Bin Xiao, Kefeng Zhang
bullets: Problem: Sparse attention can reduce computation, but searching the entire visible history makes key retrieval a bottleneck for very long contexts.

Method: Partition history into independently indexed time buckets, organize keys into balanced directional groups, and use group centers for coarse page selection before refining candidates to select Top-K positions.
Implementation: Reordered pages, fused index-construction stages, shared fixed-candidate storage, and asynchronous index maintenance improve retrieval and inference efficiency.
Result: At 1024K-token context, LRSA accelerates key selection 4.70× over DSA and combined selection plus attention 35.60× over full attention.
Scope: The reported gains target long-context inference with incrementally arriving keys and prefix reuse.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of LRSA. (a) Each completed bucket is independently partitioned into capacity-balanced directional groups, which are packed into member pages. With the default capacities, the expanded page contains eight groups of eight keys, with one center per group. (b) Queries score group centers and select the Top-Kpage pages using the maximum group score within each page. Retrieved members are combined with sink, sliding-window, and visible unindexed candidates, deduplicated, and scored to select the final Top-K positions for attention. The position map supports deduplication and recovery of original logical positions. Reordered page and slot addresses are depicted as one-dimensional indices for simplicity.

Figure 5: Ablation of directional grouping using temporal grouping as the control. The left and right columns report all-position and historical AMR, respectively. Panels (a, b) compare the two methods at matched reference page budgets, with colors distinguishing the methods. Panels (c, d) show the trade-off between AMR and selection latency as the page budget varies; colors denote context lengths, and each point corresponds to one page-budget setting. In all panels, solid lines with circles indicate directional grouping, and dashed lines with squares indicate temporal grouping.

Figure 3: Efficiency of key selection and attention across context lengths. (a) Key-selection speedup of LRSA over DSA. (b) Speedups of DSA and LRSA over full attention; both sparse methods include key selection and attention computation. Labels above LRSA bars give its speedup over the reference in each panel. Dashed lines mark equal execution time (1×).

Figure 6: Overlap between index maintenance and model execution. Colors and marker shapes identify five bucket capacities. (a) Model-only execution window. (b) Isolated index-construction time. (c) Execution-time difference relative to the model-only baseline. In (c), dashed lines with open markers indicate serial maintenance, while solid lines with filled markers indicate overlap. All points show median measurements. The vertical axis is logarithmic in (a) and linear in (b, c).

Figure 4: Ablations of index organization across five context lengths. The top row reports all-position AMR and the bottom row historical AMR. Panels (a, d) vary bucket capacity, and panels (b, e) vary group capacity. In these panels, colors denote context lengths and vertical dashed lines mark the default capacities. Panels (c, f) compare the default with two variants: one mean center per page and mean aggregation of group scores. Each variant changes only the corresponding design choice. Page capacity and selection budgets are held fixed within each comparison. Points report mean AMR.

Figure 2: Latency of recursive partitioning and fixed-candidate copying. (a) Partitioning latency for three fusion schedules as group size varies, with the total number of members per round held fixed. (b) Candidate-copying latency as chunk size varies, comparing per-query copies with a shared copy. Labels in (b) show the speedup from sharing. Panel (a) uses a logarithmic latency axis; panel (b) uses a linear axis starting at zero.

Table 2: End-to-end speedup of LRSA over DSA across context lengths and final selection budgets.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces LongCat Recall Sparse Attention (LRSA) to improve retrieval efficiency for long-context LLM inference.
papers.title: LongCat Recall Sparse Attention: Co-Designing Key Organization and Retrieval for Long-Context Inference
papers.tldr: LRSA makes long-context sparse attention substantially faster by co-designing an incrementally maintained, paged retrieval index with efficient GPU execution.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive Transformers generally fail on out-of-distribution reasoning due to two primary reasons: positional corruption over long sequences and structural state drift across deep execution steps. We introduce ORION, a framework that supervises exact canonical execution states via auxiliary heads to anchor latent trajectories to valid computational manifolds. Across Folding, GridShift, and CLRS-30, a pre-registered 2 x 2 factorial shows that RoPE and ORION address orthogonal axes. RoPE recovers length extrapolation (59.8%), while ORION recovers depth extrapolation (66.7%). Moreover, their combination complementarily achieves strict additive gain in joint length-depth extrapolation, while either method alone offers near satisfactory results. Negative controls confirm that the gain depends strictly on exact canonical alignment; hashed state statistics fail to constrain depth extrapolation.
bullets: Targets two failure modes: positional corruption over long sequences and structural state drift across deep reasoning steps.
Uses auxiliary heads to supervise exact canonical execution states and keep latent trajectories on valid computational manifolds.
Across Folding, GridShift, and CLRS-30, RoPE primarily recovers length extrapolation (59.8%), while ORION recovers depth extrapolation (66.7%).
Combining RoPE and ORION yields complementary additive gains on joint length-depth extrapolation.
Negative controls show that exact canonical alignment is necessary; hashed state statistics do not constrain depth extrapolation.

figures.caption: Figure 7: The ORION architecture on both domains. An exact simulator emits the canonical state Φ(S) = (µ, ν, ω, T, ans) at every execution step; five read-out heads decode it from one shared latent, and their losses are added to the language-modelling objective. The answer head is one probe among several rather than the privileged output. The identical wiring runs on FOLDING and GRIDSHIFT, which is what lets the contrastive term act across domains.

Figure 3: Canonical-state pretraining transfers across domains. Exact match during adaptation to the other domain under an equal 800-step budget, using five seeds. Models are initialized from scratch, from a Transformer pretrained on the source domain, or from an ORION model pretrained on the source domain. The ORION initialization improves target-domain held-out performance over Transformer pretraining by +0.085 ± 0.041 for FOLDING→GRIDSHIFT and +0.035 ± 0.013 for GRIDSHIFT→FOLDING. The improvement is positive in every seed in both directions.

Figure 2: ORION composes with RoPE on depth extrapolation. (a,b) Exact match at execution depths 5–8, after training at depths 1–4, for RoPE alone and ORION + RoPE on FOLDING and GRIDSHIFT. Bands show ± one standard deviation over three seeds. Printed values give the pairedby-example difference at each depth; stars indicate p < 0.05. Across all held-out depths, ORION + RoPE improves over RoPE by +0.016 on FOLDING (p = 0.036) and +0.024 on GRIDSHIFT (p = 0.002). (c) The corresponding difference across model widths in the five-seed scaling ladder. The gains are +0.000, +0.004, and +0.082 at 3.5M, 11M, and 26M parameters, respectively; the largest model favors the combined condition in all five seeds.

Figure 1: ORION + RoPE keeps computing the canonical state beyond the training depth. Exact accuracy of the canonical-state read-outs by execution depth (seed 0; shaded region: training depths). (a, b) The answer set read directly from the latent at the decision position, without autoregressive decoding, on FOLDING and GRIDSHIFT. (c) The occupancy map on FOLDING. With absolute positions the read-outs collapse at the first unseen depth (0.04, 0.19, 0.06); with RoPE they remain at 0.63, 0.67 and 0.85 at depth 5 and decay gradually, so the state is still being tracked where it was never supervised.

Figure 4: Canonical supervision confines the latent trajectory. The final-layer hidden state at each executed operation is one point per step, projected on the two leading principal components of the in-distribution states and expressed in units of their spread. Arrows: mean step-to-step displacement of 800 paths through each cell; bold path: mean position from step 1 (square) to step 8. The baseline moves 1.18 spreads per step with no coherent direction; ORION + RoPE moves 0.44 along a coherent field. The effect comes from the supervision, not the positional encoding (0.45 for ORION without RoPE, 1.36 for RoPE alone).

Figure 9: Layer-to-layer linear CKA within each model on FOLDING (seed 0, 384 in-distribution prompts). Both models show the same smooth block structure, with adjacent layers above 0.97 and the embedding layer the most distinct. Canonical supervision does not reorganise the layer hierarchy. Note the colour scale starts at 0.90; on an absolute scale the two panels are nearly identical, which is the point.

Figure 5: An execution trace in the FOLDING domain. Each operation reflects part of the sheet onto the rest and concatenates the stacks, so layer count grows with depth while the footprint shrinks. The canonical state Φ(St) is the stack-valued geometry at each step; the query is a punch through the final stack, scored by exact set match over the original cells it perforates.

Figure 6: An execution trace in the GRIDSHIFT domain. Cyclic row and column shifts permute origin labels over a grid whose extent never changes, so unlike FOLDING the state size is independent of program length. The canonical state is the origin-per-cell permutation and the query asks which positions hold marked origins after execution.

Figure 10: Degradation on FOLDING, from the reduced-budget surface sweep. (a) Exact match against execution depth at the training state sizes; the shaded band is the trained range and the printed values are the endpoints at 2×. The rotary conditions degrade gradually while the two absolute-position conditions fall off a cliff at the first unseen depth. (b) The joint surface for ORION + RoPE over both axes, every cell labelled with exact match; red lines mark the edges of the training region and n/a marks a combination the generator cannot produce. Reading up the left columns shows depth costing accuracy gradually; reading across to the right column shows the size axis costing all of it at once, at every depth. The size axis is not drawn as a separate curve because all four conditions coincide on it (0.195, 0.190, 0.169 and 0.170 at S/Strain = 1.33).

Figure 11: Per-algorithm exact match on the CLRS pilot (single seed). (a) In-distribution (n = 16). (b) The preregistered out-of-distribution endpoint, the mean of the length and structural axes. Only kmp matcher separates the conditions; activity selector and graham scan are at zero for every condition.

Table 2: Out-of-distribution exact-match (EM) accuracy across algorithmic benchmarks. FOLDING and GRIDSHIFT models are trained on state size Strain ≤ 6 and execution depth Dtrain ≤ 4; the joint split tests S = 8 at depth 5–8. In-domain, size-only, and depth-only results are averaged over three random seeds and reported as mean ± standard deviation. The joint split uses seed-0 checkpoints and reports the half-width of a 95% bootstrap interval over 1,000 test instances. CLRS is a single-seed pilot over eight algorithms. ↑ indicates higher is better.

Table 3: Ablation against negative controls on FOLDING and GRIDSHIFT under joint OOD extrapolation (S = 8, 2×D). Results use seed-0 checkpoints; ± denotes the half-width of a 95% bootstrap interval over 1,000 test instances. The controls retain the auxiliary-head architecture while changing the supervision target.
Table 1: Structural properties and evaluation parameters for the algorithmic reasoning task splits.

Table 11: Hyperparameter settings across model configurations. The scaling ladder of Table 13 varies dmodel ∈ {256, 384, 512} at a reduced step budget with five seeds; all other experiments use the configuration below.

Table 7: Alternative sequence backbones at a matched training budget (6,000 steps, 3 seeds, mean ± s.d.). The recurrent and long-convolution models were run because they carry sequence priors of their own and are therefore confounds for any claim about positional structure. The state-space model does not fit the training distribution in either domain and Hyena fits only FOLDING; RWKV fits both and is the strongest non-rotary backbone on the depth axis (0.099 and 0.175), but none of the three comes near what rotary embeddings reach (0.651 and 0.575).

Table 4: Sensitivity to the availability of canonical supervision on FOLDING using an exploratory seed. The auxiliary loss weight (λ) was fixed at its preregistered value. The experiment varies the fraction of supervised execution steps and the fraction of corrupted labels.

Table 9: Representation geometry of the final layer on FOLDING (seed 0, n = 600 in-distribution prompts). The preregistered hypothesis was that canonical supervision compresses the execution subspace. It does not: the participation ratio, the spectral entropy and the number of dimensions needed for 90–95% of the variance all rise under supervision. The TwoNN estimator is the one measure that moves the other way, so we report the evidence as mixed in direction but uniform in conclusion — no measure supports compression. Layer-wise linear CKA between the supervised and unsupervised models stays high throughout, so the supervised representation is a nearby one rather than a different one.

Table 10: Error taxonomy on FOLDING (seed 0): counts of each failure mode among incorrect predictions. Beyond the training depth the model almost never emits a malformed or reflected answer: the failures are well-formed answer sets that miss cells or are disjoint from the truth, which is the signature of a state that has drifted rather than of a decoder that has broken.

Table 8: Robustness to input corruption on FOLDING (seed 0, in-distribution test set). Token noise replaces a fraction p of program tokens at random. Dropped operation removes one operation from the program and scores against the answer for the shortened program. Canonical supervision leaves both curves essentially unchanged, so the robustness it confers is not visible at the level of the decoded answer.

Table 5: Scaling laws for RoPE versus ORION + RoPE on depth extrapolation in FOLDING. Values are EM percentages, reported as mean ± standard deviation over five seeds. The ladder uses a reduced training budget; therefore, its absolute values are lower than those in Table 2.

Table 13: RoPE versus ORION + RoPE on depth extrapolation in FOLDING across model width. Values are EM percentages, mean ± standard deviation over five seeds. The ladder uses a reduced training budget, so its absolute values are lower than those in Table 2.

Table 6: Three further preregistered evaluation axes on the seed set of Table 2 (mean ± s.d. over 3 seeds, exact match). Held-out operation type withholds diagonal folds (FOLDING) and the transpose (GRIDSHIFT) from training. Held-out query type withholds the multi-cell punch. Equivalent programs scores agreement on pairs of syntactically different programs that Theorem 3 certifies to have the same answer; it is an in-distribution consistency check, not an extrapolation split.

Table 12: OOD exact match on the depth-extrapolation split (2×D at the training state size) across negative controls, mean ± s.d. over 3 seeds. CLRS controls were not trained. The controls lie within the seed spread of the APE baseline and of ORION with APE (0.026 on FOLDING, 0.063 on GRIDSHIFT); the separation in this table is between the rotary column and everything else.

Table 14: Positional-bias interoperability across the size and depth axes on FOLDING. Values are EM percentages. ALiBi and other relative-bias schemes were not trained in this study and are therefore not listed; we make no claim about their interaction with ORION.

papers.selection_reason: Improves transformer length/depth extrapolation via canonical-state supervision and RoPE, relevant to LLM architecture and long-context research.
papers.title: ORION: Exact Canonical-State Supervision for Systematic Generalization in Transformers
papers.tldr: ORION improves Transformers’ systematic generalization by supervising exact canonical execution states, addressing depth-related state drift alongside RoPE’s handling of long-sequence positional corruption.

papers.abstract: Training-free activation guardrails such as kNNGuard score prompts by comparing last-token LLM hidden states (the Layer Ensemble branch, kNNGuard LE) and sentence embeddings (all-MiniLM-L6-v2, Embedding-kNN) against a small reference bank (50 examples per class), combining the two branches into a Fused Ensemble (kNNGuard FE). While effective on short inputs (up to 256 tokens), standard kNNGuard degrades substantially on long inputs (over 1000 tokens): averaged across Qwen3.5-4B and Gemma-4-E4B-it, kNNGuard LE AUROC drops from 0.742 (0.777 and 0.706) to 0.554 (0.587 and 0.521) on Content Harm Moderation (Aegis-2.0), and from 0.994 (0.995 and 0.992) to 0.556 (0.598 and 0.513) on RAG Hallucination Detection (HaluBench). We trace this degradation to three causes: (1) hidden-state drift as sequence length increases, (2) hard 256-token truncation in MiniLM, and (3) signal dilution when a long document is compressed into a single final-token vector. We then evaluate three training-free adaptations: a Length-Routed Dual Bank, a long-context embedding model (Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B), and Strided Window Pooling across intermediate token positions. On Content Harm Moderation, dual-bank routing and strided window pooling raise long-context kNNGuard LE AUROC from 0.554 to 0.828 (+0.274 AUROC) and fused kNNGuard FE AUROC from 0.721 to 0.886 (+0.164 AUROC) with no latency overhead from bank routing. On RAG Hallucination Detection, where the guardrail must verify logical consistency between a generated answer and a retrieved passage, sentence-embedding kNN remains near random chance across all lengths, while length-matched LLM hidden states (kNNGuard LE) recover medium-length detection (AUROC = 0.853) but remain limited on over-1000-token passages (AUROC = 0.607) due to final-token dilution over long contexts.
bullets: Long-context degradation stems from hidden-state drift, MiniLM’s 256-token truncation, and final-token signal dilution.
Length-routed dual banks and strided window pooling improve long-context Content Harm Moderation LE AUROC from 0.554 to 0.828 and fused FE AUROC from 0.721 to 0.886.
Bank routing adds no latency overhead, while a long-context embedding model is evaluated as another training-free adaptation.
Sentence-embedding kNN stays near random for RAG hallucination detection; length-matched hidden states recover medium-length performance but remain weak beyond 1,000 tokens.
The study evaluates training-free adaptations using small reference banks across Qwen3.5-4B and Gemma-4-E4B-it.

Figure 2: Long-context (> 1000 tokens) AUROC and 95% bootstrap confidence intervals (averaged across Qwen3.5-4B and Gemma-4-E4B-it) of kNNGuard LE (LLM hidden states) and kNNGuard FE (fused ensemble) across training-free adaptations on Content Safety (Aegis-2.0) and RAG Hallucination (HaluBench).
Table 2: Progressive ablation study on Long (> 1000-token) inputs averaged across Qwen3.5-4B and Gemma-4-E4B-it.
Table 1: Length-segmented AUROC of standard kNNGuard LE and kNNGuard FE (built from short ≤ 256-token banks B(d) short) across native prompt-length regimes.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses long-context prompt processing and hidden-state drift in LLM guardrails, fitting long-context model research.
papers.title: Auditing and Adapting kNNGuard for Long-Context Prompts
papers.tldr: kNNGuard degrades sharply on long prompts, but length-aware banks and strided pooling substantially restore harmful-content detection while hallucination detection remains difficult at extreme lengths.

papers.abstract: Recent gated linear attention models use state-independent gates, computed from token representations without directly reading the recurrent memory. This design supports efficient chunkwise computation: sequences are divided into chunks of consecutive tokens, with parallel computation within each chunk. However, the same token representation produces the same gate, even when the layer stores different information. We introduce State-Dependent Gating (SDG), which computes element-wise gates from the change in memory over a chunk and applies them at the chunk boundary. This provides state feedback for forgetting while preserving parallel computation within each chunk. We develop fused kernels for Gated DeltaNet, Kimi Delta Attention, Gated DeltaNet-2, and Mamba-3. Our theoretical analysis quantifies the potential reconstruction benefits of state-dependent, element-wise gating under a signal--noise model. We also show that boundary decay is an element-wise ridge proximal step when the gate is held fixed. Empirical evaluation of 1.3B linear attention and hybrid models trained on 100B tokens shows improvements across language modeling, commonsense reasoning, synthetic and real-world retrieval, and long-context understanding. These results demonstrate that SDG is an effective approach to enhancing existing linear attention models.
authors: Renjia Deng, Yuxi Liu, Yutong He, Xue Wang, Kun Yuan
bullets: Existing gated linear attention uses state-independent gates, which ignore the information currently stored in recurrent memory.
SDG computes element-wise gates from the memory change over each chunk and applies them at the chunk boundary.
The approach preserves parallel within-chunk computation and is implemented with fused kernels for several linear-attention architectures.
Theory connects SDG to improved signal reconstruction and interprets fixed-gate boundary decay as an element-wise ridge proximal step.
Experiments on 1.3B models trained on 100B tokens report improvements across language modeling, reasoning, retrieval, and long-context understanding.

papers.selection_reason: State-dependent gating improves linear attention efficiency and long-context modeling, directly relevant to efficient attention and LLM architectures.
papers.title: SDG: State-Dependent Gating at Chunk Boundaries for Linear Attention
papers.tldr: State-Dependent Gating improves chunkwise linear attention by using memory changes to control element-wise forgetting without sacrificing parallel computation within chunks.

papers.abstract: In our experiments on long-horizon customer-behavior forecasting, a longer observation window outweighed the observed effects of more data, more capacity and newer architectures. The window is the weeks of history a model sees before the week it forecasts from. Going from an 8- to a 16-week window adds a raw +0.070 to 0.107 log-space $R^2$ in every family at 1M. Matched test cohorts, which score the same customer-weeks at every window, show this raw comparison understates the gain in every family they cover. The direction holds on five public datasets, four spanning over a year (ridge and our transformer on all five). On our internal data, longer windows admit up to 10% more and colder training customers, which matching does not fix. Our design does not separate window length from calendar coverage, because every test anchor (the week a forecast is made from) falls in one eight-week band. On training-period anchors, the weekly ridge probe's gain persists outside the holiday season, keeping about 72% of it. We therefore report a robust positive association with longer windows and do not identify the magnitude of a calendar-independent history effect. Of four internally registered predictions, the only fully blind one failed. An activity-mixture model predicted +0.014 from 24 to 32 weeks; the weekly-aggregate probe returned -0.0004. For the sequence families, the other three levers are about an order of magnitude smaller, bounded and unresolved. Their observed effects are at most 0.006 between the nominal 1M and 10M tiers and 0.0052 among five sequence families at 16 weeks with clocks as built, both single-seed on the full test split, and 0.006 for capacity on three-seed means. These are observed intervals, not equivalence bounds. Our claim is the order-of-magnitude contrast between the window and those bounds. A team building on this class of data should start by lengthening the window.
bullets: Doubling the observation window from 8 to 16 weeks added 0.070–0.107 raw log-space R² at the 1M tier across model families.
The positive association with longer windows held across five public datasets and persisted outside the holiday season, retaining about 72% of the weekly ridge gain.
Longer windows also admitted up to 10% more and colder training customers on internal data, an effect not removed by cohort matching.
Observed effects of data, architecture, and capacity were much smaller—at most 0.006, 0.0052, and 0.006 respectively—but these are not equivalence bounds.
The study’s blind prediction largely failed, and the design cannot separate history length from calendar coverage.

figures.caption: Figure 2: The input window is the lever, across families. Among the plotted families trained with squared error, only ridge is meaningfully below the others. Scores use the matched cohort at the 1M tier, the customer-weeks present in each of the M8, M12 and M16 test sets (n=407,338). Here they extend the transformer curves to M24 on the four-window matched cohort (M8∩M12∩M16∩M24, n=372,778). The cohort changes at that step, so the dotted connectors to M24 do not trace a within-cohort trajectory. Figure 1: The observation window outweighs the observed effects of population scale and model capacity, our counterparts of the data and parameter axes swept by a compute-calibration scaling study that does not vary the window in training [Brüel Gabrielsson, 2026]. Extending the input window M8→M24 moves R2 by +0.111 (left). On our counterparts of those axes, it moves by 0.0025 across training-population tiers 1M→10M at fixed window M16 (center) and by 0.006 across width and depth at fixed window M16 and fixed data (right), both as 3-seed means. Both are observed intervals rather than resolved equivalence bounds. The scale interval sits within seed dispersion. The capacity interval does not, but it is unresolved against its own 0.016 equivalence margin (§6). The raw M24 endpoint carries the composition caveat of Table 2; the matched-cohort window climb is larger still (+0.131, 3-seed, §2.3), so the raw delta is the conservative estimate. Every ladder shares one setup (Huber objective, log-space R2, full test split). Apart from the factor each ladder varies, the only differences are a 100→500-step warmup at d512 with 8 layers (§2.1) and, on the tier ladder, the realized learning-rate schedule (§6). Window length also shifts calendar coverage (§6) and training eligibility (§4.1). Filled markers: 3-seed means ± population SD; open markers: weaker evidence, here single-seed (seed-42) runs; dashed lines: levels of the shared base configurations. The inset redraws the two M16 ladders on a y span about nine times tighter, column-aligned to the main axis. The M8 capacity replicate sits at its own level and stays on the main axis.

Figure 3: The saturating law’s 24-week prediction hits, and the activity-mixture model’s 32-week prediction misses. Both were registered internally. (a) At k=24 the observed 0.4296 lies 0.005 below the saturating prediction and 0.066 below the log-linear one, so both internally registered levels sit above the outcome. The two forms were fit on the three-window matched ladder before any 24-week evaluation and are scored across a cohort shift (both scorings in §4.5). The curve plots the log-space R2 of the weekly-aggregate ridge probe (closed-form, no training seed) against history length k=1..24 weeks. Every point is scored on the single four-window matched cohort (n=372,778) and comes from the M24 extract alone, so no training-extract mismatch enters the curve. On the test calendar it flattens (+0.00009/week at k=22→24), but a single exponential underfits it, with fit RMSE 0.0103 and an asymptote of 0.423, below the observed 0.4296. A mixture of per-decile saturation rates predicts this underfit inside the window, and panel (b) rejects the mixture’s extrapolation past k=24. Inset: the more active the customers, the sooner the curve bends. The top three deciles, 10, 9 and 8, reach the half-saturation point k1/2 of their saturating fits (circles) at 3.9, 5.2 and 10.0 weeks. In the fits, deciles 6–7 bend beyond the window (k1/2 of 27.1 and 24.7 weeks), and the bottom five are still climbing at the window’s edge. This is a claim about curve shape, not level, and it rests on the fitted parameters in §2.6. Curves show per-decile refit R2(k), k=1..16, from the M16 extract on the same matched cohort, shaded by prior-activity decile. Each (decile, k) pair has one ridge fit, evaluated on that decile’s test rows. All ten deciles are fitted, but only deciles 1, 5, 8, 9 and 10 are drawn, because the lower eight lie within 0.051 of one another at k=16 and their strokes would overlap. (b) The 32-week miss, drawn against the falsification region of the internally registered extension. This panel uses a separate M32 extract, scored on the matched-cohort rows that also fall in the M32 test split (94.2% coverage, n=351,174). Its level differs from panel (a) by −0.033, an offset between extracts in which the M32 training data and the scored rows change together. The internally registered quantity is therefore the gain within this extract, ∆(24→32), anchored at the observed k=24 point. The activity-mixture model predicted ∆=+0.0142 [0.0126, 0.0231], the internally registered band and the only interval that panel (b) draws. Its lower endpoint is the calibrated and its upper endpoint the raw 90% bootstrap bound, so it is not a single 90% interval. The flat-tail null is ≤ +0.001. The observed gain is ∆=−0.0004, with 95% CI [−0.0014,+0.0004] from the paired customer-clustered bootstrap on the same extract and rows. This observed interval reflects row-sampling uncertainty at the three test anchors, not variation across calendar anchors (§2.3). The curve enters the flat-tail null, and the observed interval excludes the entire internally registered range (discriminating threshold 0.007). The mechanism check fails in the same direction. The three lowest deciles show a mean within-decile gain of 0.018, against a predicted 0.045–0.059.

Figure 4: Through 16 weeks, cohort composition makes raw deltas understate the window effect. Full-test-split vs. matched-cohort window deltas in log-space R2 (transformer, Huber, seed 42) at 1M and 10M. At both scales the matched delta exceeds the full-set delta for every window contrast (e.g. ∆(M16−M8) +0.094 matched vs. +0.075 full at 10M). The gap arises because longer windows admit colder, less active customers, which changes both the error and the target variance in R2. Here the net effect is that raw deltas between these windows understate the window gain measured on a fixed population. The matched delta scores both windows on that fixed population, so it is unaffected by shifts in test composition. Bars are point estimates. Within seed 42, customer-clustered paired bootstrap intervals on the matched 10M deltas are tight.

M16-1M configurations, log-space R2 on the full test split (not the matched cohort of Table 2); bars are 3-seed means and dots are individual seeds {42, 123, 456}, including the stacked configuration (0.6060±0.0006). Table 15: The paper’s transformer on three public datasets. On each dataset, read on its own, the transformer gains from 16 weeks of history over 8 too. Gain = out-of-fold R2 with a 16-week history minus with an 8-week one, in log space, over all rows, each scored by the model whose test fold holds it; the mean over 5 seeds. Seed interval: t on the 5 per-seed gains (4 df). Scoring interval: a customer bootstrap with the models held fixed, 999 draws, the same draws for both windows and every seed. The intervals cover seed noise and the noise of scoring these rows, not the choice of folds. Datasets: Online Retail II, a UK online gift retailer with many wholesale buyers, 2009 to 2011; The Complete Journey, a grocer’s 2,500-household panel over about two years, with no calendar dates; CDNOW, one quarter’s new customers of an online music store, with every purchase they made over 18 months. Rows are the ridge probes’: one per customer and anchor with at least one purchase in the 56 days before the anchor, cross-fit by customer over the ridge probes’ five folds. Earlier anchors’ targets overlap later anchors’ inputs in calendar time, so this is not out-of-time validation. Target: spend over the 364 days from the anchor, as log(1 + max(0, ·)). Model: the paper’s d128, 2-layer transformer and loss, with batch and warmup scaled to these sizes and the learning rate left at 5×10−4, untuned (it was set at a batch of 8,192). It sees each line’s quantity, price and spend and its place in the sequence, oldest first, with no date and no item or category; the paper’s recipe reads no calendar or timing feature on the main data either. So the longer window adds older lines, in order, without their dates. On Online Retail II, cancellations enter as lines with negative quantity. On CDNOW every customer joined in the first quarter of 1997, and for 31% of rows the 16-week history reaches back to the first purchase, which to a model with no dates looks like a shorter sequence, as a light buyer’s does. On 3 of the 15 folds the learning-rate schedule was sized for 0.7% to 5.6% more steps per epoch than ran, so it ends at about 1.0% to 1.75% of its peak rather than at 1%, and one fold’s warmup is 76 steps, not 72. papers.selection_reason: Empirically demonstrates that longer observation windows significantly outperform increases in data, capacity, and architecture in customer behavior forecasting, highlighting the importance of long-context modeling.
papers.title: The Window Lever: Longer Observation Windows Outweigh the Observed Effects of Data, Capacity, and Architecture in Customer Behavior Forecasting
papers.tldr: For long-horizon customer-behavior forecasting, extending the history window appears far more influential than adding data, model capacity, or newer architectures, though calendar coverage prevents isolating the window’s causal effect.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly need to process long documents and codebases, making long-context attention a major prefill bottleneck. Block sparse attention reduces computation by skipping unimportant blocks of the attention matrix, but scoring blocks accurately can itself be expensive. We propose Delta-Based Tile Scoring (DTS), a training-free, content-adaptive tile scoring method for sparse block attention. DTS selects query and key anchors according to local vector changes, using fewer representatives in redundant regions while retaining more detail in heterogeneous regions. To accelerate anchor selection, parallel delta packing partitions the query and key sequences into tile-aligned chunks and performs bounded local scans over these chunks concurrently. The selected tiles are then computed using the original query, key, and value vectors. On LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct, DTS keeps average RULER and LongBench scores within 0.10 percentage points of full attention, with RULER evaluated up to 128K tokens. At 128K tokens, DTS reduces measured scoring-pipeline latency by 38% compared with XAttention. On four NVIDIA H100 GPUs, it achieves a 3.3$\times$ prefill speedup over a PyTorch full-attention baseline using FlashAttention-2 at 512K tokens.
authors: Emre U\u{g}ur, Jiawen Qi, Qinyu Chen
bullets: Addresses the prefill bottleneck of long-context attention, where accurately scoring skippable blocks can be costly.
Uses training-free, content-adaptive delta scoring with fewer anchors in redundant regions and more in heterogeneous ones.
Accelerates scoring through parallel, tile-aligned local scans, then computes selected tiles with the original vectors.
Maintains average RULER and LongBench scores within 0.10 percentage points of full attention, including RULER up to 128K tokens.
Reports 38% lower scoring-pipeline latency than XAttention at 128K tokens and 3.3× prefill speedup over a FlashAttention-2 PyTorch baseline at 512K tokens on four H100 GPUs.
