papers.selection_reason: Training-free sparse block attention scoring for long-context LLMs; directly targets efficient attention and long-context processing.
papers.title: DTS: Delta-Based Tile Scoring for Efficient Long-Context Sparse Attention
papers.tldr: DTS enables efficient long-context sparse attention by scoring tiles from local vector changes while preserving near-full-attention quality.

papers.abstract: Long-context large language model (LLM) services charge for repeated context, yet billing weights need not reflect its contribution to answer quality. We present a three-layer framework separating content relevance, observable proxies and auditable positional weights. Context-ablation experiments show that relevance dominates position and that distance-decay families do not outperform a relevance-only baseline. A measured serving stack shows that cache hits reduce repeated-prefix compute cost by over two orders of magnitude at 65,536 tokens, while cold resends constrain sustainable discounts. Cross-provider measurements separate cache value from tokenisation and list-price differences. Calibrated simulations reduce the 99th percentile of session charges by 31-42%, although revenue-matched nonlinear tariffs achieve similar reductions and median charges increase. The framework provides a bounded per-token accounting rule and measured deployment constraints, rather than a validated utility estimator.
authors: Yi Lu, Qianshi Lin, Yumeng Yang, Hongxia Wang
bullets: Separates content relevance, observable proxies, and auditable positional weights for context billing.
Context ablations find relevance dominates position; distance-decay weighting does not beat a relevance-only baseline.
Serving measurements show cache hits cut repeated-prefix compute costs by over 100× at 65,536 tokens, while cold resends limit discounts.
Calibrated simulations reduce 99th-percentile session charges by 31–42%, but revenue-matched nonlinear tariffs produce similar reductions and increase median charges.
The work offers bounded per-token accounting and deployment constraints, not a validated utility estimator.

papers.title: Measuring and Charging for Retained Context in Long-Context LLM Services

papers.abstract: Asking a model to check retrieved text can also tell it which source to trust. We introduce FutureBench, a renewable framework for evaluating knowledge-context conflict using timestamped questions, controlled passage triplets, and no-context probes. Across 3,629 questions and six models, Verify (a prompt combining checking with passage priority) raises false-answer adoption in all five models tested on pre-cutoff events, mainly by displacing answers that were correct under Baseline, which allows both passage evidence and model knowledge. On post-cutoff events, only o4-mini increases adoption (+13.7 percentage points). A four-prompt comparison on 902 post-cutoff questions finds that passage priority without checking raises adoption, while moving to Verify lowers it in all five models. Adversarial-Aware, which warns of misleading passages and prioritizes model knowledge, restores 82.5-98.9% of displaced pre-cutoff answers with under one point of change in true-passage accuracy. FutureBench supports repeated evaluation on fixed cohorts and extension to new events as models change.
bullets: Uses timestamped questions, controlled passage triplets, and no-context probes across 3,629 questions and six models.
The Verify prompt increases adoption of false answers on pre-cutoff events in all five tested models, often displacing previously correct answers.
On post-cutoff events, only o4-mini shows increased false-answer adoption; passage priority alone raises adoption, while adding checking lowers it.
Adversarial-Aware restores 82.5–98.9% of displaced pre-cutoff answers with less than one percentage point change in true-passage accuracy.
The framework supports reproducible evaluation on fixed cohorts and extension to new events as models change.

papers.title: FutureBench: A Renewable Framework for Evaluating Knowledge-Context Conflict in LLMs
papers.tldr: FutureBench evaluates how prompts and retrieved passages make LLMs resolve conflicts between context and their own knowledge over time.

papers.abstract: Interpretability for AI agents should not be confined to understanding the model's internal weights. It must also cover the agent's reasoning and decision-making process over multi-source context. We present LMLineage, an out-of-band system that attributes every output sentence of an agent session to its supporting input spans with calibrated confidences, without requiring white-box access to the model or any additional inference passes. On top of the lineage metadata, we build concept-drift micro compaction: instead of waiting for the context-length limit and summarizing everything, the system detects when previously used input documents have stopped being referenced ("drifted") and surgically compacts only those, preserving user instructions verbatim. We evaluate on a multi-tier corpus: 71 gold annotated sentences from 10 Chinese web-QA cases, plus 90 turns of independently collected multi-turn sessions across three generator models (gpt-4o-mini, qwen3.8-27b, deepseek-v4-flash). Results show that (i) window-level embedding similarity is far better aligned with LLM paraphrasing than whole document or lexical matching; (ii) the greedy-window fast path is both faster and more accurate on average than exhaustive line-matching (a multiple-comparisons bias in the latter inflates web recall at the cost of overall accuracy); (iii) per-turn attribution completes in 1s on a single GPU, remaining stable as context accumulates to 40 turns; and (iv) concept-drift detection is conservative (0% false compaction) with recall bounded by attribution accuracy. We further describe the concept-drift micro compaction design and an interactive incident-tracing/memory-cleaning case study. A companion patent application covers the lineage construction method.
authors: Wei Hou, Jingxin Geng, Xin Chen, Zheqing Jiang
bullets: Uses calibrated lineage metadata to attribute output sentences to input spans across multi-source, multi-turn contexts.
Detects concept drift and compacts only no-longer-referenced documents while preserving user instructions verbatim.
Window-level embedding similarity better captures paraphrased support than whole-document or lexical matching.
A greedy-window method is faster and more accurate on average than exhaustive line matching; attribution remains stable through 40 turns and completes in about 1 second per turn on one GPU.
Drift compaction is conservative, reporting 0% false compaction, with recall limited by attribution accuracy.

Right ribs: inflow this turn (user prompt above, tool calls/results/web below). Expanding a beat reveals per-sentence cards with (type, value, confidence) triplets. papers.abstract: Mamba models deployed on streaming data, such as limit order book updates, run far past the sequence lengths they were trained on. A guarantee on how much a small change of input can move the hidden state therefore has to hold at every length. The closest existing bound we know of measures the change of the timescale additively, and it grows linearly with the sequence length unless the timescale is bounded away from zero. In this paper, we measure the change on a log scale instead. The key observation is that the decay factor of each step then moves by at most a fixed fraction of that step's input weight, so the per-step errors cannot pile up. Using this, we prove that two runs of a selective-scan cell from a common start stay within a bound that holds at every length, shrinks to zero with the size of the change and needs no lower bound on the timescale. We give a construction showing that, for small changes, this bound is within a factor of about 2 of the best possible, and we extend it to the update used in Mamba's released code when the timescale is bounded above. We then evaluate block-level bounds built from the theorem on two small models trained on one day of order book data. With a bounded timescale, a bound built on the existing analysis is tighter than ours for at most the first 8 steps. With Mamba's softplus timescale, whose certified lower bound is as small as $10^{-21}$, it is looser at every length. Our bounds hold for every input to a block, but they remain more than five orders of magnitude above the changes that gradient attacks find.
bullets: Existing additive-timescale bounds can grow linearly with sequence length unless the timescale is bounded away from zero.
Measuring timescale changes logarithmically prevents per-step errors from accumulating and yields a bound valid at every sequence length.
The bound vanishes with the input perturbation and is within about a factor of 2 of optimal for small changes.
The analysis extends to Mamba’s released update when the timescale is bounded above.

On two small order-book models, the new bounds outperform existing analysis beyond 8 steps or at all lengths with softplus timescales, but remain over five orders of magnitude above gradient-attack changes.

papers.selection_reason: Theoretical perturbation bounds for selective state space models used in LLMs; relevant to long-context and streaming language models.
papers.title: A Log-Timescale Perturbation Bound for Selective State Space Models at Every Sequence Length
papers.tldr: A log-timescale analysis gives selective state space models a sequence-length-independent perturbation bound without requiring a positive lower bound on the timescale, though the resulting block-level bounds are still very loose in practice.

papers.abstract: Sparse attention models read a few blocks of keys for every query at a fixed budget and can lose much of their long-context retrieval accuracy at that budget. We ask where this loss is made. Using exact attention mass selection at the shipped budget as an oracle, we show that the selector under-ranks the needle rather than running out of budget. We find attention heads that miss the needle by running a calibration probe that teacher-forces the answer and reads two quantities in every head. The first is the needle attention that the selector forfeits, and the second is the share of the answer's log-probability that fixing the head's selection restores, integrated along the path from the shipped selector to full attention. Four checkpoints of the InfLLM-V2 family and NOSA-8B lose multi-key retrieval in the same three blind heads, which attend to the needle while a mean-pooled key summary dilutes its single decisive token. Full attention in those heads or a 4-bit scorer that keeps the shipped budget recovers most of the loss without training. On MiniCPM4.1-8B at 64K, either fix lifts multi-key retrieval accuracy from 54.1 to 97.5%, level with full attention in every head. In production serving engines, full attention in those heads keeps 84 to 89% of the time to first token (TTFT) that sparse attention saves at 32K to 128K context length. Beyond the InfLLM-V2 selector lineage, one unified rule flags attention heads above a threshold swept on each checkpoint until they close most of the gap to full attention on calibration prompts. A similar small set of blind attention heads carry the loss for the SeerAttention-R gates, NSA, and DashAttention, whereas many such heads exist in MoBA. On Qwen3-8B with the SeerAttention-R gates, full attention in 18 of 288 key-value heads lifts multi-key retrieval accuracy from 29.8 to 97.7%.
bullets: Exact-attention analysis shows the main issue is selector mis-ranking of relevant blocks, not exhausting the fixed budget.
A teacher-forced calibration probe identifies heads that attend to the needle but lose it when mean-pooled key summaries dilute its decisive token.
For InfLLM-V2 and NOSA-8B, the same three blind heads explain much of the multi-key retrieval loss; similar patterns appear in several other sparse-attention methods.
Repairing flagged heads with full attention or a 4-bit scorer preserves the shipped budget and recovers most of the loss without training.
Reported gains include MiniCPM4.1-8B improving from 54.1% to 97.5% at 64K, while selective full attention retains 84–89% of sparse attention’s TTFT savings; MoBA shows many more blind heads.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Method overview. (a) InfLLM-V2 scores each block from mean-pooled keys, gathers the top-k blocks and attends to them in every head. (b) A needle probe, run once per checkpoint, compares the shipped selection with exact attention mass at the same budget, which explains the failure, and keeps the heads with the largest gain of fixing their selection. (c) In the flagged heads, full attention reads every block, and every other head keeps the shipped selector. A 4-bit scorer that keeps the shipped budget can replace full attention in those heads.

papers.abstract: We present Limite 1B - Violetto, a one-billion-parameter model designed for high-throughput mathematical reasoning. Limite is trained from scratch on 237 billion tokens from a carefully curated, mathematics-centric corpus and supports context lengths of up to 131k tokens. Its architecture and training recipe were developed together to maximize reasoning capability while keeping training and inference costs low. Post-training combines knowledge distillation, targeted supervised fine-tuning, and RLVR on a curated curriculum. Limite achieves 94.01% on AIME 2026 and 74.25% on BeyondAIME, placing it among models many times its size on our evaluation suite. The model is deliberately only lightly instruction-tuned: it is intended primarily as a single-turn mathematical solver and as a fast, parallel component of larger systems, rather than as a general-purpose assistant. We release the model, its base and value checkpoints, and an optimized serving implementation under the Apache 2.0 license.
authors: Mario Prignano, Gabriele Cirillo, Alessio Morosini, Luca Cerovaz, Alessandro Bartolocci, Emanuele Rodol\`a, Giulio Starace, Francesco Pappone
bullets: Trained from scratch on 237 billion tokens from a mathematics-focused corpus.
Supports context lengths up to 131k tokens and uses a jointly designed architecture and training recipe for efficient reasoning.
Post-training combines knowledge distillation, targeted supervised fine-tuning, and RLVR.
Scores 94.01% on AIME 2026 and 74.25% on BeyondAIME, according to the report.
Released under Apache 2.0 with model checkpoints and an optimized serving implementation.

papers.abstract: Sequence models represent past context at different resolutions, using token-level keys and values, fixed-size recurrent states, or hierarchies of compressed summaries. Full attention supports strong associative recall but requires quadratic work during training and prefill and a linearly growing key-value cache during inference. Linear attention and state-space models reduce these costs through fixed-size recurrent memory, but this compression can limit recall. Log-linear attention offers a middle ground by maintaining logarithmically many state matrices. However, its hierarchy favors finer resolution near the current query while compressing earlier context into coarser summaries. To complement this allocation of resolution, we introduce bilateral log-linear attention, which pairs the existing hierarchy with a second hierarchy anchored at the sequence origin. By combining their reads, the two branches provide finer access to both early and recent context while remaining causal. We derive recurrent and chunkwise parallel formulations for the added branch, preserving log-linear training and prefill work, logarithmic decoding work per token, and logarithmic persistent state storage at fixed feature dimensions and chunk size. In multi-query associative recall, this design raises mean overall test accuracy from 76.37% to 96.12% over forward log-linear attention across multiple training seeds. For pretrained language models under approximate parameter matching, it raises the mean score on six selected RULER needle-in-a-haystack tasks from 26.97% to 50.03% at a context length of 6144 tokens. In the same setting, bilateral attention also outperforms forward log-linear attention on seven of eight downstream retrieval tasks, including question answering and information extraction.
bullets: Full attention recalls well but has quadratic training/prefill cost and a linearly growing inference cache.
The method complements the existing recent-context hierarchy with a second hierarchy anchored at the sequence start, enabling finer access to both early and recent tokens while remaining causal.
Recurrent and chunkwise-parallel formulations retain log-linear training and prefill work, logarithmic decoding per token, and logarithmic persistent state storage.
Mean associative-recall accuracy improves from 76.37% to 96.12%; selected RULER retrieval scores improve from 26.97% to 50.03% at 6,144-token context.
It outperforms forward log-linear attention on seven of eight downstream retrieval tasks, including question answering and information extraction.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly rely on long contexts, making Key-Value (KV) caches dominate memory usage and inference latency. Existing vector quantization (VQ) methods effectively compress KV caches to sub-4-bit levels but often overlook inefficiencies in memory alignment and decoding speed. This work introduces MeltKV, a memory-latency co-optimized KV cache quantization framework for long-context LLM serving. MeltKV employs a memory-aligned variable-bit index packing scheme that adaptively assigns bit-widths to grouped key channels and compactly stores indices within standard data-types, eliminating redundant bits. Additionally, head-wise codebook sharing reduces the total codebook size while maintaining accuracy. Experiments demonstrate that MeltKV effectively compresses KV representations to sub-4-bit levels down to 1 bit and, at comparable perplexity, achieves 48.1% lower memory usage and 52.9% lower latency than state-of-the-art VQ methods.
authors: Jiyun Han, Seongjoon Cho, Seungkyu Choi
bullets: Targets KV-cache memory and inference-latency bottlenecks in long-context LLM serving.
Adaptively assigns bit-widths to grouped key channels and packs indices into standard data types to remove redundant bits.
Shares codebooks across attention heads to reduce codebook storage while preserving accuracy.
Reaches sub-4-bit compression, down to 1 bit, with comparable perplexity.
Reports 48.1% lower memory usage and 52.9% lower latency than prior VQ methods at comparable perplexity.

papers.abstract: The needle-in-a-haystack (NIAH) benchmark was introduced as a test for measuring a model's ability to find small relevant facts within a very large body of input text. However, existing NIAH benchmarks each suffer from one or more of the following limitations: (1) reliance on synthetic data, so their evaluations may not generalize to real-world settings; (2) reuse of previously published datasets, leading to the risk of benchmark contamination; (3) dependence on manual annotation, which requires human effort to create and update data and is prone to future benchmark contamination; and (4) unrealistic simplification of long-context multi-hop reasoning where each next step is trivial given previous steps, while real-world reasoning often requires planning over multiple possible proof paths. To address these limitations, we introduce \Benchmark, a dynamic benchmark built from real citation relationships among scientific papers published after the evaluated models' knowledge cutoff date, which utilizes real-world information while ensuring no benchmark contamination. The fully automated benchmark construction pipeline samples representative subgraphs of the citation graph formed by these papers and converts each subgraph into a long-context QA example with a verifiable answer. We use GraphNIAH to evaluate eight LLMs from the GPT-5.6, Gemini-3, and Qwen3.5 families. We find that accuracy falls as questions require longer reasoning paths: at question depths of 16 and 32, the GPT-5.6 and Qwen3.5 models answer YES/NO questions no better than random guessing, mostly by answering NO; four of the eight models answer no counting example correctly, and the others model get worse as the subgraph size increases. These findings suggest that current LLMs often stop searching the citation relationships in their context before they reach the answer, even though every fact they need is in the context.
bullets: Addresses limitations of prior NIAH benchmarks, including synthetic data, reused datasets, manual annotation, and overly simple reasoning paths.
Automatically builds verifiable long-context QA examples from citation subgraphs of papers published after evaluated models’ knowledge cutoffs.
Evaluates eight LLMs across the GPT-5.6, Gemini-3, and Qwen3.5 families.
Accuracy declines as reasoning depth and subgraph size increase; at depths 16 and 32, some models perform no better than random guessing on YES/NO questions.
Results suggest models often stop searching citation relationships before reaching answers, despite all required facts being present in context.

papers.title: GraphNIAH: A Benchmark for Long-Context Reasoning over Real-World Graphs
papers.tldr: GraphNIAH is a contamination-resistant benchmark testing whether LLMs can perform long-context, multi-hop reasoning over real scientific citation graphs.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon language agents accumulate tool results and replies until the history no longer fits the context window. Current agents shrink this history by having a model summarize it, so each compaction rereads and rewrites the history it replaces, and cache-aware triggers decide when to compact while taking the size of the result as given. We present Folio, a context manager that records, folds, and recovers history through one set of handles. While the agent runs, Folio records three linked levels: a short turn note the model writes as part of its ordinary reply (L1), an event manifest of every call written by the runtime (L2), and the captured source records (L3). Because these views already exist, the runtime folds the context programmatically, selecting coarser views for older turns. The fold prints the handles that index L2 and L3, so recovery tools that read bounded pages, compute over full text in files, and keep findings in a persistent dossier reach the evidence the agent needs with little added input. The fold trigger prices an explicit landing point that includes the retained budget. On 75 LOCA-bench tasks with DeepSeek-V4-Pro behind every system, Folio solves 66 tasks against 54 for the same runtime with model-written compaction and 49-59 for Claude Code, Codex, and SoL-Pi, in about half their working time, at 2.4 times lower cost than that runtime; each fold takes a median of 0.6 seconds.
authors: Yubo Ruan, Tao Peng, Jiao Zhang, Chuanguo Ma, Lei Xu, Han Zhou, Wenwu Wang, Xiafei Lv, Xingjie Zhou, Guiju Fan, Hao Wang, Fenghui Zhang, Mao Miao, Shuo Li
bullets: Addresses context-window overflow from accumulating tool results and replies in long-running agents.
Records linked history views: model-written turn notes (L1), runtime event manifests (L2), and source records (L3).
Programmatically folds older turns into coarser views while preserving handles for bounded, evidence-focused recovery.
Uses a fold trigger that accounts for an explicit retained-context budget and landing point.
On 75 LOCA-bench tasks, solved 66 versus 54 for model-written compaction, with roughly half the working time and 2.4× lower cost; folds took a median of 0.6 seconds.

papers.selection_reason: Context folding and recovery for long-horizon language agents directly targets LLM memory and long-context management.
papers.title: Folio: Recoverable Multi-Resolution Context Folding for Long-Horizon Language Agents
papers.tldr: Folio manages long-horizon agent context by programmatically folding multi-resolution history and enabling targeted recovery, improving task completion while reducing time and cost in the reported evaluation.

papers.abstract: Laya is a small model that answers a multiple-choice question about a text in one pass: the question, the options (each with a name and a description) and the text form one sequence of at most 512 tokens, the window, in the English release. A longer text is silently cut at the end, and we measure what that costs. Test documents place a held-out row's text, the evidence, at a chosen token offset among distractor text; 177 items, five tasks, three checkpoints (released, short-row fine-tune, long-document fine-tune), four window sizes and 93,275 scored requests. When the evidence lies beyond the window, accuracy falls to 26.4% for the released checkpoint (27.2% for both fine-tunes), near the 27.0% of guessing and below the 35.6% of always giving the commonest label. Confidence gives no warning (AUROC 0.50 to 0.55 for telling cut from read requests; 0.5 = chance), and the runtime's truncation flag also fires on requests whose evidence was visible. The released checkpoint reads visible evidence badly once text precedes it: 38.5% pooled against 60% when the evidence comes first, so a larger window alone gains +6.2 points. Fine-tuning on long documents adds +27.6 points on visible evidence over the short-row fine-tune (95% interval +22.3 to +33.1) and nothing on cut evidence. That is an in-family result: training rows and test documents share generator and question types, and the main filler is of the training kind. With encyclopedic filler never seen in training the gain is +13.2 (+9.9 to +16.6), with rows of other tasks as filler -2.0. Among training-free rearrangements a 312-token window scan helps most (+11.9 points over the default for the released checkpoint) at six to eleven forward passes. Documents are synthetic, labels are LLM-made and one backbone is studied, so these diagnose this model, not long documents in general.
authors: Mohammed Nayeem Khan, Allan Kevin T
bullets: Evidence beyond the input window reduces accuracy to near-guessing levels, while truncation flags can also fire when evidence remains visible.
The released model reads visible evidence much better when it appears first; increasing the window alone yields only a modest gain.
Fine-tuning on long documents substantially improves performance on visible evidence but does not help when evidence is cut off.
A training-free window scan provides the strongest tested improvement, at the cost of multiple forward passes.
Results are limited to synthetic documents, LLM-generated labels, and one model backbone.

papers.title: Where in the Input Does a One-Pass Decision Encoder Look?
papers.tldr: A one-pass decision encoder often misses or mishandles evidence placed later in the input, and neither confidence nor truncation signals reliably reveal the failure.

papers.abstract: Long-context multimodal intelligence requires revisiting earlier images as conversations and documents accumulate, yet retaining an image does not guarantee reliable access to its details. By varying context length, redistributing a fixed text passage around the image, and changing positions without adding text, we identify the positional relation between images and questions as a direct influence on visual access. To address this gap, we propose Visual Position Re-Anchoring (VPR), a training-free method that shifts cached visual-key rotary phases toward a short-context reference before question processing. It operates directly on the existing KV cache, preserving standard attention computation without extracting attention maps or adding model forward passes. We develop static and continuous compensation schedules, using the static schedule by default. Across ten checkpoints and ten benchmarks, static VPR improves 97 of 100 model--task scores. Further analysis shows greater attention to regions containing answer evidence across six checkpoints, with minimal runtime overhead under fixed rotary frequencies. These findings demonstrate an efficient way to sustain visual access through positional adjustment within the cache.
authors: Juntao Xu, Qichai Zhao, Rui Sun, Zhouyang Jiang, Shiwei Wu, Zhi Li, Kaisheng Ma, Yu Liu
bullets: Image–question positional relationships can impair visual access even when the image remains in context.
VPR shifts cached visual-key rotary phases toward a short-context reference before question processing.
The training-free method works directly on the KV cache without attention-map extraction or extra forward passes.
Static VPR improved 97 of 100 model–task scores across ten checkpoints and ten benchmarks.
It increased attention to answer-relevant image regions with minimal runtime overhead under fixed rotary frequencies.

papers.abstract: Practical Web applications increasingly require agents to interpret long conversations or documents. For inputs exceeding the context windows of large language models (LLMs), memory agents process segments sequentially and retain past information in bounded memory. However, they typically divide inputs into flat token segments without preserving structure or hierarchy, causing three limitations for structured data such as API responses or HTML documents. First, fixed-length segmentation can split fields of the same record, breaking their relationships. Second, segments lack hierarchical information, obscuring their structural context and positions. Third, successive memory updates may discard details of earlier sibling records needed for reasoning on later segments. To address these limitations, we propose TreeAgent, a structure-aware agent that uses the input hierarchy to guide both segment-wise context processing and access to past information. Specifically, TreeAgent constructs segments from complete subtrees and groups of adjacent sibling subtrees to preserve local structural relationships. We provide theoretical guarantees on segment counts to guide token budget selection toward matching the segment count of fixed-length segmentation. We further attach structural paths to the segments for the agent to identify their ancestors and hierarchical positions. We also introduce residual memory links from the segments of low-level children to the segments of high-level parents, enabling direct information flows beyond successive memory updates. We evaluate TreeAgent with four representative memory agents on eight retrieval and aggregation tasks. The inputs are derived from real-world application data in JSON, HTML, YAML, and JavaScript and range from 8K to 1M tokens. TreeAgent improves the average score across the four datasets for all four agents, with 3.61% performance gain on average.
authors: Wei Gu, Weiwei Qi, Jiajun Tang, Tianhang Zheng, Bo Chen, Zhibo Zhang, Jinfei Liu, Kui Ren
bullets: Targets flat, fixed-length segmentation that breaks relationships, loses hierarchy, and forgets earlier sibling details.
Builds segments from complete subtrees or adjacent sibling subtrees to preserve local structure.
Attaches structural paths to expose each segment’s ancestors and position.
Adds residual links from low-level child segments to high-level parent segments for direct information flow.
Evaluated on retrieval and aggregation tasks over JSON, HTML, YAML, and JavaScript inputs spanning 8K–1M tokens; improved all four tested memory agents on average.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong capabilities across diverse applications, making both safety and utility essential for reliable deployment. Jailbreak attacks use diverse forms of adversarial prompting to bypass alignment safeguards and induce LLMs to generate harmful responses. Some representation-based defenses regulate internal activations using predefined steering directions or learned safety regions. However, adapting intervention to each input without a predefined representational target while limiting over-refusal remains a challenge. In this paper, we propose Target-free Entropy-guided Residual Modulation (TERM), an inference-time defense that uses prompt-calibrated attention entropy deviations to guide adaptive modulation of the model's own residual updates. Attention patterns vary across prompts and decoding steps, making raw entropy values difficult to interpret as a consistent signal for intervention. We therefore calibrate attention entropy against each prompt's own prefill baseline to establish an input-specific reference for reducing unnecessary intervention on benign requests. Adaptive scale normalization and temporal accumulation then account for differences in deviation scale and persistence to determine intervention strength. The resulting signal controls bounded scaling of the model's own residual updates, without relying on a predefined safety direction. We compare our method with seven defenses on seven jailbreak attacks and two over-refusal benchmarks across Llama, Qwen, and Gemma models, including Qwen3 models from 0.6B to 32B. Results show our method improves jailbreak robustness while maintaining low over-refusal on benign safety-sensitive requests with modest inference overhead.
authors: Haoyi Wu, Yunkai Dang, Wanyu Zhang, Lei Wang, Wenbin Li
bullets: Addresses the challenge of defending against jailbreaks without predefined safety directions or excessive over-refusal.
Calibrates attention entropy against each prompt’s prefill baseline, then uses scale normalization and temporal accumulation to estimate intervention strength.
Applies bounded modulation to the model’s own residual updates, avoiding predefined representational targets.
Evaluated against seven defenses across seven jailbreak attacks and two over-refusal benchmarks on Llama, Qwen, and Gemma models.
Reports improved jailbreak robustness, low over-refusal on benign safety-sensitive requests, and modest inference overhead.

papers.abstract: DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) reduces the computational cost of attention through token-level selection. However, its indexer still scores the entire causal prefix for each query, making indexing a dominant source of latency in long-context inference. Notably, the indexer alone can account for more than 50% of total prefill GPU time at long context lengths. To address this bottleneck, we propose ADIndex, an Adaptive and Distillation-driven Indexing method for token-level sparse attention. ADIndex integrates three key components: (i) a layer-wise calibration strategy that adaptively accommodates cross-query retrieval overlap, motivated by our observation of pronounced inter-layer heterogeneity; (ii) a group-level distillation scheme that leverages this heterogeneity to efficiently train adaptive layer-wise group indexers, capturing salient retrieval signals from individual queries; and (iii) a low-latency inference strategy that reduces repeated full-prefix scans through token bank sharing within query groups while retaining query-specific refinement. Experiments on DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5.1 demonstrate that ADIndex preserves near-lossless task performance on LongBench, LongBench v2, and RULER while delivering substantial efficiency gains over standard DSA, including prefill and decoding kernel speedups of up to 6.22x and 3.40x, respectively, at a context length of 256K across the layer-wise reuse configurations, as well as an end-to-end serving speedup of 1.54x at a context length of 128K.
authors: Jin-Fei Qi, Yiduo Li, Jiang-Xin Shi, Kan Liu, Tao Lan, Hanlin Tang, Yu-Feng Li
bullets: Targets the indexer bottleneck, which can exceed half of prefill GPU time at long context lengths.
Uses layer-wise calibration to handle heterogeneous cross-query retrieval overlap across layers.
Trains adaptive layer-wise group indexers through group-level distillation while retaining query-specific refinement.
Reduces repeated full-prefix scans via token-bank sharing within query groups.
On DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5.1, reports up to 6.22× prefill, 3.40× decoding-kernel, and 1.54× end-to-end serving speedups while maintaining near-lossless LongBench, LongBench v2, and RULER performance.

figures.caption: Figure 2 Overview of ADIndex. papers.abstract: Describing hours of audio requires accurate event timing and sustained descriptive detail throughout the recording. We present LongCap, a framework for timestamped audio captioning (TAC), with the human-annotated LongCapBench and three diarization-inspired metrics: Timeline Error Rate (TER), Granularity Error Rate (GER), and Caption Similarity (tcpCapSim). LongCap interleaves audio chunks with structured event captions, using relative timestamps and retained context to support length extrapolation within a 1M-token inference context window. Event-level reannotation restores caption detail, while systematic studies examine model scaling, dependency supervision, and self-distillation. LongCap-Diar achieves strong benchmark results and extrapolates to 16 hours of concatenated audio despite training on recordings no longer than 40 minutes. Our TAC models are competitive with Qwen3.5-Omni-Plus on short clips, outperform evaluated baselines in caption similarity and timeline accuracy in segment-level comparisons on LongCapBench-TAC-Long, and caption full recordings approaching two hours. On LongCapBench-TAC, 9B and 35B-A3B offer favorable size-performance tradeoffs, while 122B-A10B substantially improves event-dependency recovery. These findings support long-horizon general audio understanding and provide a foundation for always-on voice agents.

Models are competitive on short clips and outperform evaluated baselines in segment-level caption similarity and timeline accuracy.

papers.abstract: Existing methods enhancing an LLM's long-context reasoning capability often rely on data synthesis and follow-up LLM post-training. However, the data synthesis strategy and the post-training recipes are empirically driven and computationally intensive. In this work, we propose a new framework, dubbed LongCapHarness, to instead harness the underlying capabilities for long-context reasoning. The harnessing process recursively revises and updates capability primitive implementation, capability state and control logic through recursive self-improvement on the development set. With neither data synthesis nor LLM post-training, LongCapHarness is applied to Llama3-8B and transferred to Qwen2.5-3B. LongCapHarness substantially outperforms recent data-synthesis-based baselines on HELMET and RULER benchmarks; its estimated development cost is less than 50% of the estimated training costs of NExtLong and PolicyLong. We hope these results motivate further research into harnessing the latent capabilities of LLMs to solve tasks beyond their explicit training.
bullets: Addresses the computational cost and empirical nature of data synthesis and post-training approaches.
Recursively updates capability primitives, capability state, and control logic through self-improvement on a development set.
Applied to Llama3-8B and transferred to Qwen2.5-3B without additional LLM post-training.
Substantially outperforms recent data-synthesis baselines on HELMET and RULER.
Estimated development cost is under 50% of the estimated training costs of NExtLong and PolicyLong.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Performance superiority and cost effectiveness of LongCapHarness compared with the three recent data-synthesis-based baselines and the RSI baseline.

Figure 2: LongCapHarness uses recursive selfimprovement (RSI) on the development set to construct and refine reusable capability harnesses. papers.abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents accumulate sessions of up to millions of tokens, far more key-value (KV) cache than one GPU holds, so serving systems keep a small budget of tokens and evict the rest. Eviction methods differ in which tokens they keep but share one goal: that the tokens a later step needs are still cached. We show this is not enough. In 100K-token coding sessions on Qwen3-8B with a 2,048-token budget, a planner-guided policy that keeps over 99% of the needed tokens resident still fails late steps increasingly often: its accuracy falls from 93% to 64% as the gap between a definition and its use grows from 2K to 90K tokens, at residency 0.996. The needed tokens are resident but unretrievable: what grows is their rotary-position distance to the query. We present PACE (Planner-Aware Context Engine), a KV-cache engine that couples plan-aware retention, in which the agent's planner tells the cache which context future steps will read, with bounded positions, which renumber kept tokens so their rotary distance to the query stays below 8K at any session length. In a pre-registered evaluation on fresh tasks, PACE passes 97% of hidden unit tests at 100K tokens, against 42% for H2O and 3% for SnapKV under the same budget, and needs both components: either alone reaches 63% (the combination beats each, p < 10^-4). The result holds with length: in 1M- and 2M-token sessions on one 24 GB GPU, with definitions written 0.9M and 1.8M tokens before use, PACE passes 99% and 100% of checks and recalls every session fact, while bounded positions without foresight falls from 33% to 13%; PACE holds under 0.7 GB of KV state where the full cache would need 147-295 GB. Renumbering is exact, costs no measurable perplexity, and adds 9% wall time. On Mistral-7B, whose coding ability caps it at 40% even with nothing evicted, PACE stays at that ceiling while retention alone falls below it.
bullets: Long sessions can exceed one GPU’s KV-cache capacity, requiring aggressive token eviction.
Even when over 99% of later-needed tokens remain cached, accuracy drops as their rotary-position distance from the query grows.
PACE uses the agent’s plan to retain future-relevant context and bounds rotary distances by renumbering retained tokens.
On 100K-token Qwen3-8B coding tasks with a 2,048-token budget, PACE passes 97% of hidden-unit tests versus 42% for H2O and 3% for SnapKV.
The method scales to 1M–2M-token sessions on one 24 GB GPU, with 9% added wall time and no measurable perplexity cost.

papers.abstract: Context selection can reduce input length during long-input inference but can remove evidence required to answer a query. We introduce CoRA-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating evidence preservation under shared token budgets. We compare head and tail truncation, BM25, dense retrieval, dense retrieval with reranking, LLMLingua-2, and Provence across BABILong, LOONG Financial Spotlight, a custom NoLiMa diagnostic, and LongMemEval. Evidence-preservation results reveal task-dependent tradeoffs: BM25 achieves 0.921 supporting-fact recall on BABILong at 128K, dense retrieval and dense reranking each achieve 0.908 needle recall on NoLiMa at 64K, and dense retrieval achieves 0.993 answer-bearing-turn recall on LongMemEval at 64K. Evidence, token retention, and complementary reader evaluations use the same selected contexts. Reader evaluations use dataset-native answer metrics and three runs on the same questions, with paired bootstrap confidence intervals. At a 32K budget, BM25 achieves 46.20% BABILong answer accuracy and dense retrieval achieves 71.13% LongMemEval accuracy. The results show that method rankings vary across evidence types and between evidence recall and downstream accuracy.
bullets: Compares truncation, BM25, dense retrieval, reranking, LLMLingua-2, and Provence across four long-context benchmarks.
Evaluates evidence recall, token retention, and downstream reader accuracy using the same selected contexts.
Reports strong but task-specific recall: BM25 reaches 0.921 supporting-fact recall on BABILong, while dense retrieval reaches 0.993 answer-bearing-turn recall on LongMemEval.
At 32K tokens, BM25 obtains 46.20% BABILong answer accuracy and dense retrieval obtains 71.13% LongMemEval accuracy.
Finds that evidence-recall rankings do not consistently predict downstream answer accuracy.

papers.abstract: External state should become more valuable as a reader becomes more capable, yet long-context evaluations measure memory utility at a single model scale. This paper formulates scale complementarity: the absolute gain from external state increases when reader capacity and a compact state budget are jointly scaled. ASCENT realizes this principle with a target-blind causal writer, nested typed state, and a bounded query-conditioned readout; every language model remains frozen. Under log loss, the value of a nested refinement equals its target-relevant conditional information; a full factorial makes the reader-by-state interaction identifiable. Official 16K BABILong experiments show Qwen2.5 accuracy gains of 10.50, 78.88, and 82.63 percentage points at 0.5B, 1.5B, and 3B parameters, with both adjacent directional contrasts significant after family-wise correction. At 7B, Foundation accuracy rises to 33.25% while four-slot ASCENT answers every question, which caps the gain at 66.75 points; the 3B-to-7B accuracy increment is -15.88 points [-20.55, -11.20]. The accuracy-side claim is therefore established from 0.5B to 3B; the 7B conclusion rests on the non-saturated negative-log-likelihood factorial. A three-model by three-state factorial yields co-scaled negative log-likelihood gains of 0.388, 2.099, and 7.406 nats at 1.5B, 3B, and 7B; all interaction and gain contrasts retain positive simultaneous lower bounds. Five public 7B-8B readers obtain 66.75-85.63 point gains, and ASCENT exceeds task-trained retrieval checkpoints at the two larger shared scales. Controls, baselines, systems accounting, matched-hardware reproduction, and a cross-architecture sensitivity analysis accompany the experiments. The results establish scale-complementary external state under the evaluated benchmarks, metrics, and state schema.
bullets: Addresses the lack of scale-sensitive measurements of external-memory utility in long-context models.
Uses a target-blind causal writer, nested typed state, and bounded query-conditioned readout while keeping readers frozen.
Formalizes scale complementarity through conditional information and factorial reader-by-state interaction analysis.
On 16K BABILong, Qwen2.5 accuracy gains were 10.50, 78.88, and 82.63 percentage points at 0.5B, 1.5B, and 3B parameters.
Results support the claim from 0.5B–3B on accuracy and across 1.5B–7B on negative log likelihood, under the evaluated benchmarks, metrics, and state schema.

papers.abstract: Long-context language models often neglect information in the middle of the input, a phenomenon known as "lost-in-the-middle". Part of this gap may stem from the long-range decay of rotary position embedding (RoPE), which weakens the positional signal between distant tokens. Existing input compression deletes low-importance tokens, and attention reweighting acts only after RoPE has weakened this signal. RoPE-level methods modify positions directly but apply the same remapping to every query. To address these limitations, we propose QGPM (Query-Guided Positional Modulation), a training-free method that reshapes RoPE positions using query relevance from the model's own attention heads. QGPM builds a broad relevance map for lower layers and a sharp one for upper layers. Low-relevance tokens advance by less than one position on fast-rotating planes, pulling relevant evidence toward the query. Slow-rotating planes keep the original layout, with every token in place. Experiments on NoLiMa and RULER with multiple context lengths show that QGPM improves over base models and strong baselines, with the largest gains on retrieval tasks, and generalizes across multiple backbones. Our code is available at https://github.com/iZHpy/QGPM.
authors: Peiyu Zhang, Heng Ping, Shinibali Bhattacharyya, Anwesan Pal, Nikos Kanakaris, Kevin Cheang, Shixuan Li, Wei Yang, Paul Bogdan
bullets: Targets positional-signal decay that can cause models to overlook information in the middle of long inputs.
Uses attention-derived query relevance to reshape token positions rather than deleting tokens or reweighting attention afterward.
Applies broad relevance maps in lower layers and sharper maps in upper layers; preserves the layout on slow-rotating RoPE planes.
Experiments on NoLiMa and RULER across context lengths show gains over base models and strong baselines, especially for retrieval tasks.
Generalizes across multiple model backbones.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of QGPM. (a) A plain prefill reads the attention from the query to each context sentence in a few selected heads. The fused sentence ranking is shaped into a broad relevance map and a sharp score map. Context before the first relevant sentence is protected and keeps a score of 1. (b) Each map sets a positional stride for every token on every frequency plane. Low-relevance tokens advance by less than one position on fast planes. Slow planes, relevant sentences, and the query keep unit stride. Cumulative sums give the remapped positions. (c) In the answering pass, the lower layers use the broad map and the upper layers use the sharp map. Decoding continues in unit steps from the last position of each map.

papers.abstract: Language models lose accuracy when a prompt contains non-evidential context: irrelevant statements from unrelated domains, or random off-distribution tokens, with no competing answer and no semantic overlap with the query. Such noise pervades retrieval-augmented, tool-using, and long-context deployments, yet the failure has lacked a mechanistic account. We trace the corruption to the Intrusion Pathway, which starts with MLPs enriching both query-subject and irrelevant-token representations, parroting heads carry prefix-token content to the prediction position, and relational readers largely avoid unrelated sources. Nevertheless, preserved subject enrichment and selective reading do not prevent intrusion in the broader computation. We then localize part of this interference to a sparse set of attention heads, which we call intrusion heads. Their prefix-derived writes promote distractor-related content, while their reduced support for the correct answer arises primarily from weaker non-prefix contributions rather than direct suppression by the prefix. The same heads transfer across tasks and distractor types and are largely weight-disjoint from the heads that integrate relevant contextual evidence, enabling a class-conditional intervention. Replacing the corrupted last-token residual with its clean counterpart, an oracle probe that requires a matched clean forward pass, recovers 97.6% on average of the distractor-induced drop across four downstream tasks. A deployable mask level knockout of about ten heads, roughly 1% of the model's attention heads, recovers 57% at bounded cost to helpful context.
bullets: The study explains accuracy loss from irrelevant statements or off-distribution tokens even when they provide no competing answer.
MLPs enrich irrelevant-token representations, while parrot-like heads carry prefix content to the prediction position; relational readers mostly avoid unrelated sources.
Intrusion heads promote distractor content and provide weaker support for the correct answer, rather than directly suppressing it.
These heads transfer across tasks and distractor types and are largely distinct from heads that use helpful context.
An oracle residual replacement recovers 97.6% of the induced drop; masking about ten heads recovers 57% with bounded impact on useful context.

papers.selection_reason: Mechanistic study of how irrelevant context degrades LLM performance in long-context and RAG settings, with head-level interventions; relevant to LLM behavior and long-context robustness.
papers.title: The Intrusion Pathway: How Non-Evidential Context Degrades Language Model Performance
papers.tldr: Non-evidential prompt noise harms language models through a sparse, transferable set of “intrusion heads” that inject distractor-related content into predictions.

papers.abstract: ConvPE (Convolutional Position Embedding) improves both the performance and efficiency of Transformer models in language modeling, long-context extension, and vision. It injects a windowed, content-dependent bias into attention scores through a lightweight causal convolution over a low-dimensional projection of the hidden states. As a lightweight plug-in, ConvPE is compatible with RoPE, attention masks, and KV concatenation. It also supports high-dimensional position embeddings via high-dimensional convolutions. In a reproduction, ConvPE outperforms five 1D baselines and eight 2D baselines. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/wzhagi/convpe.
bullets: Adds a windowed, content-dependent bias to attention scores using a causal convolution over low-dimensional hidden-state projections.
Works with RoPE, attention masks, and KV concatenation, and supports high-dimensional position embeddings through high-dimensional convolutions.
Evaluated for language modeling, long-context extension, and vision.
In reproduction experiments, it outperformed five 1D and eight 2D baselines.
Code is publicly available on GitHub.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a general Transformer position-embedding method that improves language modeling and long-context extension, directly relevant to LLM architecture and long-context research.
papers.title: ConvPE: Convolutional Position Embedding Improves Transformers
papers.tldr: ConvPE is a lightweight convolutional position-embedding plug-in that improves Transformer performance and efficiency across language and vision tasks.

papers.abstract: In large language model (LLM) serving systems, the key-value (KV) cache grows linearly with sequence length and concurrency, so long-context inference easily hits the high-bandwidth memory (HBM) capacity wall and results in low concurrency. Offloading the KV cache to host dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) frees HBM space and raises concurrency, but the additional cache management and host-to-device (H2D) load overhead inflates inference latency, higher concurrency fails to translate into effective throughput. We present FlashOffloading, a host-DRAM-centric inference architecture that fully offloads the KV cache in both the prefill and decode phases. FlashOffloading builds rolling HBM cache for prefill, a hot cache for decode, a reverse sparse index with zero extra miss-lookup overhead, and a compute--load overlapped kernel, optimizing KV offloading latency across the entire pipeline and delivering throughput gains under a time-per-output-token (TPOT) service-level objective (SLO). In experiments deploying GLM-5.2 with multi-token prediction (MTP3) speculative decoding on an Ascend910C prefill--decode (PD)-disaggregated platform, FlashOffloading improves prefill throughput by up to 1.38\(\times\) and decode throughput by up to 1.91\(\times\) under a 30 ms TPOT constraint. FlashOffloading is integrated into an open-source serving framework: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-ascend/tree/releases/v0.30.0.
bullets: Long-context inference can exhaust HBM because KV-cache usage grows with sequence length and concurrency, limiting concurrency.
The architecture fully offloads KV caches for both prefill and decode while optimizing cache access across the serving pipeline.
Key techniques include rolling HBM and hot decode caches, a reverse sparse index, and compute–load overlap.
On GLM-5.2 with MTP3 speculative decoding, it improves prefill throughput by up to 1.38× and decode throughput by up to 1.91× under a 30 ms TPOT SLO.
The system is integrated into the open-source vLLM-Ascend serving framework.

papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses KV cache offloading for efficient long-context LLM serving, fitting both efficiency and long-context topics.
papers.title: FlashOffloading: Low-Latency KV Cache Offloading for Long-Context LLM Serving
papers.tldr: FlashOffloading reduces the latency cost of DRAM-based KV-cache offloading, enabling higher-throughput long-context LLM serving under strict latency constraints.

papers.abstract: EHR foundation models read medical events within a fixed context window, and long context has so far been measured only in tokens. How far back in time a model must look to capture the earliest predictive signal is unknown. We introduce time-context, the calendar lookback window before the prediction point, and provide, to our knowledge, the first systematic evaluation of decade-scale time-context for an EHR foundation model. We pretrained a decoder-only transformer (34.6M parameters) on 1.4B coded events from 3.6M primary-care patients in North West London and fine-tuned it to predict incident colorectal cancer under a 12-month pre-diagnostic buffer. A frozen cohort of 1,008 cases and 9,582 matched controls, all registered for at least 30 years, was evaluated at 15 nested lookback windows from 2 to 30 years, so that every truncation is compared within the same patients. Discrimination rose from an AUROC of 0.551 at 2 years to 0.590 at 18 years, then plateaued, with about 80% of the gain reached within 10 years; an XGBoost baseline converged to the same level (peak AUROC 0.589). A simulation further suggests that rotary position embeddings (RoPE) over elapsed time alias beyond about 20 years at the default base frequency, motivating a retuned $θ$. Time-context is a measurable design axis for clinical prediction models, distinct from token-context, and should be reported.
bullets: The study defines and evaluates calendar-based time-context—the lookback period before prediction—rather than token-context alone.
A decoder-only EHR transformer was pretrained on coded primary-care events and evaluated across 15 nested windows spanning 2–30 years.
AUROC increased from 0.551 at 2 years to 0.590 at 18 years, then plateaued; roughly 80% of the gain occurred within 10 years.
An XGBoost baseline reached a similar peak AUROC, while simulations indicated potential RoPE time aliasing beyond about 20 years.
The findings support reporting time-context as a distinct design axis for clinical prediction models.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces time-context for EHR foundation models and analyzes RoPE aliasing over elapsed time, a transferable insight for long-context position encoding.
papers.title: How Deep is the Signal? Time-Context up to 30 Years for Colorectal Cancer Prediction in a Primary-Care EHR Model
papers.tldr: For colorectal cancer prediction from primary-care EHRs, extending the model’s time-context improved discrimination up to about 18 years, with most gains achieved within 10 years.

papers.abstract: At context lengths of about 1M tokens, dense attention is costly in prefill and decoding, and training typically relies on long documents, which become scarcer as the target length increases. Most sparse attention methods score all preceding blocks or tokens, so their selection cost per query is $O(L)$ at context length $L$; hierarchical selection reduces it to $O(\log L)$, but prior trainable hierarchical methods report accuracy only within their training length. We propose RecSA (Recursive Sparse Attention), which builds a tree over the KV cache in which each node summarizes its subtree with one key and one mean-pooled value. The keys come from one pooler per layer, shared by all levels and distilled from dense attention. Each level above the tokens selects at most $k$ candidates, so each query has $O(\log L)$ selection cost and reads $O(\log L)$ entries; the summaries of unselected candidates share one softmax with the exact tokens. Each entry's RoPE position is its index among the candidates of its level, so at any length every relative distance stays within the range seen during training. Initialized from Qwen3-4B and trained on 0.62B tokens at the original model's 32K training length, RecSA outperforms all baselines on RULER at every length from 131K to 2M; at 1M, it scores 60.5, compared with 40.0 for the best baseline, Dense + DCA. With our optimized kernels, RecSA is faster than dense attention in end-to-end prefill and decoding from 64K to 2M; at 524K on one H200 GPU, it accelerates prefill by 3.2x and decoding by 3.8x.
bullets: Builds a hierarchical KV-cache tree whose nodes summarize subtrees with pooled keys and values.
Selects at most k candidates per level, reducing per-query selection and reads to O(log L).
Uses shared, dense-attention-distilled poolers and level-relative RoPE positions to support length extrapolation.
Outperforms reported baselines from 131K to 2M tokens; at 1M, scores 60.5 versus 40.0 for Dense + DCA on RULER.
With optimized kernels, achieves 3.2× prefill and 3.8× decoding speedups at 524K on one H200 GPU.

papers.title: Recursive Sparse Attention: Million-Token Length Extrapolation at Logarithmic Cost
papers.tldr: RecSA enables accurate attention over up to 2M tokens with logarithmic selection cost, using only 32K-length training.

papers.abstract: LLM agents use context compaction to manage growing interaction histories, but summarizing long histories with large models can introduce substantial delays. Compaction therefore requires balancing information retention against latency. We observe that structured summary slots can retain information when generated independently. Based on this observation, we present SpecCompact, a framework that accelerates compaction through slot-parallel semantic speculation. SpecCompact fine-tunes a small drafter and generates slots in parallel. The target model verifies each proposed line and repairs rejected content, while subsequent drafting uses the updated slot prefix. System optimizations further reduce repeated context processing and model calls. Across AppWorld and $\tau^3$ benchmarks with two target models, SpecCompact achieves $2.04$--$5.63\times$ compaction speedups over Hermes-style summarization. Separate downstream evaluations reveal model- and task-dependent performance trade-offs. A user study within Hermes further shows an $8.68\times$ median compaction speedup.
authors: Yulu An, Yifei Feng, Xiangyang Yin
bullets: Addresses the latency of summarizing growing agent histories while preserving important information.
Uses a small fine-tuned drafter to propose structured summary slots in parallel.
A target model verifies each proposed line, repairs rejected content, and guides subsequent drafting.
Reports 2.04–5.63× speedups on AppWorld and τ³ with two target models, plus an 8.68× median speedup in a Hermes user study.
Downstream quality shows model- and task-dependent trade-offs.

papers.selection_reason: Accelerates LLM agent context compaction via speculative verification, directly relevant to long-context and memory efficiency.
papers.title: SpecCompact: Accelerating LLM Agent Context Compaction with Slot-Parallel Semantic Speculative Verification
papers.tldr: SpecCompact speeds up LLM-agent context compaction by speculatively generating summary slots in parallel and having a target model verify and repair them.

papers.abstract: Looped Transformers increase effective depth by re-executing shared layers, but three limitations hinder their adoption: memory grows with the loop count, compute can only be adjusted in whole-block steps, and the loop count is hard to change after training. We propose LooM (Loop-invariant Memory), which addresses each in turn. In a causal encoder-decoder (CED), LooM loops only the decoder layers after the first, which read a global memory written once per token, and each of them publishes the key-value (KV) entry for a token only on its first visit, so the cache does not grow with the loop count. These layers loop independently, providing every budget from 3 to 21 layer executions per token, and one model trained on randomly sampled budgets covers all of them without a router. With enough loops, LooM outperforms a single-pass baseline trained on the same data on language modeling, zero-shot accuracy and long-context perplexity, while using the same cache size. Our analysis further shows that the training budget distribution decides what extra depth buys. These results suggest that a CED is a natural place to loop: memory is written once, and depth becomes a budget chosen at deployment.
authors: Lele Yang, Muxi Diao, Zhonghao Yan, Jiankang Chen, Bin Wen, Tingting Gao, Wentao Zhang, Kongming Liang, Zhanyu Ma, Weiran Xu
bullets: Targets looped Transformer limitations: loop-dependent memory growth, coarse compute control, and fixed post-training loop counts.
Loops decoder layers after the first, using global memory written once per token and publishing each token’s KV entry only on its first visit.
Independent layer loops provide budgets from 3 to 21 layer executions per token; one model supports all budgets without a router.
With sufficient looping, LooM improves language modeling, zero-shot accuracy, and long-context perplexity over a same-data single-pass baseline while keeping cache size unchanged.
Training-budget distributions determine what additional depth provides; the approach supports deployment-time depth selection.

papers.selection_reason: Novel looped transformer architecture that keeps cache size constant, improving long-context perplexity and efficiency.
papers.title: LooM: Loop-Invariant Memory for Causal Encoder-Decoder Language Models
papers.tldr: LooM enables flexible, memory-efficient looping in causal encoder-decoder language models, allowing deployment-time depth adjustment without increasing cache size.

papers.abstract: The full-attention layers of large language models (LLMs) make every generated token more expensive than the previous one, slowing models down on long-context tasks. Hybrid models reduce this cost by replacing most full-attention layers with linear-attention layers, but the first still dominate decoding at long contexts. We accelerate these remaining layers without any training or weight changes using combined sparse attention: each layer attends to a sliding window of recent tokens, a pinned prefix, and a fixed budget of most relevant tokens in the context. The window size and budget are found on a per-layer basis using a multi-objective search algorithm. Across six hybrid models from three families, from 4B to 397B parameters, the selected configurations preserve their baseline model's accuracy on 21 long-context datasets. Decoding 64k/256k tokens becomes up to 1.26x/2.22x faster on Qwen3.5-4B, 1.20x/2.23x on Qwen3.5-122B-A10B, and 1.16x/2.06x on Ornith-1.0-397B.
authors: Jo\~ao Eduardo Batista, Emil Vatai, Mohamed Wahib
bullets: Targets full-attention layers that remain costly at long contexts in hybrid models.
Combines a recent-token sliding window, a pinned prefix, and a fixed budget of salient context tokens.
Uses per-layer multi-objective search to select the window size and token budget without changing weights.
Across six models and 21 long-context datasets, configurations preserve baseline accuracy.
Provides up to 2.22× faster decoding at 256k tokens, depending on the model.

papers.selection_reason: Training-free sparse attention for long-context decoding directly fits efficient attention and long-context interests.
papers.title: Accelerating Long-Context Decoding in Large-Scale Hybrid LLMs Without Retraining
papers.tldr: A training-free sparse-attention strategy accelerates long-context decoding in hybrid LLMs while preserving baseline accuracy.

papers.abstract: Small Language Models (SLMs) are increasingly deployed on consumer-grade hardware, yet their ability to preserve information across progressively longer contexts remains insufficiently understood. Existing benchmarks primarily evaluate retrieval-oriented tasks, providing limited insight into whether successful retrieval reflects comprehensive long-context memory preservation. To address this limitation, this paper introduces Simple Retrieval-Reconstruction Memory (SRRM), a lightweight and fully reproducible benchmark that jointly evaluates Targeted Retrieval and Global Information Reconstruction. This study also proposes the Memory Preservation Ratio (MPR), a benchmark-level metric that quantifies the relationship between retrieval and reconstruction performance. SRRM was evaluated using a synthetic dataset on three Qwen2.5 models (0.5B, 1.5B, and 3B parameters) across context loads ranging from 10 to 100 factual statements. Experimental results show that reconstruction performance deteriorated substantially faster than retrieval accuracy as contextual information increased, indicating that retrieval alone is insufficient to characterize long-context memory preservation. Among the evaluated models, Qwen2.5-1.5B achieved the highest retrieval accuracy (86.7%), reconstruction performance (45.7%), and MPR (0.53), outperforming the larger Qwen2.5-3B model (72.2%, 18.5%, and 0.26, respectively). These findings demonstrate that increasing parameter count does not necessarily improve long-context memory preservation. Overall, SRRM provides a reproducible and extensible benchmark for systematically evaluating long-context memory while revealing complementary memory behaviors that remain hidden under retrieval-only evaluation frameworks.
bullets: Introduces SRRM, a lightweight benchmark combining targeted retrieval with global information reconstruction.
Defines Memory Preservation Ratio (MPR) to relate retrieval and reconstruction performance.
Evaluates three Qwen2.5 models from 0.5B to 3B parameters on synthetic contexts containing 10–100 factual statements.
Qwen2.5-1.5B performed best, while the larger 3B model performed worse, showing that more parameters do not guarantee better memory preservation.
Scope: results are based on a synthetic dataset and the evaluated Qwen2.5 models.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overall architecture of the proposed SRRM benchmark. Synthetic information is generated and organized into conversational context before being evaluated through Sequential Retrieval and Summary Reconstruction tasks. Performance is measured using retrieval accuracy, Critical Information Recall (CIR), token consumption, inference time, and hardware memory usage.

Figure 2: Overall organization of the proposed SRRM benchmark. The benchmark begins with four independently generated synthetic information categories, which are subsequently organized into a balanced benchmark sequence using a deterministic Round-Robin strategy. Each information item is assigned a sequence identifier and category identifier before being grouped into predefined context sizes. The constructed benchmark is then evaluated through two complementary tasks, namely Sequential Retrieval and Summary Reconstruction, while multiple performance metrics are collected to provide a comprehensive analysis of the short-term memory capability of the evaluated language models.

Figure 4: This figure illustrates the evaluation workflow of the Sequential Retrieval Test. After the complete conversation history has been constructed, benchmark questions are automatically generated from the corresponding ground-truth annotations. Each model response is subsequently compared with the expected answer to determine whether the retrieved fact is correct or incorrect. The final retrieval performance is then calculated using the proportion of correctly answered questions.

Figure 7: As shown in Figure 7, retrieval performance varies across the evaluated models as the context size increases. The figure presents the overall accuracy trend for Qwen2.5-0.5B, Qwen2.5-1.5B, and Qwen2.5-3B under identical benchmark conditions. The numerical retrieval accuracy corresponding to each evaluation level is summarized in Table 13.

Figure 10 visualizes the mean retrieval accuracy for each evaluated language model across the four benchmark information categories. Color intensity represents retrieval performance averaged over all evaluated context sizes, while the numerical values indicate the corresponding percentage accuracy for each model–category combination.

Figure 13: Demonstrates that all evaluated models achieved substantially higher retrieval performance than reconstruction performance. Although the magnitude of this difference varies across the Qwen2.5 model family, the same overall pattern is consistently observed, indicating that successful retrieval of previously presented information does not necessarily translate into equivalent preservation of that information during summary generation. This observation suggests that retrieval and reconstruction represent related but distinct memory capabilities, supporting the motivation for evaluating both tasks independently within the proposed SRRM benchmark.
Figure 9: Overall comparison between mean retrieval accuracy and mean CIR score.

Figure 5: Figure 5 illustrates the evaluation workflow of the Summary Reconstruction Test. After the complete conversation history has been constructed, the language model is instructed to reconstruct every previously presented factual statement as a structured summary. The generated summary is subsequently compared against the benchmark ground-truth facts through automatic line-by-line matching, producing the Critical Information Recall (CIR) score that represents the proportion of correctly reconstructed information.
Figure 11: Category-specific reconstruction performance heatmap matrix

Table 12: The SRRM benchmark records multiple computational metrics alongside memory performance to provide a more comprehensive evaluation of language models. These metrics quantify computational efficiency by measuring context size, response length, inference latency, and hardware resource utilization throughout the benchmark. Together, they complement the retrieval- and reconstruction-based evaluations by revealing the computational trade-offs associated with increasing model parameters and context sizes.

Table 5: As shown in Table 5, the benchmark evaluates three parameter scales within the Qwen2.5 family while maintaining the same inference framework and context length. This controlled selection enables the study to isolate the effect of parameter scaling on information retention performance.
Table 1 : Comparison of Existing Long-Context Benchmarks

Table 11: The SRRM benchmark evaluates language models under five progressively increasing context sizes to analyze the effect of information load on short-term memory performance. Instead of modifying the dataset itself, the benchmark gradually increases the number of information items presented to the model while preserving the same information order and distribution. This controlled context scaling enables consistent comparisons across different parameter sizes under identical experimental conditions.

Table 15 : Reports the exact CIR scores obtained by each evaluated model at every benchmark level. The tabulated values complement the graphical representation shown in Figure 8 by providing precise reconstruction scores for each context size, facilitating direct comparison across different parameter scales.

Table 4: Comparison between existing benchmark objectives and the proposed SRRM benchmark. SRRM extends previous evaluations by jointly measuring targeted retrieval, global information reconstruction, and computational efficiency under progressively increasing factual contexts.

Table 13: reports the exact retrieval accuracy obtained by each model at every evaluated context size. Presenting the numerical results in tabular form complements the graphical representation in Figure 7 by providing precise values for each experimental condition, enabling direct comparison across both models and context levels.

Table 14: summarizes the overall retrieval characteristics of each evaluated model. Mean Accuracy represents the average retrieval accuracy across all five context sizes, Max Accuracy and Min Accuracy denote the highest and lowest recorded retrieval performance, respectively, while Accuracy Drop measures the absolute decrease in retrieval accuracy between the evaluations conducted with 10 and 100 information items.

Table 16 : Summarizes the overall reconstruction characteristics of each evaluated model. Mean CIR represents the average reconstruction score across all five context sizes, Max CIR and Min CIR indicate the highest and lowest reconstruction scores observed during the benchmark, respectively, while CIR Drop denotes the absolute decrease in reconstruction performance between the evaluations conducted using 10 and 100 information items.

Table 18 summarizes the benchmark-level ranking derived from the retrieval and reconstruction evaluations presented in the preceding sections. The ranking provides a consolidated comparison of overall memory performance across the evaluated models while preserving the detailed retrieval, reconstruction, and category-level analyses reported previously. As such, it serves as a concise reference for comparing the relative benchmark performance of the evaluated Qwen2.5 model family.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a benchmark for evaluating long-context memory preservation in small language models, directly relevant to long-context processing and memory evaluation.
papers.title: SRRM: A Retrieval-Reconstruction Benchmark for Evaluating Long-Context Memory in Small Language Models
papers.tldr: SRRM shows that retrieval accuracy alone overestimates long-context memory in small language models, as reconstruction degrades much faster with increasing context.

papers.abstract: Why do language models fail on long inputs? The common answer is length. We show that, for retrieval, length is cheap and competition is not. On five open models (0.5B to 3B parameters, four families), neutral filler costs nothing: accuracy stays at 0.97 to 1.00, up to 32K tokens on Qwen2.5-1.5B. Statements in the format of the evidence, placed at the same positions, drop it to 0.16 to 0.33. A single statement that gives the queried key a rival value multiplies the loss by 9 to 110, and every additional rival adds to it. Inside the model, one quantity tracks the failure: the attention mass left on the evidence. Across 126,473 trials it explains up to 58% of the variance in loss; log length explains at most 8%. The masked-filler protocol behind the claim that length alone hurts reproduces on MMLU (11 to 18 points lost at 30K tokens), but fails a visible control in retrieval: masking costs 45 accuracy points at 32K tokens, while the same filler left visible costs none. In retrieval, context rot is a competition for attention. We release the probe and all 126K trial-level measurements.
bullets: Neutral filler preserves retrieval accuracy—even up to 32K tokens—while same-format statements sharply reduce it.
A single rival value for the queried key increases loss 9–110×, with additional rivals worsening performance.
Attention remaining on the evidence explains up to 58% of loss variance; log context length explains at most 8%.
A masked-filler protocol can make length appear harmful, but visible filler has no effect in the retrieval control.
The study evaluates five open models across 126,473 trials and releases the probe and measurements.

Mean over trials, pooled over the three neutral fillers; shaded bands are 95% bootstrap intervals.
