papers.selection_reason: Analyzes why retrieval fails on long inputs, attributing context rot to attention competition rather than length; relevant to long-context understanding.
papers.title: Length Is Cheap, Competition Is Not: Attention Predicts Context Rot in Retrieval
papers.tldr: Retrieval failures in long contexts are driven mainly by competing evidence that steals attention, not by context length alone.

papers.abstract: Later tokens are costlier to generate than earlier tokens. On frontier open weight models, the disparity in cost may rise to as much as 7x. Through frequent compaction, we show across a broad range of long-horizon and long-input tasks that frontier language models sacrifice little to no task accuracy when maintaining short contexts. We further demonstrate that LLM performance does not collapse on long-horizon software engineering tasks even when taking at most one action per context, and based on that we outline the concept of semantic state space models (SSSMs). Our findings question the need for long-context language models.
authors: Peter Belcak, Saurav Muralidharan, Jindong Jiang, Yonggan Fu, Wonmin Byeon, Hanrong Ye, Ryan Angilly, Ali Taghibakhshi, Shih-Yang Liu, Siru Ouyang, Greg Heinrich, Pavlo Molchanov
bullets: Later tokens can cost up to 7× more to generate than earlier tokens in frontier open-weight models.
Across diverse long-input and long-horizon tasks, short contexts cause little to no reported accuracy loss when compacted frequently.
Software-engineering performance remains robust even with at most one action per context.
The authors propose semantic state space models (SSSMs) and challenge the necessity of long-context LLMs.

papers.selection_reason: Directly challenges long-context necessity and proposes compaction-based alternatives for frontier LLMs.
papers.title: You don't need long context
papers.tldr: Frequent context compaction can preserve frontier LLM accuracy on long-input and long-horizon tasks while substantially reducing the need for long contexts.

papers.abstract: Parameter-efficient linearization turns a pretrained autoregressive Transformer into an efficient model by hybridizing sliding-window attention (SWA) with a constant-size recurrent memory. But does every layer's recurrent state contribute to long-context retrieval? Investigating an SWA and Test-Time Training (TTT) hybrid, we find that retrieval is sparse across depth, concentrated in a few anchor layers, and that the remaining states hold similar information expressed through layer-specific transformations. We exploit both observations in Anchor: TTT memory placed only at the anchor layers, and a cross-layer recurrent state written once and read by many layers, each through its own learned read map that realizes a layer-specific stretch and rotation, along with demonstrated generalization to other hybrid attentions. On Llama-3.1-8B and Mistral-7B, Anchor delivers 2.3-3.1x higher recall and 6.7-8.9 points higher MMLU accuracy than LoLCATs with a 10x smaller recurrent state, retains 91-95% of the teacher's MMLU accuracy, and cuts end-to-end latency by up to 4.3x relative to softmax attention.
authors: Vimal William, Yuanzhe Li, Danella Zhao, Huanrui Yang
bullets: Long-context retrieval is concentrated in a small number of layers, while other recurrent states encode similar information via layer-specific transformations.
Anchor places recurrent TTT memory only at these anchor layers and uses a cross-layer state read by many layers.
Evaluated on Llama-3.1-8B and Mistral-7B, it achieves 2.3–3.1× higher recall and 6.7–8.9 points higher MMLU accuracy than LoLCATs.
It uses a 10× smaller recurrent state, retains 91–95% of teacher MMLU accuracy, and reduces latency by up to 4.3× versus softmax attention.
The approach also generalizes to other hybrid-attention designs.

figures.caption: Figure 5. Anchor architecture and recurrent-state coverage. Left: Anchor-F maintains a private recurrent state in every layer, while Anchor keeps one shared state per anchor group and removes the interior states entirely, reducing recurrent state by 16× (201.0 → 12.6MB at 32k context). Each reader accesses the shared state through its own learned read map χ(·). Right: coverage over query (rows) and key (columns) positions. Green marks the local sliding window, red the span served by the recurrent state. Anchor-F requires one such state per layer; Anchor serves layers l1, . . . , L from a single shared state.

Figure 9. Cross-layer similarity generalizes across linearization methods. Debiased CKA against mean cosine similarity for every pair of layers, on the recurrent-state readouts of our TTT hybrid (Anchor-F), LoLCATs, and Liger on Mistral-7B over identical PG-19 and WikiText inputs. In all three models, layers share information while their cosine similarity remains small, indicating that this information is encoded in different bases.

Figure 7. Hybrid architecture of ANCHOR and full self-attention. ANCHOR and full self-attention layers are interleaved at a 3:1 ratio, so that softmax attention accounts for 25% of all layers. Within each group, the three ANCHOR layers retain their own sliding-window attention for local context but share a single recurrent state for long-range context: the leading layer writes the state, and each layer reads it through its own learned read map χℓ(·). The subsequent full self-attention layer attends over the entire sequence, providing exact retrieval at regular depth intervals, while the recurrent state per group remains constant in sequence length.

Figure 2. Layer-wise contribution of each branch to long-context retrieval. ∆CE (nats) on AR-32k when the TTT (top) or SWA (bottom) branch is removed at a single layer, broken down by the distance between a query and its target. Warm cells indicate degradation, that is, a larger increase in loss when the branch is removed. papers.tldr: Anchor improves long-context retrieval and efficiency by storing TTT memory only in a few anchor layers and sharing it across layers through learned read transformations.

papers.abstract: We introduce a training-free sparse attention method that builds a prompt-specific key index to accelerate both prefill and decoding. The method clusters the keys into large semantic blocks that group tokens from noncontiguous positions. Each query position selects blocks by scoring their centroids and attends to the original keys and values within them. Queries that select the same block are processed together, so prefill stays fast even though each query chooses its own blocks. Large blocks make centroid scoring and this grouped processing cheap, so each query can attend to more tokens in the same time. Larger blocks with a larger token budget can thus be both faster and more accurate on long-context tasks than smaller blocks with a smaller budget. We evaluate two hybrid LLMs, Qwen3.5-4B and 35B-A3B, on one NVIDIA H200. Including the cost of building and using the index, whole-model wall-clock speedups over dense attention are 2.3-2.4x for prefill and 1.7-2.0x for decoding at 512K tokens, and 2.9-3.0x for prefill at 1M. The 35B-A3B model stays close to dense attention on five RULER tasks through 1M, on LongBench-v2 overall, and on MRCR through 256K. The 4B model loses accuracy mainly on multi-key retrieval, yet outperforms dense Qwen3.5-2B, whose latency is similar at 512K, on all three benchmarks.
authors: Sosuke Kobayashi, Shoichiro Yamaguchi, Seiya Tokui
bullets: Builds a prompt-specific index by clustering noncontiguous keys into large semantic blocks.
Each query scores block centroids, then attends to the original keys and values within selected blocks.
Groups queries selecting the same blocks to keep prefill efficient despite query-specific routing.
On one H200, whole-model speedups reach 2.3–2.4× for 512K prefill, 1.7–2.0× for 512K decoding, and 2.9–3.0× for 1M prefill.
The 35B-A3B model remains close to dense attention on several long-context evaluations; the 4B model mainly degrades on multi-key retrieval.

papers.selection_reason: Training-free sparse attention with semantic block selection, directly relevant to efficient attention and long-context LLM inference.
papers.title: Coarse Semantic Blocks for Efficient Training-Free Sparse Attention
papers.tldr: A training-free semantic-block index makes sparse attention substantially faster for long-context prefill and decoding while largely preserving accuracy.

papers.abstract: Sparse attention cuts the cost of long-context inference by making the attention matrix sparse: each query attends only a subset of the sequence, chosen by a fixed pattern or, in recent production LLMs, learned per query. In DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA), the attention of DeepSeek-V3.2 and the GLM-5 family, every layer is preceded by a lightning indexer that scores the whole cache and keeps the k=2048 highest-scoring tokens for the layer to attend. At long context this indexer scan, not the sparse attention it feeds, is where the decode time goes. But adjacent layers select nearly the same tokens, so a layer can attend the selection of the previous indexer layer instead of its own. This removes the dependency: each indexer then runs concurrently with the attention of its layer. The resulting Multi-layer Indexer (MLI) needs no retraining and no new weights. Its default realization changes no kernel, running inside SGLang's production decode graph; an optional fused decode kernel accelerates it further on DeepSeek-V3.2. MLI composes with IndexCache (the cross-layer reuse GLM-5.2 ships as IndexShare): IndexCache drops the indexer from some layers, and MLI hides the scan on the rest. We serve DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5 under IndexCache's protocol at retentions 1/2 to 1/32 (the fraction of layers that keep an indexer) and contexts 10K to 195K. At equal retention the composition decodes faster than IndexCache: up to 14.5% faster on DeepSeek-V3.2 and 9.8% on GLM-5 at 1/2, and 7.9% and 5.1% at 1/4, largest where IndexCache keeps the most indexers and growing with context. At retention 1/r it is faster still than IndexCache at 1/(2r) while keeping twice the fresh selections: at 128K it reaches 1.32x the unmodified model's decode throughput at 1/4, above IndexCache's 1.28x at 1/8. Its LongBench, RULER and LongBench v2 accuracy stays within a few percentage points of IndexCache's.
authors: Serdarcan Dilbaz, Arjun Krishna, Kiran Kamble, Daniel M. Bikel
bullets: DSA’s full-cache indexer scan dominates decode time at long contexts, while adjacent layers choose nearly identical tokens.
MLI lets each layer attend to the preceding layer’s selection, allowing indexer computation to overlap with attention.
It requires no retraining or new weights; the default implementation runs in SGLang without kernel changes, with an optional fused kernel.
Combined with IndexCache, MLI improves decoding speed by up to 14.5% on DeepSeek-V3.2 and 9.8% on GLM-5 at equal retention.
Long-context accuracy on LongBench, RULER, and LongBench v2 remains within a few percentage points of IndexCache.

papers.abstract: LLM agents compact long histories to fit their context windows, but the compacted context must still carry the operating rules that govern later actions. Prior work shows that violations rise after compaction, but measures compliance outside a complete agent harness and does not identify where each violation comes from. We introduce ARCBench(Agent Rule Compliance Benchmark), a configurable benchmark built on the open-source pi agent harness. Its tool-calling agent loop lets us measure rule compliance from actions taken during execution, bringing the evaluation closer to deployed agent workflows. Using ARCBench, we examine where violations after compaction come from, and how different compaction configurations and adversarial settings change their sources. We find that compaction rarely deletes the rule: most violations after compaction occur while the rule is still in the compacted history, with the agent treating a later request as permission, ignoring the rule, and proceeding anyway. Where violations come from depends on the configuration: how the rule is delivered decides whether the agent would break it even without compaction, while the compaction strategy and budget decide whether the rule survives. The strongest compactor-targeted attack more than doubles violations by corrupting the rule in the summary and changing how the agents behave, whereas the strongest defense restores the rule in most summary but still violates. Finally, retaining a rule does not guarantee compliance: compacted runs that retain the rule violate more than twice as often as runs with the full history.
bullets: Introduces ARCBench, a configurable benchmark that measures rule compliance through tool-calling actions in an open-source agent harness.
Most post-compaction violations occur even when the rule remains in the compacted history: agents treat later requests as permission or ignore the rule.
Violation sources depend on configuration: rule delivery affects baseline willingness to break rules, while compaction strategy and budget affect rule preservation.
A compactor-targeted attack more than doubles violations by corrupting summarized rules; the strongest defense restores rules in most summaries but does not eliminate violations.
Retaining a rule is insufficient: compacted runs with retained rules violate more than twice as often as full-history runs.

papers.selection_reason: Studies how context compaction affects LLM agent rule compliance, relevant to long-context processing and context management.
papers.title: Do Agents Still Follow the Rules? Benchmarking Rule Compliance under Agent Context Compaction
papers.tldr: ARCBench shows that context compaction usually preserves rules but can still sharply reduce agent compliance, especially when summaries corrupt rules or alter behavior.

papers.abstract: Long-context LLM inference is costly because attention repeatedly reads a growing key-value (KV) history. We introduce Chunk-Indexed Sparse Attention (CISA), which retrofits pretrained dense attention models without gradient updates. CISA selects fixed-size KV chunks using compact summaries of existing keys, avoiding token-level indexing and a separate full-length index cache. It uses one indexing query per KV group and shares selected chunks across queries in that group. During prefill, QShare reuses selections across adjacent queries to reduce indexing cost and improve KV reuse and GPU utilization. We evaluate CISA on NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano and Ultra, and Inkling-Small. In one-layer BF16 benchmarks at batch size 32 using Ultra's per-device attention dimensions, core attention is 11.7x faster for prefill queries near the end of a 1M-token prompt and 13.0x faster during decode. Including chunk scoring, selection, and all other measured GPU work, speedups are 8.6x and 3.0x. On Ultra NVFP4 with a 4,096-chunk budget, aggregate scores stay within 1.5 percentage points of dense attention on MRCR, LongBench v2, and GraphWalks. RULER sweeps on Nano and Ultra BF16 up to one million tokens show scores within 2.05 percentage points of dense attention with 8-16x fewer KV reads. Serving million-token prompts with 32 concurrent requests and 4K output tokens per request, CISA achieves 2.29x the end-to-end throughput of dense attention using Nemotron 3 Ultra NVFP4 on four NVIDIA B300 GPUs. Selecting fewer chunks increases throughput to 2.61x; in separate GraphWalks evaluations, the smaller budget widens the aggregate score gap from 1.49 to 3.59 percentage points. These results expose a practical quality-speed tradeoff without sparse training.
bullets: Targets the high cost of repeatedly reading growing KV histories during long-context inference.
Indexes fixed-size KV chunks using compact key summaries, with one query per KV group and shared selections across group queries.
QShare reuses chunk selections across adjacent prefill queries to reduce indexing overhead and improve KV reuse.
Reports up to 8–16× fewer KV reads, 2.29× end-to-end throughput, and quality within roughly 1.5–2.05 percentage points of dense attention in evaluated settings.
Using fewer chunks raises throughput to 2.61× but widens the GraphWalks quality gap to 3.59 percentage points.

papers.title: CISA: Retrofitting Dense Attention Models with Chunk-Indexed Sparse Attention
papers.tldr: CISA retrofits pretrained dense-attention LLMs with chunk-level sparse attention, achieving substantially faster million-token inference while keeping quality close to dense attention without retraining.

papers.abstract: Theoretical limitations of transformers on state tracking---the ability to track information about entities or variables over long contexts---have motivated new recurrent language modeling (LM) architectures such as Gated DeltaNet (GDN). These architectures have, in particular, been benchmarked against the $S_5$ word problem, a theoretically hard state-tracking task that captures abilities such as code evaluation under arbitrary variable assignment. It, however, remains open whether other, simpler forms of state tracking might both be more relevant in practice and already explain observed differences between these architectures. We propose evaluating state tracking using a hierarchy of word problems with four increasing levels of difficulty: r-trivial, corresponding to immutable assignment to variables in programming; aperiodic, where assignments are mutable; soluble, where assignments are self-referential; and general finite state tracking. Theoretically, we show that the class of problems transformers are thought to length-generalize on does not even contain all aperiodic state tracking. On the other hand, we prove that GDN with positive eigenvalues expresses all aperiodic problems, and the regular languages recognized by certain transformers are precisely all soluble ones, thus providing a fine-grained picture of state tracking capabilities of various architectures. Taking these ideas to practice, we construct StateBench, a 4-tier long-horizon state-tracking benchmark. Our systematic direct training experiments across architectures largely align with theoretical expectation, albeit with interesting observations at very large scale length-generalization. Additionally, we also evaluate pretrained models---both open hybrid and closed frontier ones---on StateBench, finding that none of them robustly solves even soluble state tracking, suggesting a direction for future improvement.
bullets: State tracking is organized into r-trivial, aperiodic, soluble, and general finite-state problems of increasing difficulty.
Theoretical results show transformers may fail on some aperiodic tracking, while Gated DeltaNet can express all aperiodic problems; certain transformers correspond precisely to soluble problems.
StateBench provides a four-tier, long-horizon benchmark for systematic evaluation across architectures.
Direct training results broadly match theory, but pretrained open and closed models do not robustly solve even soluble state-tracking tasks.
Very large context lengths reveal additional, notable deviations from expected length-generalization behavior.

papers.abstract: Long-context large language model (LLM) inference is increasingly constrained by the cost of maintaining an ever-growing KV-cache. Low-rank K/V projections provide a promising way to compress the KV-cache with minimal quality loss, but prior work has largely optimized KV-cache compression in isolation, leaving distributed inference, especially with tensor parallelism where attention computation is partitioned across multiple GPUs, largely underexplored. We make two observations: (i) tensor-parallel communication is an important cost when deploying low-rank KV-cache compression in distributed inference; and (ii) Value compression can be associated with the output projection, allowing the same low-rank Value representation to reduce both Value-cache width and tensor-parallel communication. Based on these observations, we propose BasisKV, a low-rank KV-cache compression method for communication-intensive, long-context LLM inference. BasisKV jointly optimizes the low-rank factors across per-GPU attention partitions against the complete attention output, rather than fitting each partition in isolation. The compressed Value cache is further reused to help identify which Key pages should be accessed: it predicts part of the Key information needed for routing, while a Key-specific residual stores what cannot be recovered from Value. The original Keys are then retrieved only for the selected pages to compute exact QK scores. Across multiple LLM families and system settings, BasisKV achieves a better quality--efficiency tradeoff than existing low-rank baselines, reaching up to 1.42x end-to-end speedup under 8-GPU tensor-parallel inference. Our code is available at https://github.com/alexz949/BasisKV
bullets: Targets KV-cache growth and communication overhead in distributed, tensor-parallel inference.
Jointly optimizes low-rank factors across GPU attention partitions against the complete attention output.
Uses compressed Values to predict routing-relevant Key information, with a Key residual for unrecoverable details.
Retrieves original Keys only for selected pages to compute exact query–key scores.
Reports a better quality–efficiency tradeoff than low-rank baselines, with up to 1.42× end-to-end speedup in 8-GPU tensor-parallel inference.

papers.abstract: Query-conditioned sparse KV selection reduces long-context inference cost by attending to a subset of historical KV entries at each decoding step. Existing selectors must wait for the target-layer query before scoring candidates and generating indices, placing routing on the immediate pre-attention path. We introduce EarlySelectKV, a training-free transformation that uses proxy queries from earlier hidden states to precompute selected KV indices while retaining the real target-layer query for final attention. Tests with RocketKV, Quest, and Loki show no consistent pattern of quality degradation across the evaluated settings. In the primary RocketKV evaluation, ES-RocketKV differs by +0.018 points on LongBench, approximately -0.01 points on RULER, and +0.25 percentage points on representative NIAH/Passkey settings. In a TensorRT-LLM deployment with CPU-offloaded routing, ES-RocketKV improves end-to-end output throughput by up to 12.4% and reduces GPU-resident memory by 11.1% of the combined KV/K-summary pool. This makes routing timing an explicit optimization target alongside KV subset selection in sparse long-context decoding. Code is available at https://github.com/sea-with-sakura/EarlySelectKV.
bullets: Addresses routing latency caused by waiting for each target-layer query before selecting historical KV entries.
Uses a training-free transformation to anticipate selected KV indices from proxy queries in earlier hidden states.
Evaluated with RocketKV, Quest, and Loki, with no consistent quality degradation reported across tested settings.
In TensorRT-LLM with CPU-offloaded routing, improves output throughput by up to 12.4% and reduces combined KV/K-summary GPU memory by 11.1%.
Frames routing timing—not only KV subset selection—as an optimization target for sparse long-context inference.

papers.selection_reason: Novel anticipatory KV selection for sparse long-context decoding, directly relevant to inference efficiency.
papers.title: EarlySelectKV: Anticipatory KV Selection via Cross-Layer Query Proxies
papers.tldr: EarlySelectKV accelerates sparse long-context decoding by precomputing KV selections from earlier-layer query proxies while preserving the target-layer query for attention.

papers.abstract: Causal masking obstructs the column balancing used by optimal-transport (OT) attention. We study an unbalanced OT operator that uses only current and earlier rows and characterize its induced positional prior. For bounded scores and any fixed balancing strength below one, its fixed point assigns vanishing mass to every fixed window as context grows. With constant scores, the prior has an exact scale-invariant form. We classify positional encodings by whether they prevent this dilution. We also derive finite-length window-mass bounds for log-distance priors with exponents near one. Preregistered experiments use 25M- and 100M-parameter language models. The OT operator improves loss extrapolation over softmax, while exploratory comparisons favor an explicit distance bias at a fraction of the cost. Changing only the bias beyond the training length moves long-context loss in the predicted direction on all 30 tested checkpoints. During training, learned exponents approach one even when constrained above it. A margin chosen from prior calculations controls distant-mass growth in the tested setting.
bullets: Causal masking prevents standard OT column balancing, motivating an unbalanced OT operator over current and earlier rows.
For bounded scores and fixed balancing strength below one, mass in any fixed-size window vanishes as context length grows; constant scores yield an exact scale-invariant prior.
The work classifies positional encodings by whether they prevent this dilution and derives finite-length bounds for log-distance priors with exponents near one.
Experiments with 25M- and 100M-parameter language models show improved loss extrapolation over softmax, while explicit distance bias performs favorably at a fraction of the cost.
Modifying only the bias beyond the training length shifts long-context loss as predicted across 30 checkpoints; learned exponents approach one in training.

papers.selection_reason: Studies causal optimal-transport attention, positional priors, and length extrapolation for language models, directly relevant to long-context LLM research.
papers.title: Causal Optimal-Transport Attention: Positional Priors and Length Extrapolation
papers.tldr: Causal OT attention develops a scale-invariant positional prior that can dilute local attention over long contexts, but suitable distance-based biases can improve length extrapolation at lower cost.

papers.abstract: Language agents read code, tool output, and dialogue in contexts that grow at every step. Dynamic sparse attention lets a small indexer choose the earlier tokens each query attends to, but the indexer still scores the whole prefix at every layer. Cross-layer reuse methods such as IndexCache rerun the indexer at only some layers, with one fixed pattern for every input. In an agent, the relevant evidence can change abruptly when a traceback or test result arrives, so fresh selections matter more at some steps than at others. We propose Adaptive Index Reuse (AIR), which keeps IndexCache's execution and learns, for each segment of an agent episode, how many layers refresh their selection. A small controller reads signals from completed computation and the latest tool event, chooses a pattern from a nested library, and learns from terminal task reward under an expected compute budget. On Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 with a 128K context, AIR improves success over the strongest static schedule at matched cost on SWE-bench Verified (27.0% to 32.4%), Terminal-Bench 2.0, and three $τ^2$-bench domains, and it lowers time per successful task on all five. Across 50 backbone, context, and benchmark settings, it matches or exceeds that schedule in 44.
bullets: Long agent contexts make repeatedly scoring the full prefix expensive, while fixed cross-layer reuse schedules cannot react to new tool evidence.
AIR uses a small controller to select a nested index-refresh pattern for each episode segment based on prior computation and the latest tool event.
The controller learns from terminal task reward under an expected compute budget.
On Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 with 128K context, success rose from 27.0% to 32.4% on SWE-bench Verified at matched cost.
AIR matched or exceeded the strongest static schedule in 44 of 50 tested backbone, context, and benchmark settings, while reducing time per successful task across five benchmarks.

papers.title: When Should an Agent Refresh? Adaptive Index Reuse for Efficient Long-Horizon Reasoning
papers.tldr: Adaptive Index Reuse dynamically decides when to refresh attention indices, improving long-horizon agent success and efficiency at matched compute cost.

papers.abstract: Relative-position attention mechanisms offer compelling alternatives to RoPE across various transformer architectures, delivering superior performance in domains such as audio. These mechanisms typically modify attention scores by adding content-position or bias-position terms. Unlike RoPE, which encodes position via per-token rotations directly on the queries and keys, relative-position terms generally require pairwise offset-dependent computation or lookups, complicating their integration into fused attention kernels and introducing severe memory, bandwidth, and compute overheads as sequences scale. To address this bottleneck, we propose an exact attention algorithm that incorporates additive relative-position terms into FlashAttention-style tiled computation. Our method (1) uses offset-aware tiling to avoid redundant indexing and memory accesses, (2) computes only the necessary key/query-relation products and reuses them across token pairs in both forward and backward passes, and (3) uses offset-based gradient sharding and aggregation, eliminating atomic contention. We provide a unified, efficient Triton implementation across diverse relative-position attention mechanisms and evaluate it against naive and specialized implementations. For 8K-token sequences, our method speeds up the forward (backward) pass by 1.8-6.4$\times$ (2.0-21$\times$) and reduces peak memory up to 2.9-128$\times$ (1.4-54$\times$) over the strongest baseline for each mechanism, enabling long-context end-to-end transcription that is 1.8$\times$ faster and uses 2.4$\times$ less memory. Our method thus provides a drop-in, hardware-efficient solution for scaling relative-position attention transformers.
bullets: Addresses the pairwise offset computation and memory overhead that hinder efficient relative-position attention.
Introduces offset-aware tiled computation, reusable query/key relation products, and offset-based gradient aggregation without atomic contention.
Provides a unified Triton implementation supporting diverse relative-position attention mechanisms.
At 8K tokens, reports 1.8–6.4× faster forward passes, 2.0–21× faster backward passes, and up to 2.9–128× lower peak memory than the strongest mechanism-specific baselines.
Enables end-to-end long-context transcription that is 1.8× faster and uses 2.4× less memory.

papers.abstract: Continuous diffusion language models show promising potential in text generation tasks, but are prone to problems such as text repetition, semantic drift, and generation quality degradation when the generation length exceeds the training length. To address these challenges, we propose RangeSWA, a training-free length extrapolation method. The method combines local sliding-window attention, remote block summaries, and dynamic content retrieval to preserve local details and support long-range context access. In addition, generation degradation caused by length extrapolation is mitigated through positional remapping, conditioning attention correction, and denoising-stage-adaptive window scheduling. We conducted experiments on multiple continuous diffusion language models, and the results show that RangeSWA can effectively reduce generative perplexity and text repetition rates in long-text generation.
bullets: Addresses repetition, semantic drift, and quality degradation when generation exceeds the training length.
Uses local sliding-window attention, remote block summaries, and dynamic content retrieval to balance local detail with long-range context.
Applies positional remapping, conditioning-attention correction, and denoising-stage-adaptive window scheduling to mitigate extrapolation degradation.
Experiments across multiple continuous diffusion language models show reduced perplexity and text repetition in long-text generation.

papers.abstract: Agentic workflows are increasingly shifting towards long-horizon tasks, such as open-ended scientific work, where models benefit from long context windows. However, at ultra-long context (above 1M tokens), full attention is prohibitively expensive. A promising approach is sparse attention, in which a dedicated indexer selects a subset of keys for the attention. Yet current methods of indexing either still have quadratic cost in context size or lose accuracy at ultra-long context scale. We address this with Latent Sparse Attention (LSA), an efficient attention method that maintains accuracy at ultra-long context. In LSA, keys are hierarchically clustered in a learned latent space, and queries score the hierarchy of clusters instead of scoring every key, making prefill, decode and training faster at long context. We propose two variants, Distilled-LSA (D-LSA), which can be applied to pre-trained models via distillation, and Native-LSA (N-LSA), which is trained natively on the next-token loss alone. On GLM-5.3-FLASH (QWEN-3.8-27B) at 10M tokens, D-LSA speeds up one attention layer by 22.7x (72.4x) in prefill and 4.6x (42.5x) in decode over its original sparse attention (full attention), while keeping similar accuracy across a variety of tasks. N-LSA matches the accuracy of full attention with a training speedup of 1.6x per layer at 128k tokens. LSA offers practical and efficient attention for models to benefit from ultra-long context.
authors: Ales Kubicek, Andrea Caciolai, Liangzu Peng, Sukrit Sumant, Benjamin Hoover, Fraser Greenlee, Ruairidh M. Battleday, Radim Urban, Torsten Hoefler, James C. R. Whittington
bullets: Targets the prohibitive cost and accuracy degradation of existing sparse attention beyond 1M tokens.
Organizes keys into a learned latent hierarchy, allowing queries to score clusters rather than all keys.
Introduces Distilled-LSA for adapting pretrained models and Native-LSA for native next-token-loss training.
At 10M tokens, D-LSA substantially accelerates prefill and decode while maintaining similar accuracy across evaluated tasks.
N-LSA matches full-attention accuracy and provides per-layer training speedups at 128k tokens.

papers.selection_reason: Subquadratic sparse attention for ultra-long context via latent hierarchical key selection; directly fits efficient attention and long-context models.
papers.title: Latent Sparse Attention: Towards Subquadratic Ultra-Long Context Attention
papers.tldr: Latent Sparse Attention enables efficient ultra-long-context attention by hierarchically routing queries to learned key clusters instead of examining every key.

papers.abstract: The quadratic scaling of attention is a fundamental bottleneck limiting the long-context capabilities of large language models (LLMs). A variety of approaches have attempted to circumvent this, but they either fail to match attention's expressiveness (e.g., sliding-window or linear attention variants with fixed-size state) or only achieve constant-factor speedups (e.g., sparse attention methods whose indexers themselves scale quadratically). In this paper, we derive an asymptotically subquadratic sparse attention method based on a hierarchical, tree-structured indexer, which we call Zyphra Hierarchical Attention (ZHA). ZHA constructs a tree of recursively compressed key summaries over the KV cache, which future queries traverse from the top down to retrieve a sparse subset of keys. Crucially, by iteratively growing the tree's depth, the total cost including routing and final attention grows sublinearly in sequence length, resulting in overall subquadratic (but superlinear) scaling for attention. We demonstrate that ZHA can be cheaply applied to existing pretrained models with only a short KL distillation training stage over a few billion tokens, and maintains performance on long-context retrieval and challenging reasoning, mathematical, and agentic coding evaluation tasks. Moreover, we show that our method is highly robust to tree geometry including very deep trees of up to 6 levels. Finally, we develop a detailed performance model and show that our approach scales subquadratically, dramatically outperforms competing methods beyond 1 million context, and ultimately has the potential to extend effective context windows to the hundreds of millions or billions of tokens.
authors: Leon Lufkin, Cutter Dawes, Alexander Speicher, Kamesh Krishnamurthy, Tom\'as Figliolia, Beren Millidge
bullets: Addresses quadratic attention cost, which limits long-context scaling.
Builds a hierarchical tree of compressed key summaries that queries traverse to select sparse keys.
Joint routing and attention cost grows subquadratically—sublinear in sequence length for the relevant computation, but still superlinear overall.
Can be added to pretrained models using a short KL-distillation stage and maintains long-context retrieval, reasoning, math, and coding performance.
The authors report strong scaling beyond 1 million tokens and potential context windows of hundreds of millions to billions of tokens; performance depends on the method’s tree-based indexing scope.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of the ZHA architecture: (a) tree construction and (b) sparse routing. During tree construction, for each chunk of contiguous key nodes, we construct a compressed key node at the higher level by an attention-weighted sum of the keys, where the attention is computed with respect to the learned reference queries. In practice, we use multiple reference queries and store the key nodes for each in parallel. This process continues recursively with higher level key nodes being constructed from the summaries of lower levels. During routing, we start at the top of the tree and compute dot-product similarity scores between our query and the key nodes of that level. We select the set of nodes to expand using top-p, and then recursively descend the tree until we reach the leaf nodes corresponding to raw KV cache entries. The union of all the leaves we reach defines the sparse KV cache subset that we dispatch to the main attention.

Figure 8: For a fixed top-p, and hence sparsity level, ZHA (here, R = 1, C = 8, p = 0.75) scales subquadratically according to our decode roofline model, eventually dramatically outperforming both dense attention and the MSA sparse attention variant. Importantly, we have not empirically validated the scaling at these ultra-long context lengths due to the lack of existing LLMs which can operate at these contexts. Because of this, while we can obtain subquadratic latency, it is unclear to what extent reasoning and retrieval performance degrades at the level of depths required for these ultra-long contexts. Latencies are modeled per-token decode times for the attention subsystem of one layer at batch size 1.

papers.abstract: Linear attention scales linearly with sequence length, but its finite-state memory can limit long-context retrieval. In gated linear recurrences, memory retention depends on state decay, which is shaped jointly by gate parameters A_log and dt_bias and by input activations. In controlled Gated DeltaNet (GDN) experiments, both parameters remain highly correlated with their initial values after training, highlighting the importance of initialization. Therefore, we introduce Dual-Axis Memory Initialization (DAMI), which jointly configures these parameters before training. DAMI assigns geometric timescales across heads for varied retrieval distances and a low-high-low input-sensitivity profile across layers. A small activation sample calibrates the GDN-family implementation to match both behavioral targets without adding trainable parameters. Across GDN, KDA, GDN2, Mamba-2, and RWKV-7, DAMI improves average RULER-style retrieval accuracy by 5.29 to 16.71 percentage points over the corresponding random-initialization baselines. Performance on language modeling, commonsense reasoning, and 2K real-world retrieval remains broadly comparable to those baselines. Our code is available at https://speedai.com/research/dami.
authors: Zhangchi Feng, Harry Jiang, Yangyifei Luo, Ray Zhang, Richong Zhang
bullets: Finite-state memory and initialization can limit long-context retrieval in linear attention.
DAMI jointly configures gate parameters before training using geometric head-wise timescales and a low-high-low layer-wise sensitivity profile.
A small activation sample calibrates the implementation to these targets without adding trainable parameters.
Across five gated linear-attention families, DAMI raises average RULER-style retrieval accuracy by 5.29–16.71 percentage points over random initialization.
Language modeling, commonsense reasoning, and 2K real-world retrieval performance remains broadly comparable to baseline initialization.

papers.abstract: Long-context diffusion repeatedly pays for both token interaction and feed-forward computation. We formulate these costs as two separate budgets: the edges available to an attention graph and the experts activated for each token. This view connects local, dilated, and global attention with conditional expert computation without assuming that sparsity alone preserves document-level information. We specify normalized masked attention, distinguish denoising depth from sampling iterations, and derive graph and compute bounds. A reported sparse-expert configuration, denoted DualBudget, is analyzed across scientific summarization, multi-hop question answering, dialogue, and sentence-pair prediction. All supplied table measurements are retained. The length study shows gains over the listed baselines through 16K, together with measurable degradation as length increases. Ablations reveal mixed changes across the three reported scores, while the cost record indicates a 20% reduction relative to DiffuSeq under an unspecified timing convention. The analysis separates these observations from unmeasured claims about training speed, absorbing states, global coherence, and deployment memory.
authors: Alexandros Christoforos, Chadbourne Davis, Paul Raj
bullets: Models long-context diffusion costs using two budgets: attention-graph edges and activated feed-forward experts.
Unifies local, dilated, and global attention with conditional expert computation without assuming sparsity preserves document-level information.
Defines normalized masked attention, distinguishes denoising depth from sampling iterations, and derives graph and compute bounds.
Evaluates the DualBudget configuration on scientific summarization, multi-hop QA, dialogue, and sentence-pair prediction.
Results show gains over listed baselines through 16K, mixed ablation effects, and measurable degradation as sequence length grows.

papers.abstract: Gated Delta Networks (GDNs) offer linear-time sequence modeling, yet long-context prefill remains costly due to dense intra-chunk computation, recurrent-state updates, and intermediate state storage. We introduce SparseGDN, a hardware-aware framework that combines structured intra-chunk approximation with input-dependent recurrent-event selection while producing outputs for every token. A block-adjacent solver reduces local Delta-solve computation, while a dynamic selector allocates recurrent-update budgets across head pairs. The GPU implementation materializes updates only for selected events and reconstructs token outputs using compact state snapshots and group-local interactions, reducing computation and memory traffic. We evaluate SparseGDN on Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-9B across RULER tasks and context lengths from 4K to 128K. Retaining approximately 29% of recurrent events on average, SparseGDN achieves 1.50-1.94x GDN-core prefill speedups over native FLA kernels, including online selection overhead.
authors: Jiedong Zhuang, Peng Zhao, Jialin Tang, Haoji Hu
bullets: Targets the high cost of dense intra-chunk computation, recurrent-state updates, and intermediate storage in long-context GDN prefill.
Uses a block-adjacent solver for approximate local Delta computation and an input-dependent selector for recurrent-event allocation across head pairs.
Materializes only selected updates and reconstructs token outputs from compact state snapshots and group-local interactions.
On Qwen3.5-4B/9B across RULER and 4K–128K contexts, retaining about 29% of recurrent events yields 1.50–1.94× GDN-core prefill speedups over native FLA kernels, including selection overhead.

figures.caption: Figure 3 End-to-end SparseGDN execution pipeline. The block-adjacent intra-chunk kernel computes transformed values U, compact update coefficients, and selector scores. The dynamic selector converts these scores into a structured event mask. Only selected events trigger deferred W materialization and recurrent-state updates, producing compact event states. During output reconstruction, the mapped output kernel retrieves the appropriate preceding event state from HBM and applies the accumulated gap decay, while computing group-local interactions and producing outputs for every token.

papers.abstract: Why does length generalization (LG) depend so sharply on the positional encoding (PE)? Relative schemes extrapolate fixed offsets, absolute schemes fix positions, and neither handles growing offsets. We give a realizability theory for a deliberately controlled abstraction, a single positional-only attention head, that derives this well-documented empirical pattern and says precisely where it holds and breaks. The device is a simulation transfer operator $T_L$ that re-evaluates a selected length-$L_0$-realizing positional kernel on the longer grid, with a scalar $\alpha_L \in [0,1]$ read off before any training from $(\Phi, t_n)$ alone. Here $\alpha_L$ serves as the computable witness of that taxonomy's derivation, not as a stronger empirical predictor. Our results are a relative-head deep-row characterization for kernels with a strict unique global maximizer (Theorem 2), an absolute/relative duality that derives the pattern (Proposition 4), a learned-absolute underdetermination result, and a static expressivity bound; a sufficiency theorem (Theorem 1) bridges $\alpha_L$ to LG, and the general deterministic case is a precise open conjecture (correcting a tempting but invalid "outside-colspan" argument). Experiments confirm the structure: in the controlled single-head regime $\alpha_L$ exactly separates the taxonomy's generalizing and non-generalizing (PE, task) cells (2625 trained-model measurements; stable at vocab 64/d=128). Together, these results turn the received PE taxonomy into a positional-kernel transfer theorem, and identify the content and depth mechanisms that escape it. The theory concerns the positional channel alone: tasks whose targets depend on token content, including the standard length-generalization suite such as addition and sorting, fall outside Theorem 2.
authors: Jiasong Han, Yunkai Chai, Jintao Wang
bullets: Defines a transfer operator that reevaluates a length-$L_0$ positional kernel on longer grids and computes a pre-training witness $\alpha_L$.
Characterizes relative-head generalization for kernels with a strict unique global maximizer and establishes an absolute/relative duality.
Shows that learned-absolute schemes are underdetermined and derives a static expressivity bound.
Experiments on 2,625 controlled trained-model measurements show $\alpha_L$ exactly separates the studied generalizing and non-generalizing positional-encoding/task cells.
The theory does not cover content-dependent tasks such as addition or sorting; the general deterministic case remains an open conjecture.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the method. Select (fit) a single positional head’s kernel at length L0 realizing the task’s target pattern RL0 ; transfer the same kernel to a longer grid via TL (re-evaluate ΦLWΦ⊤ L , no retraining); old rows keep their argmax by the causal-mask identity (Thm 1); score the new rows [L0, L) to read off αL ∈ [0, 1]. The whole pipeline uses only (Φ, tn), with no Transformer training, no data samples, and no learned Transformer parameters (only a deterministic kernel-selection on the PE basis).

Figure 2: The offset taxonomy, derived (Theorem 2, Prop. 4). A relative kernel length-generalizes a fixed relative offset; a clamped learned-absolute encoding does the reverse; and neither handles a growing offset (the shared blind spot, right column). Throughout, the relative statements are for kernels with a strict unique global maximizer, the hypothesis of Theorem 2; the accompanying text explains why it is needed and what the L0-fit contributes. This 2 × 3 verdict is exactly the empirical PE taxonomy, here a consequence of what a single positional head can realize.
Figure 4: Empirical LG (solid) and training-free αL (dashed) vs. test length L (train L0=20), 1L1H. αL tracks both who generalizes and how LG decays with L.

Figure 5: Training-free α60 (left) and empirical LG@60 (right) over (PE, task), 1L1H. Agreement is strong in this single-head regime; the content-driven disagreements (which emerge at depth, not shown here) are characterized in §7.

Figure 3: Training-free αL vs. empirical LG across the three tiers (5 seeds). Left (1L1H, the setting the theory describes): learnable cells (blue) give Spearman ρ=0.90. Center, right (scale, 2L4H, 4L4H): the graded rank correlation weakens (its bootstrap CI includes 0) as the content channel rescues low-αL cells, yet high αL remains a sufficient screen at every depth (precision ≥ 0.92).

Figure 6: H3: learnable-cell Spearman ρ(αL, LG) (circles) drops with depth (its bootstrap CI includes 0 at depths 2, 4), while sufficiency precision (squares) stays ≥ 0.92 with tight CIs. αL remains a sufficient screen at all depths.

Table 1: Positioning against the closest LG frameworks. αL’s niche: pre-training, keyed to the PE’s feature map, continuous, single-head, with matched sufficiency and relative-head necessity (the general necessary condition is conjectural).

Table 3: Training-free αL (at L=60) vs. empirical LG accuracy (mean over 5 seeds), 1-layer 1-head and scale (2L4H) tiers. Top: αL tracks 1L1H LG. Bottom: at scale, the content/recency channel (outside the positional-only abstraction, S3) lets ALiBi/NoPE generalize where αL=0, making the predictor’s onesidedness visible.

Table 10: RoPE frequency sweep on content-neutral skip-3 (1L1H). No discriminating cell: where the model generalizes the taxonomy is right; at scale 0.03 αL under-predicts (false negative); at 0.01 the model cannot learn at all.
Table 2: The evaluation grid. Each axis follows the theory’s categories or standard practice; the reason given for each level is the reason it was included.

Table 6: Interior fixed-absolute positions (1L1H, mean over 5 seeds). Absolute encodings realize and transfer them; relative encodings do not learn them at all. Compare first, where RoPE scores α60 = 0.20 purely because position 0 is the causal boundary.

Table 8: L0-sensitivity (1L1H, predictor αL / empirical LG at L=3L0). The screen AUC is 1.0 at every training length and the per-cell verdicts are stable; the separation is not an artifact of L0=20. Generated by experiments/l0_sensitivity.py.

Table 7: Scale robustness: cell-level Spearman ρ(αL, LG) on learnable cells, at the paper’s default size vs. a larger model. The predictor is identical; only the trained models change. The scale study uses 2 seeds (700 rows), and both columns are computed on the cells the two studies have in common, so the 2L4H entry (0.36) is over 19 cells rather than the 20 of Table 4, where the same quantity over all 20 cells is 0.31.

Table 9: Content-driven induction (target = token after the previous occurrence of xi): positional αL = 0 for all PEs, yet 2-layer models generalize (LG up to 0.84). α+ L flags the realizable through the content channel regime αL misses; residual PE-modulation of content LG is future work.

Table 12: αL for sinusoidal under the same sweep. The absolute verdict is invariant (first≈1 everywhere; growing offsets ≈0). The bounded-offset cells (prev/skip3) are the only entries whose verdict moves with frequency – they degrade as frequencies are added (num:8→32 drives prev 0.47→0.00); the other cells’ raw αL shifts stay sub-threshold (e.g. first 0.93→1.00) and never flip the verdict. This is what the theory predicts: enlarging the realizable space does not help the L0-fit select a transferring kernel (existence ̸= selection, Prop. 3). papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) draw on parametric knowledge and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to solve knowledge-intensive tasks. Yet problem solving in unfamiliar domains calls for tightly coupled knowledge acquisition and reasoning, beyond factual retrieval and aggregation or learning solely from a preassembled context. We study self-learning -- autonomously retrieving, studying, and applying knowledge from long-form reference materials on the fly. To investigate this capability, we formulate a textbook-based mathematical problem-solving task. LLMs must navigate textbook exposition, learn and apply relevant principles, and construct proofs for exercises, with reference solutions withheld. We introduce a BookNavigator interface to support this human-inspired study process and incentivize self-learning through reinforcement learning (RL) with fine-grained rewards. Experiments show that our method improves performance across in-domain and out-of-domain textbooks and subjects, raising Intern-S2-Preview-35B's overall proof accuracy from 51.5% to 79.5% and outperforming RL-trained textbook-free and fixed-retrieval baselines. These gains extend to complex long-context benchmarks involving different task types, with improvements over the base model of 1.7 and 2.3 percentage points on BrowseComp-Plus and CL-bench, respectively. Together, these findings suggest that RL can foster a domain-agnostic self-learning strategy, highlighting the potential of self-learning from long-form corpora to strengthen broader problem-solving capabilities on complex, long-context tasks.

papers.abstract: We introduce Nemotron 3.5 Super and Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, open and efficient Mixture-of-Experts Hybrid Mamba-Transformer models designed for reasoning, long-context understanding, and agentic workloads. Super is a 120B-parameter, 12B-active multimodal model, while Lightning is a smaller 30B-parameter, 3B-active text model; both designed for efficient deployment. Both models combine large-scale distillation, long-context training, and native speculative decoding, while Super further incorporates Indic continued pretraining and agentic software-engineering mid-training. We develop a comprehensive post-training pipeline spanning supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning (RLVR and RLHF), complemented in Super by specialized teacher training and multi- teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD). This transforms Super from a text-only base model into a multimodal agent capable of reasoning over text, images, video, and interactive tool environments. We further explore test-time scaling through parallel agent execution and self-verification. Across training and deployment, we jointly optimize capability and efficiency. Indic continued pretraining improves Indian-language benchmarks by up to 9.82 percentage points, while agentic mid-training strengthens software-engineering capabilities and robustness across agent harnesses. The post-trained Super model achieves 51.78% on SWE-bench Pro, surpassing Nemotron 3 Ultra despite using approximately 4.6x fewer active parameters. Post-training MTP boosting improves speculative- decoding acceptance length by up to 21.8% under probabilistic draft sampling, while NVFP4 quantization achieves 99.62% median accuracy recovery relative to BF16. Inference optimizations enable up to 4,856 output tokens/s/GPU on GB200 while sustaining at least 50 tokens/s/user.

papers.abstract: Self-attention plays a key role in long-sequence modeling, but its quadratic time complexity fundamentally limits the scaling of Large Language Models. Recently, Multi-State Linear Attention (MSLA) mechanisms have been proposed to make sequence modeling more efficient by splitting the context into segments and compressing each in its own memory state. MSLA aggregates the information extracted from each memory state using only the mean alignment between a query and each segment's keys, ignoring how the alignment is distributed within the segment. In order to model the relevance of a segment to a query more comprehensively and incorporate the variance of the alignment in the aggregation, we propose MERLIN (MomEnt Routing for multi-state LINear attention), a method that tracks the first and second moments of each segment's keys. Using the moments of keys, a query can recover both the mean and the variance of its alignment with each segment to perform a more content-aware aggregation of per-state readouts. Experiments on multi-state variants of Gated DeltaNet-1.3B and Mamba-2-780M show that MERLIN consistently outperforms existing aggregation methods on various long-context tasks. In particular, MERLIN outperforms baselines on RULER needle-in-a-haystack and long-context QA (+8.3% for Gated DeltaNet-1.3B and +7.0% for Mamba-2-780M) and diverse subtasks in LongBench (+13.5% and +12.0%). It even outperforms baselines that consume 4x more memory. MERLIN provides a simple and general routing mechanism for improving long-context capabilities of MSLA models.
authors: Hee Seung Hwang, Sanghyuk Chun, Xindi Wu, Olga Russakovsky, Zhiwei Deng
bullets: MSLA reduces the cost of long-sequence modeling by compressing context segments into separate memory states, but standard routing uses only mean query–key alignment.
MERLIN tracks each segment’s first and second key moments to estimate both mean and variance of query alignment.
This enables more comprehensive, content-aware aggregation of per-state readouts.
On RULER, long-context QA, and LongBench, MERLIN consistently outperforms existing routing methods, including baselines using 4× more memory.
Reported gains include up to 8.3% on RULER/QA and 13.5% on LongBench for the evaluated models.

figures.caption: Figure 1: (a) A multi-state linear attention (MSLA) model aggregates segment-level outputs via a weighted sum. Prior methods compute the weights λt,i from position or from the mean of each segment’s keys. MERLIN instead reads both the first and second moments of the keys. (b) On retrieval-augmented generation samples in HELMET (Yen et al., 2025), we measure the aggregation weight each method places on the ground truth (GT) segment at the query token. Position-based aggregation largely misses the GT and mean-based aggregation recovers more, while MERLIN places the most weight on it.

Figure 2: MERLIN Overview. The context is split into segments Ci (middle row). Each segment stores a memory state (top row) and the first and second moments of its keys (bottom row). At position t, the query qt reads segment-level outputs from memory states (step 1). The query computes the mean and variance of the key-query alignment from the moments (step 2). The final output is a weighted sum of segment-level outputs, where the weights are derived from a gated mix of the alignment mean and variance (step 3).

papers.abstract: Self-attention mechanisms have established the Transformer as the dominant backbone across natural language processing, source code intelligence, and automated theorem proving. However, all-to-all pairwise token comparison enforces a quadratic $\mathcal{O}(N^2)$ compute and memory barrier alongside severe softmax attention dilution as sequence length $N$ scales beyond the training horizon. Inspired by recent advances in algebraic graph learning (\textbf{WPNet}), this work introduces \textbf{GTFormer}, a syntax-free hierarchical Graph Neural Network (GNN) that replaces flat self-attention for general long-context sequence modeling. GTFormer organizes raw token streams into a bounded-degree hierarchy combining a balanced binary reduction tree ($\lceil \log_2 N \rceil$ depth), horizontal boundary-bridging shift edges, random expander shortcuts, multi-channel convex highway gating, and a top-down broadcast pass. Across eight long-context code, log, and multi-hop retrieval benchmarks trained exclusively on sequences of length $N \le 512$, GTFormer extrapolates zero-shot to $N = 4{,}194{,}304$ ($8192\times$) on a single commodity GPU in linear $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, maintaining near-perfect accuracy where standard and RoPE Transformers suffer from out-of-distribution attention collapse and out-of-memory exhaustion.
bullets: Targets quadratic compute and memory costs, plus attention dilution, in very long sequences.
Uses a bounded-degree hierarchy with binary reduction, boundary-bridging edges, expander shortcuts, convex highway gates, and top-down broadcasting.
Trained only on sequences of length ≤512 and evaluated zero-shot at lengths up to 4,194,304 tokens.
Across eight code, log, and multi-hop retrieval benchmarks, it reportedly maintains near-perfect accuracy on a commodity GPU.
The abstract reports scope limited to the benchmarked long-context tasks and extrapolation setting.

Bottom-up tree edges Etree and horizontal expander shortcuts Eexp compress sequence state in log2 N steps, while top-down broadcast edges Edown resolve remote pointer queries (PTR).

(b) Flat Transformer: All-to-all O(N2) self-attention connects every filler token to every other token, causing severe softmax attention dilution on out-of-distribution lengths and quadratic VRAM exhaustion.

papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models exhibit an astonishing capacity to generalize to longer and more difficult problem instances than those seen in training. However, theoretical understanding of this phenomenon still lags behind. Unlike most machine learning models, the generalisation abilities of transformers inherently require considering two axes. On one hand, one must examine in-distribution statistical generalisation, which concerns the ability of a model to broaden a function from training samples to novel samples of the same distribution. On the other hand, given the sequential nature of language data, one must also consider length generalisation, which reflects whether a model trained on inputs of a given length can extrapolate to longer ones.These two notions have mostly been studied separately, leaving open how they interact. In this work, we give a joint treatment of both axes for fixed-precision transformers. We give generalisation guarantees in terms of the parameter sizes of the involved models, as well as the quantization space and the alphabet size that supply the sequences. Finally, we illustrate how the requirements in the sample count and training length trade off. In particular, we find that increasing training length can be exponentially more efficient than increasing the sample size. Experiments support predictions of the theory.
authors: Marius Henry, Michael Rizvi-Martel, Michael Hahn
bullets: Addresses the interaction between in-distribution generalization and extrapolation to longer sequences.
Derives guarantees based on model parameter sizes, quantization space, and sequence alphabet size.
Characterizes the trade-off between the number of training samples and their lengths.
Shows theoretically that increasing training length can be exponentially more efficient than increasing sample count.
Experiments support the theory’s predictions.

papers.title: Quantitative Generalization Bounds for Multi-Layer Transformers: A Few Long Strings can Beat Many Short Ones
papers.tldr: The paper develops joint theoretical generalization bounds for fixed-precision, multi-layer transformers across both sample distribution and sequence length, showing that longer training strings can be far more valuable than more samples.

papers.abstract: Long-sequence models must retain earlier information. Full attention keeps all past tokens but grows expensive, and recurrent-memory models compress history into fixed slots for linear-time processing. Limited capacity makes writes consequential: distractors can interfere with useful content, while skipped evidence cannot be recalled. Existing multi-slot memories write every token to the same number of slots, merging whether to store it with how many slots to update. We introduce Factorized Write Routing (FWR), which first keeps or skips each token and then chooses a fixed or token-adaptive number of slots. Queries still read all slots. Across ten seeds on two synthetic tasks that query facts after long contexts, we observe a density-dependent reversal. With four slots per write, long-context accuracy favors always writing on dense Feature Recall (0.472 vs 0.337), but learned selective writing on sparse-fact Passkey (0.222 vs 0.048). The tested adaptive rule underperforms fixed allocation under the learned gate on both tasks. A diagnostic oracle given fact labels unavailable at deployment reaches 0.372 on Passkey, showing headroom in filtering distractors. The results suggest avoiding missed writes in information-dense contexts and filtering distractors when they dominate.
bullets: Recurrent memories compress long histories into fixed slots, making write decisions critical: distractors cause interference and skipped evidence is unrecoverable.
Factorized Write Routing (FWR) first decides whether to keep or skip each token, then selects a fixed or token-adaptive number of slots to update.
Across two synthetic long-context tasks and ten seeds, always writing outperformed selective writing on dense Feature Recall (0.472 vs. 0.337).
Selective writing outperformed always writing on sparse-fact Passkey (0.222 vs. 0.048).
The tested adaptive slot-allocation rule underperformed fixed allocation, while an oracle fact filter showed remaining headroom on Passkey.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Comparison of context storage and retrieval mechanisms between existing methods and ours. Standard attention retains token-level keys and values and allows the query to attend directly to all preceding tokens, whereas Linear attention compresses the context into a shared recurrent state to alleviate the huge KV cache memory. RAVEN maintains M recurrent slots but routes every token to a fixed number K of slots. Our Factorized Write Routing (FWR) first uses a token-level gate zt to decide whether to write, and then allocates the retained token to a token-adaptive number Kt of slots. Both RAVEN and FWR read densely over all M slots, they differ in their write policies. The labels fi and di illustrate tokens that are relevant and irrelevant, respectively, to the future query q; these relevance labels are unavailable to the learned gate at inference time.

Figure 2: FWR separates token selection from slot allocation. A skipped token changes no slot; a kept token updates either a fixed or token-adaptive number of slots. Reading remains dense, so a query need not predict the write-time slot identity.

papers.abstract: Long-context language models can increasingly process entire documents, making full-context prompting a practical alternative to passage retrieval. However, greater capacity determines how much information a model can receive, but not which information best supports a query. This distinction motivates rethinking retrieval: when the full document already fits, can selecting and organizing its evidence improve answering? The challenge is to retain supporting facts and relations while keeping the context focused on the question. To reconcile these goals, we introduce \ours, a training-free framework that uses semantic abstraction to guide selection while retaining original text for answering. \ours constructs a reusable semantic hierarchy from the full document in a single generation, linking node descriptions to source spans. Given a query, structural--semantic scoring and fine-grained lexical attribution nominate shared source nodes; their union with ancestor context preserves structural relations and complete local text. Across four frontier answer models, \ours improves average QA-F1 by 1.72 points over full-context prompting on three LongBench tasks, surpassing the evaluated baselines on the four-model average while reducing answer-context length by 58.55\%. Our code is available at the $\href{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/treefuse-ECFE}{repository}$.
authors: Zhe Xu, Tianhao Liao, Zhenqing Ling, Ying Shen, Yaliang Li, Daoyuan Chen
bullets: Addresses the limitation that long-context models can fit entire documents but still need help identifying query-relevant information.
Builds a reusable semantic hierarchy once, linking abstract node descriptions to original source spans.
Uses structural-semantic scoring and fine-grained lexical attribution to select evidence while preserving ancestor context and local text.
Across four answer models and three LongBench tasks, improves average QA-F1 by 1.72 points over full-context prompting.
Reduces answer-context length by 58.55% and surpasses evaluated baselines on the four-model average.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of TreeFuse. (a) A single generation constructs a semantic hierarchy whose nodes are aligned to original source spans. Figure 3: Three paradigms for constructing an answer context. Flat methods organize text as independent units and retrieve, prune, or rewrite them; prior hierarchical methods build methoddependent trees and retrieve, expand, merge, or refine tree regions; TreeFuse constructs a reusable source-grounded semantic hierarchy from the full document, prunes it to an ancestor-closed retained subtree for each query, and serializes the complete local source spans while preserving the original parent–child relations and sibling order.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a training-free framework using semantic trees to guide adaptive context construction, improving long-context QA performance.
papers.title: Rethinking Retrieval in the Long-Context Era: Training-Free Semantic Trees for Adaptive Context Construction
papers.tldr: A training-free semantic-tree framework selects and organizes the most relevant evidence from full documents, improving long-context QA while substantially shortening answer contexts.

papers.abstract: We present HyScale, a long-context training system for learned sparse attention. Learned sparse attention is a promising architecture for million-token contexts, widely adopted in production since DeepSeek-V3.2. Selection, however, grows into the training bottleneck. For each query, it scores every previous token whereas sparse attention reads only $k$; worse, current systems materialize a full score table and repeat selection during recomputation. Our key insight is that the output of selection is not an activation, but rather a set of indices. Building on it, HyScale introduces HyTopK and selection replay. HyTopK finds each query's exact top-$k$ on the fly without a score table, while selection replay reuses forward-pass selection in recomputation. Together with holistic system optimizations tackling end-to-end training challenges, HyScale speeds up GLM-5.1 training on 1M-token sequences by 2.07$\times$ over Megatron-LM on 512 H20 GPUs. It also speeds up the CSA layers of DeepSeek-V4-Flash and the QSA layers of Qwen3.8-Flash-Next by 2.01$\times$ and 1.57$\times$ at 1M tokens on 32 H800 GPUs.
authors: Yangshen Deng, Xinjing Huang, Yulong Wang, Yunzhuo Liu, Jun Hu, Shuyong Tan, Chun-Chih Tseng, Mingji Han, Ray Ying, Key Zhang, Luo Mai
bullets: Learned sparse attention makes selection a training bottleneck because each query scores all prior tokens, despite reading only top-k tokens.
HyTopK computes exact top-k indices on the fly without materializing a full score table.
Selection replay reuses forward-pass selection during recomputation, reducing redundant work.
Combined with end-to-end system optimizations, HyScale achieves reported speedups of 2.07×, 2.01×, and 1.57× on 1M-token training workloads.
The evaluation covers GLM-5.1, DeepSeek-V4-Flash CSA layers, and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next QSA layers on H20 and H800 GPUs.

papers.selection_reason: System for scaling learned sparse attention training directly targets efficient attention and long-context models.
papers.title: HyScale: Scaling Long-Context Training for Learned Sparse Attention
papers.tldr: HyScale accelerates million-token training for learned sparse attention by avoiding full score tables and replaying selection during recomputation.

papers.abstract: Full-duplex speech models can listen and speak at the same time, enabling natural, low-latency interaction. In counseling, however, these models often focus on the latest utterance and lose track of the seeker's underlying problem. We call this failure Stressor Blindness. We propose CounselPlex, a stressor-aware full-duplex framework that uses two operations. CounselPlex updates a short stressor state during seeker silence and injects this state into positions while listening. We also introduce RoPE Position Shift Augmentation (RPSA), which broadens positional coverage during training and improves performance at longer turn depths in our evaluation. LLM-judge evaluations show improved counseling quality and stressor grounding over strong baselines.
authors: Yeonju Kim, Bella Godiva, Yong Man Ro
bullets: Addresses “Stressor Blindness,” where models overfocus on the latest utterance and lose the underlying problem.
Updates a short stressor state during seeker silence and injects it while listening.
Uses RoPE Position Shift Augmentation to broaden positional coverage for deeper conversation turns.
LLM-judge evaluations report better counseling quality and stressor grounding than strong baselines.
The evaluation focuses on counseling quality and stressor grounding, with no quantitative results specified.
papers.selection_reason: Stressor state as persistent dialogue memory and RoPE position augmentation for long turn depth are transferable to LLM memory and long-context methods.
papers.title: CounselPlex: A Stressor-Aware Full-Duplex Counseling Model
papers.tldr: CounselPlex improves full-duplex counseling by maintaining and injecting an evolving representation of the seeker’s underlying stressor.

papers.abstract: Multi-head attention retrieves and combines context representations through query--key interactions and value aggregation, with head dimension constraining the per-head representation space. In long-context processing, it remains unclear whether allocating a fixed parameter budget to fewer, wider heads improves information retrieval. In this paper, we investigate how head dimension affects the performance of long-context retrieval tasks. Our empirical studies reveal that pretraining loss and short-context non-retrieval task performance are not affected much by head dimension, while long-context retrieval performance improves with wider heads at fixed model sizes. We find that models with wider heads have a higher proportion of retrieval heads, associating more parameters with retrieval. Our ablation studies also show that the retrieval performance improves with wider heads even when the projection weights in attention modules are frozen during long-context continual pretraining, suggesting that wider heads not only benefit updates in attention modules but lead to more effective adaptation of components such as embeddings and MLPs.
authors: Seiya Tokui, Shoichiro Yamaguchi, Sosuke Kobayashi
bullets: The study examines whether fewer, wider heads better support retrieval under a fixed parameter budget.
Pretraining loss and short-context, non-retrieval performance change little with head dimension.
Long-context retrieval improves as head dimension increases.
Wider-head models contain a higher proportion of retrieval heads, allocating more capacity to retrieval.
Improvements persist with frozen attention projection weights, indicating benefits beyond attention-module updates.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates head dimension effects on long-context retrieval in language models; directly relevant to LLM architecture and long-context methods.
papers.title: Head Dimension Matters in Language Models for Long-Context Retrieval
papers.tldr: Wider attention heads improve long-context retrieval at fixed model size, even when attention projections are frozen during continual pretraining.

papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) process increasingly long sequences, attention becomes a major computational bottleneck. Sparse attention mostly targets inference, yet many methods still train densely or cannot support sparse training, and their added complexity makes sparsity hard to turn into wall-clock speedups, leaving dense attention widely used in practice. This paper introduces LazyFlash, a forward-dense, backward-sparse attention method built on the observation that attention training is dominated by the backward pass. LazyFlash keeps the forward pass exactly dense, so the trained model remains a standard dense model that existing systems such as vLLM can serve without any change. For the backward pass, LazyFlash proposes a gradient-aware block sparsification design that ranks query blocks by their attention-output gradient norms and skips those contributing negligibly to parameter updates, turning the dense backward into a block-sparse one. A gradient-mass budget adapts the amount of skipped computation to each head and training step, while importance sampling preserves the dense gradient in expectation. These designs are implemented inside the tiled FlashAttention backward kernel, where skipped blocks are never loaded or computed, translating gradient sparsity into real wall-clock acceleration. Experiments on long-context text and speech LLMs show that LazyFlash maintains downstream performance while achieving up to 5.7x attention-backward speedup over FlashAttention and 1.7x end-to-end training speedup.
authors: Keqi Deng, Ruchao Fan, Jinyu Li
bullets: Addresses the training-time bottleneck of dense attention, which limits practical speedups from sparse methods.
Uses gradient-aware block sparsification to rank query blocks by attention-output gradient norms and skip negligible updates.
Adapts sparsity with a per-head, per-step gradient-mass budget while importance sampling preserves dense gradients in expectation.
Integrates skipping into the tiled FlashAttention backward kernel, avoiding loads and computation for skipped blocks.
Maintains downstream performance while delivering up to 5.7× attention-backward and 1.7× end-to-end training speedups.
papers.selection_reason: Backward-sparse attention accelerates long-context LLM fine-tuning, directly fitting efficient attention and long-context methods.
papers.title: LazyFlash: Forward-Dense, Backward-Sparse Attention for Accelerated Long-Context Fine-Tuning
papers.tldr: LazyFlash accelerates long-context fine-tuning by keeping attention dense in the forward pass while skipping low-impact blocks during the backward pass.

papers.abstract: Deepresearch (DR) agents interact with real-world web environments through multi-turn search and visit, causing their contexts to grow rapidly over time. We observe that, even after DR Agentic Reinforcement Learning (DR-RL), 61.6% of the model's remaining prediction errors can still be attributed to insufficient long-context understanding, including longcontext hallucination and failures in cross-document evidence integration. It motivates us to further break the bottleneck of DR-RL by strengthening the model's long-context ability.
