However, effective LongContext training requires more than simply increasing context length. To bridge the data gap, we propose `DR Rollouts to LongContext-QA (DR-to-Long)'. The method repurposes DR-RL trajectories, which naturally contain search histories, visited webpages, evidence snippets, and final-answer supervision. It then replaces the compact snippets and webpage summaries in each trajectory with the full contents of their corresponding URLs, producing substantially longer multi-document contexts while preserving the original evidence relationships. Building on DR-to-Long, we introduce DLD (DR -> LongQA -> DR)-RL. DLD-RL first performs a short DR-RL stage to collect rollout trajectories, which are then converted into LongQA instances at zero annotation cost. The model is subsequently optimized with LongQA-RL to strengthen LongContext ability, followed by full DR-RL to continue improving its DR capability. Experiments show that DLD-RL outperforms standard DR-RL by 7.3% on three Deepresearch benchmarks and improves performance by 13.5% on three long-context benchmarks.
bullets: Deep-research agents still face substantial errors from long-context failures, including hallucination and poor cross-document evidence integration.
DR-to-Long expands existing DR-RL trajectories by replacing snippets and webpage summaries with the full contents of their source URLs.
DLD-RL alternates short DR-RL, zero-cost conversion to LongQA, LongQA-RL, and subsequent DR-RL.
The method improves over standard DR-RL by 7.3% across three Deepresearch benchmarks and 13.5% across three long-context benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Focuses on improving LLM long-context understanding using DR rollouts converted into LongQA data plus reinforcement learning.
papers.title: Boosting Deepresearch and LongContext Ability with Self-Generated Deepresearch Rollouts Traces
papers.tldr: DLD-RL strengthens deep-research agents’ long-context understanding by converting self-generated research trajectories into full-context QA training data, improving both research and long-context performance.

papers.abstract: Large language models can repeat an instruction while failing to keep obeying it. We study this recall-compliance dissociation in long-horizon dialogue and define State Integrity Collapse: a model preserves a stated constraint in memory but stops applying it to later turns. We introduce StateTrack-Bench, a controlled suite of conversations covering numerical, format, role/persona, factual-memory, and logical-rule constraints. Across seven provider-pinned model snapshots and five dialogue-depth probes, strict joint retention ranges from 62.4% to 100.0%, with degradation concentrated in symbolic constraints and in one especially brittle model. A forked recall audit shows that 88.6% of observed failures are behavioral-drift failures rather than ordinary forgetting; excluding the brittle outlier preserves this diagnosis (84.4% of failures). Extended evaluations at depths up to 50 turns confirm that the dissociation persists beyond the core benchmark, while Structured State Anchoring recovers up to 24.4 points on immutable constraints. The results show that reliability cannot be inferred from single-turn instruction following alone; evaluation must track whether remembered constraints remain operational as dialogue state grows. Code and artifacts are available at: https://github.com/xzzvsxd/StateTrack.
bullets: The paper defines State Integrity Collapse: recall of a stated constraint remains intact while later behavior violates it.
StateTrack-Bench evaluates numerical, format, role/persona, factual-memory, and logical-rule constraints across dialogue depths and seven model snapshots.
Strict joint retention ranges from 62.4% to 100.0%, with failures concentrated in symbolic constraints and one particularly brittle model.
A forked recall audit attributes most failures to behavioral drift rather than ordinary forgetting; the effect persists through 50-turn dialogues.
Structured State Anchoring improves retention of immutable constraints by up to 24.4 points, though long-horizon reliability remains a concern.
papers.selection_reason: Characterizes LLM constraint retention failures in long-horizon dialogues; relevant to long-context reliability and memory.
papers.title: When LLMs Forget What They Believe: Characterizing State Integrity Collapse in Long-Horizon Dialogues
papers.tldr: Long-horizon dialogue can cause LLMs to remember constraints but stop following them, revealing a distinct state-integrity failure that targeted anchoring can partially mitigate.

papers.abstract: Long-context models often use answer-bearing evidence less effectively when it appears away from a prompt boundary. We compare this position bias across Transformer, state-space, and hybrid Mamba architectures by moving one gold document through a fixed set of nine distractors. The evaluated Transformers show a beginning advantage that the evaluated state-space models lack, while both families favor evidence near the end. A matched pure-versus-hybrid Mamba comparison points in the same direction but remains statistically uncertain. The family difference appears among models that can answer the task. Transformer primacy reappears on synthetic retrieval, where state-space ceiling prevents a family comparison. A corpus swap within one state-space architecture changes overall accuracy without a detectable change in curve shape. Prompt changes can create or nearly remove a beginning advantage. Position remains decodable across architectures even when response curves differ, and attention concentration near initial tokens covaries with beginning sensitivity in the tested Transformer family. These exploratory results show that effective context use depends on the evaluated architecture family, capability, task, and prompt, without isolating the sequence mixer as the sole cause.
authors: Aman Behera, Namit Solanki, Mehul Anand
bullets: Evaluated Transformers favor evidence near the beginning and end, while tested state-space models lack the same beginning advantage but still favor the end.
A matched pure-versus-hybrid Mamba comparison trends similarly, though the difference is statistically uncertain.
Transformer primacy returns in synthetic retrieval, but state-space performance ceilings prevent a clean family comparison.
Changing the corpus alters overall accuracy without clearly changing the position-bias curve; prompt changes can create or remove beginning bias.
Position remains decodable across architectures, and initial-token attention correlates with beginning sensitivity in the tested Transformers.
papers.selection_reason: Compares position bias across sequence mixers in long-context QA, directly relevant to long-context language modeling.
papers.title: Mixing Matters: Evidence Position Bias Across Sequence Mixers in Long-Context Question Answering
papers.tldr: Evidence position bias in long-context QA varies with architecture, capability, task, and prompt, so the sequence mixer alone does not explain it.

papers.abstract: Long-context continual pre-training (LCCP) is widely used to improve long-context capability, but how its benefits scale with the number of tokens used for LCCP remains unclear. We investigate this question through modeling, monitoring, and validating the benefits of scaling LCCP. First, we establish an empirical additive power law relating long-context performance to model size and the respective token budgets of short-context pre-training and LCCP. Experiments across five model scales and more than one hundred short- and long-context budget configurations show that the fitted law reproduces the observed trends and extrapolates well to held-out model scales. Second, we introduce \textsc{Constant-Last4}, a training and observation protocol that averages the four most recent consecutive checkpoints from a constant-learning-rate run to enable stable monitoring along a single extensible training trajectory. Under this protocol, the same scaling-law form fits well and accurately predicts the LCCP performance trajectory of a 1.22B-parameter model trained on approximately 100B LCCP tokens. Finally, downstream evaluations along this trajectory show continued improvements in long-context performance, with no clear sign of saturation within the evaluated range. These gains persist after both 128K context extension and supervised fine-tuning, with benefits extending to long-context understanding and agentic tasks. Together, these results argue for continuing to scale LCCP rather than stopping early: its gains are stably observable along an extensible trajectory, quantitatively predictable, and transferable to downstream tasks.
bullets: The study examines how long-context performance scales with model size, short-context pre-training tokens, and LCCP token budgets.
It fits an empirical additive power law that reproduces observed trends and extrapolates to held-out model scales.
The Constant-Last4 protocol stabilizes monitoring by averaging the four latest checkpoints from a constant-learning-rate trajectory.
A 1.22B-parameter model’s performance trajectory is accurately predicted while training on approximately 100B LCCP tokens.
Improvements persist after 128K context extension and supervised fine-tuning, benefiting long-context understanding and agentic tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Empirical scaling laws for long-context continual pre-training directly advance long-context LLM methods and continual learning.
papers.title: Don't Stop Long-Context Continual Pre-Training Too Early: An Empirical Scaling Law
papers.tldr: Long-context continual pre-training keeps improving long-context and downstream capabilities without clear saturation in the evaluated range, and its gains can be modeled predictably as training tokens increase.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is an effective way to strengthen the long-context reasoning of large language models (LLMs), but it needs training data that are long, diverse, challenging, and verifiable. Human annotation of such data is expensive, naturally occurring data are too scarce to sustain RL, and existing synthesis methods depend on external corpora or stronger teacher models, which become harder to obtain as the trained models get stronger. Recently, RL from zero data, in which a model learns from tasks it proposes itself, has achieved excellent performance, but existing methods target short-context tasks. Therefore, we propose $\textbf{LongZero}$, a method that lets an LLM improve its own long-context reasoning without any external data. Instead of writing questions and answers over existing documents, LongZero first has the model synthesize the question and answer with its supporting evidence in a compact structured form, and only then separately expands the evidence into a long multi-document context. LongZero combines these self-written multi-hop reasoning tasks with self-written multi-round retrieval tasks and trains the model with GRPO. We evaluate LongZero on two LLMs across five long-context reasoning benchmarks and compare it with RL on data synthesized from external corpora. Experimental results show that LongZero can generalize to real tasks, and outperforms both baselines, suggesting a viable and promising path to improving long-context reasoning of LLMs.
bullets: Addresses the scarcity, cost, and difficulty of obtaining long, diverse, challenging, verifiable RL training data.
Generates compact multi-hop questions, answers, and evidence first, then expands the evidence into long multi-document contexts.
Combines self-generated multi-hop reasoning and multi-round retrieval tasks, trained with GRPO.
Evaluated on two LLMs across five long-context reasoning benchmarks; it generalizes to real tasks and outperforms the stated baselines.
Scope: the approach is designed for long-context reasoning and relies on self-generated tasks with verifiable evidence.
papers.selection_reason: Self-supervised RL method for improving long-context reasoning in LLMs without external data.
papers.title: LongZero: Enhancing Long-Context Reasoning in LLMs from Zero Data
papers.tldr: LongZero improves LLM long-context reasoning through reinforcement learning on self-generated, verifiable tasks without external data.

papers.abstract: Large language models can solve complex problems across a variety of subjects, such as mathematics and coding. For such complex analytical tasks, models with a long context perform better. Serving models with long context is currently mostly done on powerful systems with multiple GPUs, which are too expensive for most users. An alternative is local inference, or serving a model on a user's own machine, which removes per-token costs and rate limits, besides keeping sensitive data private and giving users full control over the models they run. The common understanding, however, is that local LLMs need compression (e.g., quantization) to run on a single GPU. In this paper, we set out to study the limitations that prevent serving long-context models for single users, besides the capacity issue. Rather than characterizing a single model on one GPU, we analyze how different models behave across several GPU generations. This lets us uncover not just individual bottlenecks but broader trends in where inefficiencies arise. Our analysis confirms that, as expected, self-attention dominates the runtime for long-context inference. More unexpectedly, our evaluation reveals that the current structure of self-attention leaves key GPU resources significantly underutilized, and the newest GPU is often the least well served. Many of these findings are fundamentally data management problems, from paging the KV cache to improving cache utilization and synchronization in the GPU, which is why we bring this study to the Data Systems community. To engage this community, we present our findings as a series of experimental observations and formulate recommendations for future work.
bullets: Local inference can reduce serving costs and rate limits while improving privacy and user control.
The study analyzes multiple models across several GPU generations rather than focusing on one model-device pair.
Self-attention dominates runtime for long-context inference.
Self-attention underutilizes important GPU resources, with newer GPUs often receiving less effective utilization.
Key challenges include KV-cache paging, cache utilization, and GPU synchronization; the paper offers observations and recommendations for future work.
papers.selection_reason: Analysis of long-context LLM inference bottlenecks with focus on self-attention and KV-cache data management.
papers.title: Local Inference of LLMs on Long Contexts: A Data Systems Perspective
papers.tldr: Long-context LLM inference on a single local GPU is constrained not only by memory capacity but also by substantial self-attention and data-management inefficiencies.

papers.abstract: Context compression improves long-context efficiency but may introduce faithfulness issues through an information bottleneck. Existing evaluations rely on QA metrics, but a reader can still answer correctly from an unfaithful compression, so these metrics underestimate such loss. To bridge this gap, we introduce KEEP-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark that directly assesses compression faithfulness with 4,102 cases across three challenging settings that require keeping evidence for plausible reference resolutions, explicit qualifiers, and minority perspectives. Experiments show that even with tailored prompting, the strongest models remain unreliable: despite context windows exceeding 100K tokens and inputs averaging only 3.1K tokens, the best open-weight model (31B) preserves all required evidence in only 66.8% of cases, and the best proprietary model in only 61.6%. Performance also varies sharply across evidence structures, so conclusions from limited structures may be biased. We further introduce a metric, Evidence Preservation Return (EPR), to relate evidence recall to inference FLOPs, and find that it peaks at moderate scales (4B-8B), where recall remains low. Additional output budget mainly benefits already strong models and widens capability gaps, yet the stronger preservation of these models comes at a steep computational cost. These findings highlight the importance for future work to investigate compressors with strong information preservation under a small computation budget, rather than relying on a large output budget or model scaling.
authors: Ziqing Man, Di Wu, Jia-Chen Gu, Junyi Zhang, Kai-Wei Chang, Nanyun Peng
bullets: Introduces a 4,102-case diagnostic benchmark covering reference resolution, explicit qualifiers, and minority perspectives.
Directly evaluates evidence faithfulness, addressing the gap between answer correctness and faithful compression.
Even the strongest evaluated models preserve all required evidence in only 66.8% and 61.6% of cases for the best open-weight and proprietary systems, respectively.
Evidence-preservation performance varies substantially by evidence structure, making narrow evaluations potentially misleading.

Proposes Evidence Preservation Return (EPR), finding that preservation efficiency peaks at moderate model scales but remains low; extra output budget mainly helps stronger models at high computational cost.
papers.selection_reason: Context-compression faithfulness benchmark is directly relevant to long-context and efficient inference.
papers.title: KEEP-Bench: Evaluating Evidence Preservation in Context Compression
papers.tldr: KEEP-Bench shows that context compressors often lose crucial evidence despite strong QA performance, motivating efficient methods that preserve information reliably.

papers.abstract: Long-context language models (LCLMs) power agents that act over long trajectories, from improving a codebase to running research experiments to forecasters that condition on lengthy histories. These applications draw on three distinct long-context capabilities: recall, where the answer is a fact present in the context; state tracking, where the outcome can be computed by performing a series of transformations to a specified state; and pattern learning, where the goal is to make a prediction by sampling from a distribution inferred from many observations. Existing benchmarks primarily focus on the first capability. In this work, we introduce LEAPS (Long-context Evaluation of Adaptive Pattern learning and State tracking), a collection of 12 novel datasets, spanning agentic workflows, behavioral modeling, and forecasting of market and world events. By construction, LEAPS is resistant to data contamination, extends to millions of input tokens, and uses reliable metrics. We evaluate 30 API and open models from 8K to 512K input tokens. LEAPS distinguishes models that perform near perfectly on recall tasks, finding that such models' state tracking and pattern learning abilities can vary significantly and degrade much more dramatically with increasing input lengths--even for pattern learning, where more observations should make learning a theoretically easier task. Moreover, thinking models often underperform their base counterparts, exhausting their generation budget or oversimplifying the task. We hope LEAPS can guide the development of the next generation of LCLMs.
authors: Howard Yen, Nitya Mani, Alex Renda, Christopher S. Hardin
bullets: Introduces 12 datasets covering agentic workflows, behavioral modeling, and market/world-event forecasting.
Tests recall, state tracking, and pattern learning across inputs up to millions of tokens.
Evaluates 30 API and open models with context lengths from 8K to 512K tokens.
Finds that models strong at recall can degrade sharply on state tracking and pattern learning with longer contexts.
Reports that thinking models can underperform base models by exhausting generation budgets or oversimplifying tasks.
papers.selection_reason: New benchmark for long-context capabilities (recall, state tracking, pattern learning) in LCLMs, directly relevant to long-context model evaluation.
papers.title: LEAPS: Long-context Evaluation of Adaptive Pattern Learning and State Tracking
papers.tldr: LEAPS evaluates long-context models beyond recall, revealing substantial weaknesses in state tracking and pattern learning as contexts grow.

papers.abstract: State space models (SSMs) combine fast inference and fixed state size with competitive language-modeling performance. Recently, state souping has been proposed as a procedure whereby an SSM independently encodes chunks of tokens like documents, tool definitions, or memory records. The resulting state encodings may be cached and recombined to cheaply construct a context for downstream queries. However, both state souping and vanilla SSMs deteriorate on long, crowded contexts, limiting their utility for long-horizon domains. To address this issue, we propose weighted state souping, a simple method that learns query-dependent weights for composing cached states. The resulting models improve long-context performance substantially across both single- and multi-hop document question answering, needle-in-a-haystack retrieval, variable tracking, and tool use. Our method can be further adapted into an efficient sparse variant, yielding near-constant encoding cost with respect to context length while preserving (and sometimes improving) performance. We also present simple theoretical arguments that illustrate why souping works and when it may fail, and discuss informally the advantages of weighted souping. Weighted state souping thus combines reusable context representations with selective retrieval, offering an efficient approach to language modeling over large collections of documents, tools, and other forms of structured context that increasingly dominate modern agentic workloads.
authors: William L. Tong, Aryo Lotfi, Emmanuel Abbe, Josh Susskind, Cengiz Pehlevan, Eran Malach
bullets: Addresses performance degradation of vanilla SSMs and standard state souping on crowded, long contexts.
Learns query-dependent weights to compose independently encoded and cached context chunks.
Improves performance across document QA, needle-in-a-haystack retrieval, variable tracking, and tool use.
A sparse variant offers near-constant encoding cost as context length grows while maintaining or sometimes improving performance.
Includes theoretical arguments describing why state souping works and when it may fail.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes weighted state souping for efficient long-context retrieval, directly relevant to long-context language models and efficiency.
papers.title: Weighted State Souping for Efficient Long-Context Retrieval
papers.tldr: Weighted state souping improves long-context retrieval in state-space models by selectively combining cached document or memory states based on the query.

papers.abstract: Agents that work for many turns outgrow the context window of the model that serves them, and on small language models (SLMs) and constrained inference systems that window is small. Context compaction replaces older turns with a summary so a session can continue, but it is lossy, costs a model call, and can help or hurt depending on when it runs. We describe Bud ContextCompact 2.0, the compaction built into the Bud agent runtime, and evaluate it in two settings. On recall questions over recorded agent sessions, compaction to a 16K budget raised a 1.2B-parameter model's accuracy to 0.335, from 0.247 with truncation and 0.176 with its full 32K history (p < 0.001), and raised a 9B model from 0.515 (truncation) to 0.577 (p = 0.04). On 100 SWE-bench Verified tasks run end to end by a 27B reasoning model on a 49K-token window (556 graded sessions), compaction raised the resolve rate on long sessions from 41% to 53% (+12.3 points, 95% CI +1.6 to +23.0, McNemar p = 0.043), left short sessions unchanged, and used 13% fewer tokens per solved task at equal total cost. The main failure without compaction was not the history overflowing but a reasoning turn exhausting the room the history left. The gain has limits: it vanished under a 45-minute session budget, because each summary took a median of 161 s, and in a threshold study it appeared only when compaction triggered early enough to leave room. An 8B model submitted after about ten turns at 5-8K tokens and never needed compaction. We argue that the accuracy results transfer across hardware, including CPU inference, for an equivalent model and window, while the time cost scales with the hardware and must be budgeted for.
bullets: Compaction replaces older agent turns with summaries to prevent long sessions from exhausting usable context.
On recall tasks, compaction improved accuracy for both 1.2B and 9B models versus truncation.
In 100 SWE-bench Verified tasks, long-session resolution rose from 41% to 53%, with 13% fewer tokens per solved task at equal total cost.
Benefits appeared when compaction triggered early enough to preserve room for reasoning; short sessions did not benefit.
The gain disappeared under a 45-minute session budget because summaries took a median of 161 seconds; an 8B model often avoided compaction entirely.
papers.selection_reason: Context compaction for constrained windows addresses long-context processing and memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: Bud ContextCompact 2.0: Context Compaction for Agent Success and Accuracy with Small Language Models and Constrained Context Windows
papers.tldr: Early context compaction improves long-session agent accuracy on constrained context windows, but its latency cost can erase the benefit under tight time budgets.

papers.abstract: How well can transformer-based Large Language Models (LLMs) retain and recall memories in long contexts of dialogue? LLMs are known to forget long-range factual information in their context, yet the field lacks a comprehensive benchmark to quantitatively assess these shortcomings. We present DiaLong, a long-context dialogue dataset and accompanying memory task that standardizes evaluation in this space. It consists of 100 unique conversations created by humans and then augmented with LLMs, extending beyond lengths found in existing datasets. Our selected memory task is fact recall: classify 40 candidate facts about a dialogue as true or false. This task directly probes the model's ability to actively retain and retrieve information, serving as a critical measure of memory within extended conversational contexts. In testing both the latest LLMs and proposed memory enhancements on DiaLong, we demonstrate that more work needs to be done to enable LLMs with better memory performance. By enhancing memory capabilities, LLMs can improve in maintaining coherence, relevance, and human-like interaction over extended conversation. Improving these capabilities will help LLMs fulfill diverse user needs and expectations in various conversational scenarios.
authors: Owen Bianchi, Samer Aslan, Ryunosuke Saito
bullets: Addresses the lack of standardized evaluation for long-range memory in conversational contexts.
Introduces 100 human-created conversations augmented by LLMs, extending beyond existing dialogue lengths.
Uses a fact-recall task: classifying 40 candidate dialogue facts as true or false.
Evaluates current LLMs and memory enhancements, finding that substantial memory improvements remain necessary.
Better long-context memory could support more coherent, relevant, and human-like conversations.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for long-context dialogue memory and fact recall, directly relevant to long-context processing and LLM memory.
papers.title: DiaLong: Benchmarking Reminiscence in Long-Context Dialogues
papers.tldr: DiaLong is a benchmark for measuring how well LLMs retain and recall facts in very long dialogues.

papers.abstract: Sparse attention speeds up long-context decoding by reading few keys of the KV cache, but existing methods do not control the error of a query, and on real KV caches their errors have heavy tails. We show that perturbing the score of every key with an independent Exp(1) variable turns threshold retrieval into sampling keys with probability proportional to their attention weights. Lowering the threshold along a geometric grid gives nested samples, a Horvitz--Thompson estimate of the output at every level, and confidence bounds that hold simultaneously over all levels, so each head stops at the first level whose certificate meets the target error $\varepsilon$. With fresh perturbations at every decoding step, each certificate fails with probability at most $\delta$ during generation. At a suitable threshold, the estimator reads $O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log(1/\delta))$ values regardless of the context length, and no adaptive method reads fewer, up to constants. A 4-bit scan with deterministic bounds, shared across a grouped-query-attention group, generates the candidates exactly but reads every key. On three LLMs and ten settings at 16K--128K tokens, no certificate is violated, and at equal keys read our 90th-percentile error is 4.6--7.9$\times$ lower than that of the best of 15 baseline families. At equal bytes, the best baselines have 0.6--1.6 times our 90th-percentile error and at least 4.9 times our largest. End to end, our method stays within one point of dense attention on tasks and within 0.1\% in PG-19 perplexity, and the strongest baselines at equal bytes score as well. On CPU, decoding steps at 32K--128K tokens run 1.1--1.4$\times$ faster than dense attention on the same 16-bit cache.
bullets: Perturbing key scores with independent Exp(1) noise converts threshold retrieval into sampling proportional to attention weights.
Nested samples across thresholds enable Horvitz–Thompson output estimates and simultaneous confidence certificates.
Each head stops when its estimated error is below ε; with fresh perturbations, certificate failure is bounded by δ during generation.
The estimator needs O(ε⁻² log(1/δ)) reads, independent of context length, and this read complexity is optimal up to constants.
Across 16K–128K contexts, certificates were never violated; decoding was 1.1–1.4× faster than dense attention on CPU while maintaining near-dense task quality.
papers.selection_reason: Certified sparse attention with perturbed retrieval reduces KV-cache reads for long-context decoding, fitting efficient attention and long-context model interests.
papers.title: Certified Sparse Attention via Perturbed Retrieval
papers.tldr: Certified Sparse Attention uses perturbed retrieval and adaptive sampling to provide high-probability error guarantees while reading far fewer KV-cache values during long-context decoding.

papers.abstract: Jev and its open replicas choose among the options a caller supplies with a single forward pass, fast enough to decide inside an agent loop. We ask what such a model cannot decide, and find a simple limit: Jev cannot make a decision that an LLM makes only by writing out intermediate steps. On a benchmark that varies one factor at a time, Jev finds and selects records without error up to 20k tokens and 64 options, but once the answer depends on two or more updates of one user, accuracy falls, to 53-80% at sixteen updates, because similar records interfere. Given a stale summary of the state, Jev follows it. On real decision items graded by how many thinking tokens a reference LLM needs, Jev answers 97.5% of the items that one forward pass of that LLM solves, but only 74% of the others. Jev also does not know its limit: its confidence flags the errors it makes itself but not those it inherits from a stale input, and neither an explicit nor a trained hand-off option catches the latter. The open models we evaluate share these limits. Checking the state such models rely on requires a model that reasons.
authors: Wang Yang, Xinpeng Li, Yanyan Zhang, Chuang Ma, Shouren Wang, Jianzhe Wei, Liqin Ye, Xiaoran Cai, Mohsen Hariri, Vipin Chaudhary, Xiaotian Han
bullets: Jev selects records accurately up to 20k tokens and 64 options when only one factor changes.
Accuracy drops to 53–80% at sixteen updates to the same user because similar records interfere.
It follows stale state summaries rather than independently checking whether they are correct.
Jev solves 97.5% of items solvable by a reference LLM in one pass, but only 74% of items requiring more reasoning.
Confidence detects some self-made errors but not errors inherited from stale inputs; evaluated open models show the same limits.
papers.selection_reason: Probes the limits of one-pass decision models (Jev) in terms of context length and reasoning steps. This is directly relevant to Long-Context Models and the constraints of LLM inference.
papers.title: What Can't Jev Decide? Probing the Limits of One-Pass Decision Models
papers.tldr: One-pass decision models handle simple selection well but fail when decisions require multi-step state updates or reasoning beyond their inputs.

papers.abstract: Long-context large language model (LLM) inference is important for modern intelligent applications but remains constrained by peak memory during prompt prefill. Existing KV cache compression reduces decoding memory but typically requires full-prompt prefill to preserve global context, retaining a high construction peak. Online chunk-level eviction lowers memory earlier but selects before each layer has observed the complete prompt, potentially degrading cache construction and decoding. We present TideKV, an on-GPU cache-construction architecture using layer-major delayed eviction. TideKV processes all prompt chunks within each Transformer layer, retains full-prompt KV only for the active layer, and evicts at layer end. This schedule preserves full-prompt-aware selection while reducing activation and temporary memory. Experiments across multiple computing platforms show that TideKV preserves the inference quality and final cache size of the evaluated compression methods. At 64K on A100, it reduces the construction-time transient footprint by 83.89%. On RTX 4090, it increases time to first token by only 1.06% at 64K and enables 128K prefill. TideKV also completes 128K on Jetson, whereas matched post-prefill compression runs out of memory on both resource-constrained platforms. These results show that delayed layer-end eviction substantially expands feasible context lengths without sacrificing cache utility.
authors: Yu Wang, Zhu Wang, Ning Hu, Yifan Guo, Xiu Ma, Bin Guo, Zhiwen Yu
bullets: Targets high transient memory from full-prompt KV-cache construction, which limits long-context inference.
Processes prompt chunks layer by layer, retaining full-prompt KV only for the active layer before evicting it.
Preserves full-prompt-aware cache selection while reducing activation and temporary memory.
At 64K context, cuts construction-time transient memory by 83.89% on A100; on RTX 4090, TTFT increases only 1.06%.
Enables 128K prefill on RTX 4090 and Jetson, where matched post-prefill compression runs out of memory.
papers.selection_reason: Layer-wise delayed KV eviction reduces long-context LLM prefill memory; fits KV cache/memory efficiency and long-context inference.
papers.title: TideKV: Delayed KV Eviction via Layer-Wise Chunked Prefill for Memory-Efficient Long-Context LLM Inference
papers.tldr: TideKV reduces peak memory during long-context LLM prefill by delaying KV-cache eviction until each Transformer layer finishes processing the full prompt.

papers.abstract: Natural long documents are widely used for context extension, but which selection pipelines are effective remains unclear. We conduct a controlled comparison on Qwen2.5-3B at 128K under matched 6B-token continued-training budgets. Random sampling of natural long documents (random-long) outperforms repacking at longer evaluation lengths. Within the same candidate pool, selecting documents with high LongPPL key-token density yields further gains, unlike the evaluated generic-quality and LLM-judge selectors. We introduce truncLongPPL to reduce scoring cost by computing key-token density over a truncated prefix. At 128K, scoring the first half of the reference span yields downstream performance close to full-span scoring with a measured $2.28\times$ end-to-end scoring speedup. Across three training seeds, truncLongPPL achieves the highest mean scores among evaluated pipelines, exceeding random-long by 4.54 points on validation HELMET and 3.28 on held-out RULER, with gains most consistent in retrieval. At a 256K target context, it gains 2.82 average RULER points over random-long on Qwen2.5-3B. In short/long mixed training across Qwen2.5-3B, Qwen3-8B, and OLMo~3-7B, it gains 1.47--7.31 average RULER points over random-long mixing, with seven-task short-context averages within 0.23 points of the corresponding baselines. After supervised fine-tuning (SFT), Qwen3-8B and OLMo~3-7B models trained with selected long documents outperform their random-long counterparts by 1.13--1.67 points on LongBench v2 and 0.62--1.44 points on MRCR.
authors: Junlong Jia, Jiang Zhou, Xing Wu, Chaochen Gao Tinghao Yu, Feng Zhang, Lilin Wang
bullets: Random sampling of natural long documents outperforms repacking at longer evaluation lengths under matched training budgets.
Within the same candidate pool, LongPPL key-token-density selection improves downstream performance, while evaluated generic-quality and LLM-judge selectors do not.
truncLongPPL scores only a truncated prefix, achieving performance close to full-span scoring with a measured 2.28× end-to-end scoring speedup at 128K.
Across context-extension, mixed-length training, and SFT evaluations, selected documents yield consistent gains, particularly on retrieval-focused tasks.
The study evaluates Qwen2.5-3B, Qwen3-8B, and OLMo 3-7B across 128K–256K target contexts, with short-context performance largely preserved.
papers.selection_reason: Controlled study of long-document selection for context extension; directly relevant to long-context LLM training.
papers.title: Which Long Documents Matter? A Controlled Study of Data Selection for Context Extension
papers.tldr: A controlled study finds that selecting natural long documents by LongPPL key-token density—especially with an efficient truncated-prefix scorer—improves context extension more reliably than random or generic-quality selection.

papers.abstract: Masked diffusion language models expose an inference-time choice: which positions become visible after each denoising pass. Many existing decoding methods use hand-designed rules or require visibility to grow monotonically. We present a $\textbf{T}$iny $\textbf{I}$nference-time $\textbf{P}$olicy for $\textbf{S}$caling ($\textbf{TIPS}$), an approximately $600$K-parameter controller that learns both unmasking and remasking while keeping the underlying language model frozen. TIPS uses visibility-aware confidence features and a shallow transformer to select which tokens should be visible, while a fixed schedule controls the expected visible fraction. We train the controller through supervised warmup followed by reinforcement learning from terminal correctness rewards. On GSM8K and MATH-500 with LLaDA-8B-Instruct, the full-canvas and two-block TIPS variants achieve $58.46\%$ and $57.97\%$ micro-averaged accuracy at a budget of $32$ decoder evaluations, exceeding the strongest baseline in our main comparison by $12.1$ and $11.6$ percentage points, respectively. Both variants are trained at a budget of $32$ evaluations and remain competitive at higher budgets without retraining. These results demonstrate that learning when to reveal and reconsider tokens can improve the accuracy-compute trade-off without updating the decoder backbone.
authors: Ya-Shi Zhang, Jian Tang, Pierre-Andr\'e No\"el, Oleksiy Ostapenko
bullets: Addresses the limitation of hand-designed or monotonically expanding visibility schedules in masked diffusion language models.
Uses visibility-aware confidence features and a shallow transformer to select token visibility, with a fixed schedule controlling the expected visible fraction.
Trains a roughly 600K-parameter controller using supervised warmup followed by reinforcement learning from terminal correctness rewards.

With LLaDA-8B-Instruct at 32 decoder evaluations, TIPS reaches 58.46% and 57.97% micro-averaged accuracy on GSM8K and MATH-500, respectively, outperforming the strongest cited baseline by 12.1 and 11.6 percentage points.
The full-canvas and two-block variants remain competitive at higher inference budgets without retraining.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a small inference-time controller (TIPS) for diffusion language models to optimize the accuracy-compute trade-off by dynamically managing token visibility, directly relevant to LLM memory and long-context management.
papers.title: TIPS: A Tiny Inference-time Policy for Scaling in Diffusion Language Models
papers.tldr: TIPS is a small learned inference-time controller that improves diffusion language model decoding by deciding which tokens to reveal or remask while keeping the backbone frozen.

papers.abstract: Long-context language models support ever longer context windows, and evaluations typically treat context length as the main indicator of difficulty. However, context length alone cannot explain why models fail on long-context tasks that require reasoning over complex information. Contexts of equal length can pose very different challenges: a task may be solvable from a single local passage, or it may require integrating evidence distributed across the full context. We quantitatively characterise this difficulty through three properties: evidence scope, how much necessary information must be found; evidence dispersion, how widely that information is scattered within the context; and reasoning depth, how many dependent steps are needed to derive an answer from it. We construct LURCH, a multi-domain question-answering benchmark of 6,550 instances with supporting evidence and reasoning graphs, enabling all three properties to be quantified. Evaluations of proprietary and open-weight models show that: (1) at fixed context length, all our three properties are strongly negatively correlated with model performance; (2) as context length increases, performance degrades sharply on samples with dispersed evidence, whereas it remains relatively stable on samples with localised evidence; and (3) difficulty compounds across properties, as questions with moderately high values on all three are harder than those with an extreme value on just one. These findings establish evidence scope, dispersion and reasoning depth as measures of long-context reasoning difficulty that complement context length.
authors: Shiwen Qin, Cameron Barker, Henry Gouk, Elliot J. Crowley, Shay B. Cohen, Mirella Lapata, Miao Li
bullets: Introduces three difficulty dimensions: evidence scope, evidence dispersion, and reasoning depth.
Presents LURCH, a 6,550-instance, multi-domain QA benchmark with supporting evidence and reasoning graphs.
Across proprietary and open-weight models, all three dimensions negatively correlate with performance at fixed context length.
Performance degrades more sharply with increasing context length when evidence is dispersed rather than localized.
Difficulty compounds when moderately high scope, dispersion, and reasoning depth occur together.
papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses long-context reasoning difficulty with new difficulty measures and a benchmark.
papers.title: Beyond Context Length: Characterising the Difficulty of Long-Context Reasoning
papers.tldr: Long-context reasoning difficulty depends not just on context length, but on how much evidence must be found, how dispersed it is, and how many reasoning steps connect it.

papers.abstract: Frontier models, general-purpose and domain-specific alike, now include a midtraining stage between pretraining and post-training, but little has been published about how this stage is built. We present an open midtraining recipe that primes base models for agentic post-training, and we show its effectiveness on two Nemotron models of different sizes. Pretraining typically runs at short context and sees almost no agent interactions, while SFT data is mostly synthetic, and very long SFT stages can hurt the model's later RL trainability. Our midtraining stage sits between the two. It trains at 256K context for hundreds of billions of tokens on a diverse mixture of natural software-engineering data like packed repositories, pull requests, commit histories, and build logs together with a small share of agentic traces. On Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, 500B midtraining tokens improve SWE-bench Verified from 60.7 to 64.5, SWE-bench Multilingual from 55.8 to 62.8, and SWE-bench Pro from 32.0 to 35.5 after identical full SFT. On the larger Nemotron 3.5 Super, 280B midtraining tokens improve DeepSWE, a harder benchmark of long-horizon tasks, from 11.7 to 15.7 and SWE-bench Verified from 72.9 to 74.3 after identical full SFT. Midtraining also improves robustness across agent harnesses on both models. We report the ablations behind the recipe and an evaluation protocol built on short fixed SFT runs, since base-model proxy metrics did not correlate reliably with post-training results.
authors: Soumye Singhal, Joseph Jennings, Ka Shun Shum, Alexander Bukharin, Khushi Bhardwaj, Zirui Liu, Venkat Srinivasan, Jonathan Li, Yash Jain, Kezhi Kong, Markus Kliegl, Olivier Delalleau, Sanjeev Satheesh, Mostofa Patwary
bullets: Addresses the underexplored midtraining stage between pretraining and post-training, where short-context pretraining and synthetic-heavy SFT may limit agentic capabilities.
Trains at 256K context on hundreds of billions of tokens from repositories, pull requests, commit histories, build logs, and a small amount of agent traces.
After identical SFT, gains appear across SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Multilingual, SWE-bench Pro, and the long-horizon DeepSWE benchmark on two Nemotron models.
The recipe also improves robustness across agent harnesses.
Proxy metrics from base models were unreliable; the authors instead use short fixed SFT runs and report supporting ablations.
papers.selection_reason: Open midtraining recipe for agentic post-training of LLMs at 256K context; fits LLM training and long-context.
papers.title: Priming Base Models for Agentic Post-Training: An Open Midtraining Recipe
papers.tldr: An open midtraining recipe using long-context software-engineering data and limited agent traces improves models’ subsequent agentic post-training performance and robustness.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding pairs a cheap drafter with parallel verification against the target. At ultra-long context it stops paying, because a drafter that attends over the full prefix inherits the target's context-dependent cost, so the speedup it was meant to provide first erodes and then reverses. The standard response is to build a long-context drafter, by training or fine-tuning one, or by using a multi-token-prediction head shipped inside the target checkpoint. We argue this is unnecessary, because the drafters in use are target-conditioned, reading hidden states the target computed over the entire prefix, so distant context already reaches them without their own attention, and verification corrects what they miss. We therefore freeze released short-context drafters and run them far past their training length under two inference-time mechanisms, one bounding the attention cache they see, which fixes their cost, and one re-basing their rotary position indices into the trained range. No weight is touched and the only tunable saturates early, so one vLLM-side configuration spans 4k to two million tokens, costing at most 0.16x of speedup at short length. We prove when a common index shift leaves the drafter's computation exactly unchanged, and decompose acceptance into two measurable gaps with sharp bounds. Whatever speedup a frozen drafter delivers at short context, it retains out to two million tokens, across three target-drafter pairs and five corpora. The claim concerns the flatness rather than the multiple, and removing either mechanism eliminates it. The gain is conditional on the speculative cost per emitted token staying below the matched target-only cost.
authors: Aref Jafari, Vansh Bhatia, Matt Qin, Subhajit Dutta Chowdhury, Ben Lee, Vikram Appia, Ali Ghodsi, Mehdi Rezagholizadeh
bullets: Long-context drafting becomes uneconomical when the drafter attends over the full prefix.
The approach freezes existing drafters and uses bounded attention-cache visibility plus rotary-position re-basing, with no weight updates.
A single vLLM-side configuration covers 4k–2M-token contexts; tuning saturates early and costs at most 0.16× short-context speedup.
Across three target–drafter pairs and five corpora, the drafter retains its short-context speedup up to two million tokens.
The result concerns stable speedup rather than its absolute magnitude and depends on speculative decoding remaining cheaper per emitted token than target-only decoding.
papers.selection_reason: Long-context speculative decoding with frozen short-context drafters.
papers.title: Long-Context Drafting Does Not Require Long-Context Drafters
papers.tldr: Frozen short-context drafters can support speculative decoding at up to two-million-token contexts when inference-time cache and position handling prevent their cost from growing with context length.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon failures of language models are usually measured as end-task success or as a horizon length. We instead score, step by step, three components of a 400-step ledger task in which every step is easy in isolation and the model's own answers are re-injected into its context: recognising a record already seen 5 to 300 steps earlier, processing the current record locally, and writing a counter incremented at every step. On Qwen3-8B (non-thinking, 20 seeds, replicated on a second machine and backend), with every step scored component by component, two results hold. First, duplicate-recognition errors rise late in the episode -- from 0.0019 to 0.011 per step at risk across step 200 -- while the counter makes no error in 8,000 steps and local processing is descriptively stable; the rise combines long-distance recall errors and rising false alarms. Second, a block of irrelevant content inserted before each step makes the counter fail in 20 of 20 seeds on each machine, against none without it, while its effect on local processing is much smaller and not distinguishable from none. Three pre-registered follow-ups probe the counter. Its value depends on the value present in the response history: a corrupted value persists without correction in every seed, and an exact external reminder, repeated before each message, re-aligns it within one to two steps. Under the irrelevant block, no counter error was observed when an exact compact reminder of the state, supplied externally by an oracle, preceded each message (0 of 20 seeds with an error, against 15 without it), and this reminder outperformed a length-matched neutral text; whether a single reminder suffices was not conclusive, and the absence of damage to the other components was not established. An aggregate or exclusive error classification can hide the difference we report.
bullets: A 400-step ledger task separately scores duplicate recognition, local processing, and counter updates with model outputs re-injected into context.
Duplicate-recognition errors increase late in the episode, reflecting both missed long-distance recalls and rising false alarms.
The counter remains error-free without interference, but irrelevant content causes failures in all tested seeds, with little effect on local processing.
Counter errors persist after corruption, whereas exact external state reminders can restore tracking within one to two steps.
Aggregate success or exclusive error metrics can conceal these distinct failure modes; some reminder effects remain inconclusive.
papers.selection_reason: Component-wise analysis of long-horizon LLM reliability under context re-injection; relevant to long-context behavior and memory.
papers.title: Context Injection and Long-Horizon Reliability: Separating Duplicate Recognition, Local Processing, and Counter Tracking
papers.tldr: Step-by-step evaluation shows that long-horizon failures arise mainly from duplicate-recognition drift and context-sensitive counter tracking, while local processing remains comparatively stable.

papers.abstract: Long-context decoding is limited by memory bandwidth, because every output token reads the KV cache of every layer. Sparse decoding reduces this cost by reading only part of the KV cache. We observe that the number of pages a query needs varies widely across KV heads, layers and steps. Fixed budgets are simple, but they are sized for demanding cases and tuned per workload; adaptive budgets follow this variation more flexibly, but existing designs pay for it with extra selection cost or training. At the kernel level, FlashAttention-3 (FA3) and FlashInfer are designed for rows of similar length: with page lists whose length differs per KV head, they either pad the lists (forfeiting much of the sparse saving), leave thread blocks unbalanced, or rely on a host-side plan that runs outside the CUDA graph. We propose MOIRA, a training-free sparse decode path in vLLM whose budget adapts per KV head and per layer. For every request, layer, KV head and step, a coverage rule keeps the smallest set of pages whose estimated attention mass reaches a fraction $γ$. A new kernel, self-planning attention, lets each thread block derive its own share of the work from the list lengths, so the whole decode step stays inside the CUDA graph. On an H200, at RULER's 128k context, MOIRA with $γ=0.99$ matches dense accuracy while reading about 30% of the pages and reduces the time per output token (TPOT) by 2.2-2.5$\times$ relative to dense FA3; with $γ=0.98$ it reduces TPOT by 2.7$\times$ and stays within the noise of dense. Under high serving load it raises throughput by up to 51%. These results suggest that a budget adapted per head and layer, paired with a kernel that keeps such budgets inside the CUDA graph, makes sparse decoding both flexible and fast.
bullets: Long-context decoding is memory-bandwidth-bound because each token accesses every layer’s KV cache.
MOIRA selects the smallest set of pages reaching a target attention-mass coverage per request, layer, KV head, and decoding step.
Its self-planning attention kernel handles variable page-list lengths without padding, imbalance, or host-side CUDA-graph breaks.
On an H200 with 128k-token contexts, it reads about 30% of pages at γ=0.99 and achieves 2.2–2.5× lower TPOT than dense FA3 while matching dense accuracy.
At γ=0.98, TPOT improves by 2.7× and serving throughput increases by up to 51%, according to the abstract.
papers.selection_reason: Sparse adaptive-budget KV-cache decoding for long-context LLMs; strong efficiency contribution.
papers.title: MOIRA: Mass-Oriented Indexing with Ragged Attention for Long-Context Decoding
papers.tldr: MOIRA enables fast, training-free long-context decoding by adaptively reading only the KV-cache pages needed by each layer and KV head while preserving dense-model accuracy.

papers.abstract: Long contexts enlarge key--value (KV) caches, increasing memory use and attention costs during generation. Compressing these caches must preserve information for unseen questions. We introduce **Latent Compaction**, which learns a compact document-specific cache through test-time training. We initialize cache entries using reconstruction importance, teacher attention, and key-space diversity. Training first fits attention outputs and log-normalizers to those of the full cache, with reconstruction-selected entries held fixed. It then jointly optimizes the entire cache through end-to-end distillation from the full-cache model. Model weights remain frozen throughout, and training uses only generic prompts about the document, without access to downstream questions or answers. Experiments on RULER, LongBench, and Phonebook Lookup demonstrate substantial gains over budget-matched compression baselines. On a RULER, for example, our method achieves 96.7% accuracy at 32$\times$ compression, compared with 40.0% for KVZip+. The method also transfers across model scales and families, with retrieval gains on both Qwen3 and MiniCPM5. These results show that treating the KV cache as a neural network and optimizing it with test-time training can preserve retrieval accuracy under aggressive compression. The code is released at https://www.github.com/THUNLP/latent-compaction
authors: Yingfa Chen, Xingyu Shen, Chaojun Xiao, Xu Han
bullets: Targets the memory and attention costs of large KV caches during generation.
Initializes compact caches using reconstruction importance, teacher attention, and key-space diversity.
Distills attention outputs and log-normalizers from the full cache, then jointly optimizes the cache while freezing model weights.
Uses only generic document prompts, without downstream questions or answers.
Achieves 96.7% accuracy at 32× compression on a RULER task versus 40.0% for KVZip+, with gains across RULER, LongBench, Phonebook Lookup, Qwen3, and MiniCPM5.
papers.selection_reason: Test-time training compresses KV caches for long contexts; directly fits KV-cache efficiency and test-time learning.
papers.title: Latent Compaction with Test-Time Training
papers.tldr: Latent Compaction uses document-specific test-time training to compress KV caches while preserving long-context retrieval accuracy.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates LLM generation through lightweight drafting and parallel verification. It is particularly promising for long inputs, where KV-cache access costs can be amortized over multiple accepted tokens. Yet most drafters are trained on short sequences and degrade on long inputs, while long-context training is costly. Existing training-free approaches restrict the context window, rescale positions, or augment recent context with retrieved distant entries. Drafters, however, read target hidden states that already encode contextual and positional information, and their lightweight architecture makes full-history attention affordable. We propose FOLD, a training-free method that preserves exact local positions and treats all distant entries as far memory at a shared position. To counter attention dilution as the memory grows, we sharpen attention within it to emphasize relevant entries while separately controlling its total weight relative to the local window. Across six target-drafter pairs and diverse benchmarks of up to 256K tokens, FOLD predominantly delivers the highest speedup, with the best case more than doubling the speedup over autoregressive decoding, from 2.08$\times$ to 4.22$\times$.
authors: Shuxuan Li, Jialiang Kang, Yanghao Zhou, Ziye Zhu, Xiao Yang
bullets: Addresses drafter degradation on long inputs without costly long-context training.
Preserves exact positions for recent tokens while assigning distant entries a shared far-memory position.
Sharpens attention over distant memory and controls its total influence to reduce attention dilution.
Evaluated across six target–drafter pairs and benchmarks up to 256K tokens.
Predominantly achieved the highest speedups; the best case improved from 2.08× to 4.22× over autoregressive decoding.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free long-context speculative decoding with position-free far memory; fits KV-cache efficiency and long-context language modeling.
papers.title: FOLD: Position-Free Far Memory with Local Order for Long-Context Speculative Decoding
papers.tldr: FOLD is a training-free long-context speculative-decoding method that improves drafting by combining exact local positions with sharpened, weight-controlled far-memory attention.

papers.abstract: Reasoning over infinitely long documents is becoming a reality with recurrent memory agents. However, increasing context length exacerbates the trade-off between reasoning performance and inference efficiency. Inspired by Kahneman's account of fast and slow thinking, we propose MemDuet, a dual-process memory framework that learns to coordinate a small language model for fast, parallel evidence selection from raw context chunks (System 1) with a large language model for memory-update verification and memory updates in document order (System 2). We train MemDuet in three stages: supervised fine-tuning of System 1 for evidence selection, Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) of System 2 for verification and memory rewriting, and joint optimization of both policies to coordinate selection and updating for long-context reasoning. Experiments on diverse long-context reasoning benchmarks (RULER-HQA, LongBench v2, and 2WikiMultiHopQA) demonstrate a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off as context length grows. Averaged across evaluation settings on the three datasets, MemDuet achieves an end-to-end inference speedup of 9.74x and an output-token reduction of 73.91% relative to RL-MemAgent.
authors: Jiangcheng Song, Haodong Jing, Yulin Mu, Lesong Tao, Jixin Wang, Jin Cui, Tianjing Ren, Runxuan Xie, Yongqiang Ma, Nanning Zheng
bullets: Addresses the accuracy–inference-efficiency trade-off in reasoning over very long documents.
Uses a small language model for parallel evidence selection and a large language model for ordered memory verification and updates.
Trains the two systems through supervised evidence-selection tuning, GRPO-based memory optimization, and joint coordination.
Evaluated on RULER-HQA, LongBench v2, and 2WikiMultiHopQA, achieving a 9.74× end-to-end speedup and 73.91% fewer output tokens than RL-MemAgent.
The abstract scopes results to the reported long-context benchmarks and evaluation settings.
papers.selection_reason: Dual-process memory framework for long-context reasoning with improved accuracy-efficiency trade-off.
papers.title: MemDuet: Learning Dual-Process Memory for Long-Context Reasoning
papers.tldr: MemDuet coordinates fast evidence selection with slower memory verification to improve long-context reasoning efficiency while preserving accuracy as contexts grow.

papers.abstract: Summary-token architectures such as Kwai Summary Attention (KSA) compress distant context into learnable Summary token per chunk, and hybrid variants interleave these layers with full attention to retain exact access to the original text. In such hybrid KSA-Full architecture, the interleaving inserted summary tokens are served as a streaming flow role across different layers. Although effective, however, it also introduce some bottlenecks: (1) the different layers summary compression chunk must be same, therefore hard to reach a flexible KV Cache compression, e.g., different layer set different summary compression chunk window. (2) in the full-attention layers, the summary token introduced additional computation cost, but such layer ignore them and still pay quadratic prefilling, therefore unfriendly to the computation side. Motivated by them, we developed the KSA V2, which not only achieves a more flexible KV cache memory compression but also reduces the computation cost in Full attention layer. Specifically, we found that the summary tokens can serve two roles: the KV memory and sparse indexer.
authors: OneRec Team, Chenglong Chu, Guohong Mu, Guowang Zhang, Hao Peng, Hui Wang, Jian Liang, Jiangxia Cao, Jiao Ou, Jiaxin Deng, Lu Ren, Muhao Wei, Ruiming Tang, Tianle Xu, Wenwu Ou, Xingmei Wang, Zhixin Ling, Zhiyuan Liang, Ziqi Wang, Chaoyi Ma, Haixiao Gao, Kuo Cai, Renpu Liu, Ruochen Yang, Wenlong Xu, Xinqi Jin, Yan Sun, Yifan Wang, Yingzhi He, Yiyu Wang, Yusen Huo, Zhaojie Liu, Zihan Zhou
bullets: Addresses fixed summary-compression windows across layers, which limit flexible KV-cache compression.
Reduces wasted computation in full-attention layers that previously ignored summary tokens while still incurring quadratic prefilling cost.
Uses summary tokens in two roles: compressed KV memory and sparse indexing.
Targets both more flexible KV-cache memory compression and lower full-attention computation cost.
papers.selection_reason: Summary-token attention with flexible KV cache compression and reduced full-attention cost; fits efficient AI and long-context LLM methods.
papers.title: Kwai Summary Attention V2 Technical Report
papers.tldr: KSA V2 makes hybrid summary-token attention more flexible and efficient by separating summary tokens’ KV-memory and sparse-indexing roles.

papers.abstract: Long-context inference makes the key-value (KV) cache a major memory bottleneck for large language models. We propose BELT, a low-rank KV cache compression framework. Its key-side objective targets attention distributions rather than raw keys or pre-softmax logits, yielding a quadratic surrogate with a closed-form low-rank solution. A learned global rank allocator uses differentiable soft selection during training and hard selection at deployment to meet a user-specified component budget. Experiments demonstrate improved model quality under aggressive compression and increased decoding throughput at comparable accuracy. Evaluated across three LLMs and multiple benchmarks, BELT achieves up to 70% low-rank KV cache compression while outperforming the strongest baseline by up to 23.3 points on LongBench, and up to 17.8x overall KV cache reduction when combined with quantization. With Triton-based GPU kernels and a quantized cache, BELT delivers up to 2.7x speedup for the attention module and 3.3x end-to-end decoding throughput.
authors: Yaoyang Liu, Shuwei Shen, Jincheng Tang, Jinguang Liu, Jinbao Xue, Hailong Yang, Ke Zhang, Yinjun Wu
bullets: Targets attention distributions rather than raw keys or logits, producing a quadratic objective with a closed-form low-rank solution.
Learns global top-k rank allocation using differentiable soft selection during training and hard selection at deployment.
Across three LLMs and multiple benchmarks, achieves up to 70% low-rank KV-cache compression and up to 17.8× reduction with quantization.
Reports up to 23.3-point LongBench gains over the strongest baseline and up to 3.3× end-to-end decoding throughput.
Uses Triton GPU kernels and quantized caches to reach up to 2.7× attention-module speedup.
papers.selection_reason: Low-rank KV cache compression with learned rank allocation for long-context LLM inference, directly targeting KV-cache memory efficiency.
papers.title: BELT : BEhavior-Aligned Low-Rank KV Cache Compression with Learned Top-k Rank Allocation
papers.tldr: BELT compresses long-context KV caches with behavior-aligned low-rank representations and learned rank allocation, improving memory efficiency and decoding speed while preserving quality.

papers.abstract: The design of attention mechanisms in long-context large language models faces an ``impossible triangle'' among KV cache size, training and prefill FLOPs, and model quality. GQA achieves strong quality but incurs high KV cache overhead; alternative approaches such as MLA and MFA can compress the cache, but MLA suffers from quality loss while MFA substantially increases training and prefill compute. We propose Virtual Head Attention (VHA), which simultaneously improves all three vertices through two lightweight linear operations: Q Premix applies a near-identity transformation to queries within each KV group to recover virtual head diversity from halved physical query heads, and Linear Postmix fuses inter-head features via a low-rank $I + AB^\top$ residual structure. Since VHA introduces no nonlinear operations, Premix can be folded into the query projection and Postmix into the output projection at inference time, reducing the model to a standard GQA-2 architecture that directly reuses all existing GQA inference optimizations. With only two KV heads, the group size in large models readily reaches 64, fully exploiting Tensor Core parallelism during decoding. Across four scales with 4K-context 50B-token pretraining, VHA consistently surpasses the standard GQA baseline at every scale ($+$0.05\% to $+$0.81\%), while reducing KV cache by $4\times$ vs.\ GQA-8 at dense scales and $2\times$ vs.\ GQA-4 at the MoE scale, and lowering training and prefill FLOPs by 7.9\% (1.7B, $S{=}4096$). On an industrial 30B-A3B MoE model trained on 500B tokens at 8K context, VHA outperforms both MLA and GQA-4 by $+$0.70\,/\,$+$2.60\,\% on a 12-benchmark base-model evaluation suite; in a separate matched 10B-A1B MoE comparison after long-context mid-training, VHA attains an average RULER score of 84.4 over 8K--128K versus 73.0 for GQA, while using two rather than four KV heads in the full-attention layers.
authors: Xibo Ding, Guoxia Wang, Jinle Zeng, Jiabin Yang, Sirui Tao, Chao Yang, Dianhai Yu
bullets: Targets the trade-off among KV-cache size, training/prefill compute, and model quality in long-context LLMs.
Uses two lightweight linear operations: Q Premix restores virtual query-head diversity, while Linear Postmix fuses inter-head features with a low-rank residual structure.
The operations can be folded into existing projections at inference, yielding a standard GQA-2 model compatible with GQA optimizations and Tensor Core decoding.
Across four model scales, VHA improves over GQA while reducing KV cache by 2–4× and training/prefill FLOPs by 7.9% in one reported setting.
On industrial MoE evaluations, VHA outperforms MLA and GQA and achieves higher long-context RULER scores than GQA while using fewer KV heads.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a linear attention variant that reduces KV cache size and training/prefill FLOPs for long-context LLMs, directly advancing efficient attention and KV-cache efficiency.
papers.title: Virtual Head Attention
papers.tldr: Virtual Head Attention (VHA) reduces KV-cache and compute costs while maintaining or improving long-context language-model quality over standard attention alternatives.

papers.abstract: Long-context training of large language and multimodal models couples structured attention masks (document, prefix-LM, share-question, sliding-window, block-sparse) with multi-node context parallelism, making the mask a dominant bottleneck. FlashMask's column-wise sparse mask compresses them from $O(n^2)$ to $O(n)$ via four query-axis boundary vectors, covering broad structured patterns. Implemented for Ampere GPUs, it neither exploits FlashAttention-3's TMA/WGMMA warp-specialized pipeline on Hopper nor supports distribution. The column-wise sparse mask is indexed by key positions but stores query-axis interval boundaries. Under any multi-chunk context-parallel assignment, it reduces per-rank mask localization to a provably zero-communication \emph{clip--shift--max} on the boundary vectors, compatible with the single-GPU kernel. FlashMask-3 introduces a mask-aware Hopper kernel with three-role warp specialization atop FlashAttention-3's TMA/WGMMA pipeline, plus a mask-aware distributed extension: zero-communication mask localization, a sparsity-aware load balancer (HCC-IPO), and a mask-aware compute-communication overlap with mask-driven communication pruning, whose forward all-gather uses topology-aware hierarchical routing. On a single H100 across 12 masks at 4K--128K context, it improves achieved TFLOPs over FlashMask, FlexAttention, and MagiAttention by 45--141%, 34--71%, and 2--44%. At context-parallel degrees 4--32 with 8K sequence per device, it attains 31--75% compute-communication overlap efficiency and improves throughput over Megatron-Core CP ring, Megatron-Core CP all-gather, and MagiAttention by $1.80\times$--$3.71\times$, $1.71\times$--$2.92\times$, and $1.09\times$--$1.46\times$. In end-to-end training of a 118B-A14B MoE at 128K on 128 H100 GPUs, it raises throughput by 7.3--11.0% over a Dual Chunk all-gather baseline, with attention forward+backward 24.5--44.9% faster.
authors: Guoxia Wang, Qianyue He, Siming Wu, Haoyang Xie, Qiwen Bao, Jinle Zeng, Jiabin Yang, Tian Wu, Dianhai Yu
bullets: Targets the bottleneck of structured attention masks in long-context, multi-node training.
Uses a Hopper-optimized FlashAttention-3 kernel with TMA/WGMMA and three-role warp specialization.
Provides zero-communication mask localization via a clip–shift–max operation, plus load balancing and mask-aware communication overlap with pruning.
On a single H100, improves achieved TFLOPs by 2–141% over prior mask-aware attention systems across 12 masks and 4K–128K contexts.
Across 4–32 context-parallel degrees, improves throughput by up to 3.71×; in 128K end-to-end MoE training, raises throughput by 7.3–11.0%.
papers.selection_reason: Mask-aware distributed attention for long-context LLM training; directly improves attention efficiency and long-context capability.
papers.title: FlashMask-3: Efficient and Expressive Mask-Aware Distributed Attention
papers.tldr: FlashMask-3 makes structured, mask-aware attention efficient on Hopper GPUs and across distributed context parallelism, delivering substantial kernel and end-to-end training speedups.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models apply bidirectional attention over the whole context at every denoising step, so a longer context makes each step substantially more expensive. Sparsifying only at inference leaves the pretrained weights unchanged, so the model is never trained under the sparse pattern it runs with. We propose Prefilling-dLLM v2, which continues training a diffusion language model so that it routes with its native mask token. One mask is appended at the end of each chunk, and a learned role offset marks it as a routing slot. On every fourth layer, a query keeps a bidirectional local window and the top-K chunks scored from that mask; the other layers use a bidirectional sliding window. Starting from Dream-v0-Base-7B extended to 16K with YaRN, we compare Prefilling-dLLM v2 with bidirectional NSA, DSA, and SWA under the same layout, key budget, and dense initialization, using the same Fast-dLLM decoder. With the YaRN factor scaled to the evaluation length, Prefilling-dLLM v2 leads the other sparse methods on all three RULER tasks from 16K to 128K. Its mean accuracy at 128K is 7.4 points above NSA, the next sparse model, while DSA and SWA remain near zero. At the same length, decoding is 172x faster than with full dense attention.
authors: Qi Han, Jing Xiong, Ziyuan Zhang, Ngai Wong
bullets: Addresses the high per-step cost of bidirectional full-context attention in diffusion language models.
Adds one learned routing mask per chunk; every fourth layer selects the top-K chunks while other layers use local sliding-window attention.
Continued training aligns the model with the sparse attention pattern used at inference.
Outperforms bidirectional NSA, DSA, and SWA across three RULER tasks from 16K to 128K; at 128K, it is 7.4 accuracy points above NSA.
Achieves 172× faster decoding than dense attention at 128K, within the evaluated setup and context range.
papers.selection_reason: Learned chunk routing and sparse attention for long-context diffusion language models directly address efficient attention and long-context processing.
papers.title: Prefilling-dLLM v2: Learned Chunk Routing for Long-Context Diffusion Language Models
papers.tldr: Prefilling-dLLM v2 trains a diffusion language model to route attention through learned chunk-level mask tokens, enabling efficient long-context decoding while preserving strong retrieval performance.

papers.abstract: Linear-time sequence models typically store long-context information in a recurrent state. A fixed-size state limits how much information can be stored, while hybrid architectures that add full attention for better recall incur quadratic sequence cost. Alternatively, sparse attention with continued pretraining (CPT) can extend the effective context length. Generalization beyond the trained length remains challenging, however, and CPT can be costly. We introduce FreeSolo, a native sparse attention mechanism with a short-range sliding window branch and a long-range branch that selects keypoint cells for direct token attention. Its linear-time variant, FS-L, learns to prune the prefix before query-dependent selection through short CPT. FS-B searches balanced trees with $O(N\log^2 N)$ algorithmic cost including radix-sort construction. FreeSolo demonstrates better zero-shot length extrapolation than the baselines without long-context fine-tuning.
authors: Zekun Shi, Alastair James Arthur Price
bullets: Addresses the limited memory of fixed-size recurrent states and the quadratic cost of full attention.
Combines a short-range sliding-window branch with a long-range branch that selects keypoint cells for direct token attention.
FS-L prunes the prefix before query-dependent selection, while FS-B searches balanced trees with O(N log² N) cost.
The method shows better zero-shot length extrapolation than baselines without long-context fine-tuning.
papers.selection_reason: Linear-time sparse attention with zero-shot length extrapolation, relevant to efficient attention and long-context processing.
papers.title: FreeSolo: Linear-time Sparse Attention with Zero-Shot Length Extrapolation
papers.tldr: FreeSolo is a sparse-attention mechanism that enables linear-time long-context modeling and stronger zero-shot length extrapolation without long-context fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: State space models provide efficient linear-complexity processing for long sequences, but their performance frequently degrades as context length grows. We propose SuPER-Mamba, a training-free framework that uses Surprisal as a model-intrinsic signal for long-range state routing in pretrained Mamba models. SuPER-Mamba computes position-wise Surprisal from next-token predictions, aggregates neighboring responses through Local Pooling, and uses the resulting scores to prioritize Global-Channel updates without query-dependent scoring or additional training. We evaluate SuPER-Mamba on three state-space models across the LongBench-E benchmark. The results show that SuPER-Mamba improves the average score from 8.06 to 15.69, corresponding to a 94.7% relative gain over the Base Models and a 13.1% improvement over the state-of-the-art prior baseline. Ablation and length-wise analyses further support the effectiveness of the proposed routing framework.
bullets: Addresses performance degradation in state space models as context length increases.
Computes position-wise surprisal from next-token predictions and smooths it with Local Pooling.
Uses surprisal scores to prioritize Global-Channel state updates without query-dependent scoring or additional training.
Evaluated across three state-space models on LongBench-E, improving the average score from 8.06 to 15.69.
Ablation and length-wise analyses support the effectiveness of the routing framework.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free surprisal-based routing improves long-context Mamba performance; fits long-context language model methods.
papers.title: SuPER-Mamba: Surprisal Prioritization for Extended-Context Routing in Mamba
papers.tldr: SuPER-Mamba is a training-free surprisal-based routing method that substantially improves long-context performance in pretrained Mamba models.

papers.abstract: Serving stacks for large language models manage context through four recurring mechanisms: incremental edits to a growing context, branching and snapshotting for tree search, identification of reusable prefixes for KV-cache reuse, and encoding of repeated segments. Each mechanism is served today by a different specialist structure.
