We show that all four reduce to a single persistent weight-balanced rope whose every node carries a polynomial hash of its subtree over a Mersenne prime, so that the structure supports logarithmic edits and logarithmic verified content-identity queries at the same time. We validate each mechanism with pre-registered, replicated experiments, then compare against a deployed specialist per mechanism: the Ropey editing library, a faithful PagedAttention copy-on-write block table, and the vendored SGLang radix matcher. On workloads that interleave edits with identity queries, Hashrope is net-superior to Ropey by a factor that grows without bound (369.7x at one million characters). Against the radix matcher on a live vLLM stack serving Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct-1M on four A100 GPUs, Hashrope identifies a one-million-token shared prefix exactly and 1.20x faster, at a context length the dense engine cannot even prefill.
authors: Muntaser Syed (Florida Institute of Technology), Ameerah Alsulami (Florida Institute of Technology), Marius Silaghi (Florida Institute of Technology)
bullets: Targets incremental editing, branching/snapshotting, KV-cache prefix reuse, and repeated-segment encoding.
Stores a polynomial subtree hash over a Mersenne prime in every rope node to support content-identity checks.
Uses persistent structure sharing for logarithmic updates and queries across evolving contexts.
Validated through pre-registered, replicated experiments against Ropey, a PagedAttention copy-on-write table, and SGLang’s radix matcher.
Reported 369.7× advantage over Ropey at one million characters and 1.20× faster exact detection of a one-million-token shared prefix than the radix matcher in a live vLLM setup.
papers.selection_reason: Persistent data structure for LLM context and KV-cache management; directly relevant to efficient serving and long-context handling.
papers.title: Hashrope: A Persistent Data Structure for Mechanisms of LLM Context Management
papers.tldr: Hashrope unifies four LLM context-management mechanisms in one persistent, hash-augmented weight-balanced rope with logarithmic edits and verified identity queries.

papers.abstract: Linear attention promises the efficiency needed for long-context language modelling, yet its fixed-size recurrent state must simultaneously support ongoing computation and preserve information from an ever-growing history. This coupling has reinforced a prevailing view that the state's memory capacity defines the model's long-context capability. We challenge this presumed ceiling: \emph{recurrent computation need not bear the full burden of long-term storage}. We introduce NoteBank, a sparse episodic memory that archives selected text before future queries are known, uses the backbone's native features for writing and addressing, and reads retrieved evidence through its native forward computation via replay. This \emph{training-free, plug-and-play} interface requires no external embedding model, separately trained retriever, or separate neural reader. At one million tokens, it raises Gated DeltaNet's mean accuracy across six RULER retrieval tasks from 1.7% to 70.3%, with no observed significant retrieval degradation from 4K to 1M tokens. This recovery adds $\leqslant$0.025% to analytical FLOPs, with persistent context storage approximately 1/2,600 that of a Transformer's full MHA KV cache at matched width, depth, and precision. Experiments extend from three 1.3B recurrent backbones to Mamba-2-8B and post-trained Qwen3.5-9B, demonstrating gains on LongBench v1/v2 and MemoryAgentBench. Together, these results show that sparse evidence storage and native replay can substantially expand the long-context capability of pretrained linear attention models while retaining the efficiency of recurrent computation.
authors: Li Nanbo, Firas Laakom, Yilan Zhang, Piotr Pi\k{e}kos, Yimeng Chen, Liangyu Wang, Yifan Xu, Mateusz Ostaszewski, Dandan Guo, Wenyi Wang, Yanning Dai, Yuhui Wang, J\"{u}rgen Schmidhuber
bullets: Linear attention’s fixed recurrent state must handle both computation and long-term storage, limiting context retention.
NoteBank archives selected text before queries are known, addresses it using native backbone features, and replays retrieved evidence through the model’s forward computation.
The training-free, plug-and-play method requires no external embedder, separately trained retriever, or separate neural reader.
On one-million-token RULER retrieval tasks, Gated DeltaNet’s mean accuracy improves from 1.7% to 70.3%, with no significant retrieval degradation from 4K to 1M tokens.
The approach adds at most 0.025% analytical FLOPs and uses far less persistent storage than a Transformer KV cache; evaluations cover multiple recurrent backbones and long-context benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Sparse episodic memory and native replay expand long-context capability of linear attention, directly relevant to memory efficiency and LLM memory.
papers.title: History Replays Itself: Unleashing Long-Context Capability in Linear Attention
papers.tldr: NoteBank substantially extends linear-attention models’ long-context memory by sparsely storing and natively replaying past evidence without retraining or external retrieval components.

papers.abstract: Language models are becoming infrastructure, and infrastructure built in the open, by public institutions, on documented data, is the alternative to dependence on a few providers; Apertus shows this is viable at scale. Apertus 1.5 extends the fully open Apertus family from text to multimodal reasoning. Continued pretraining of the Apertus 1.0 models, on 4T additional tokens for the 8B and 2T for the 70B, adds image and audio understanding and extends the context window fourfold to 262,144 tokens; multimodality enters through the tokenizer, the language-model head remains restricted to text, and the architecture is unchanged. Supervised finetuning, long-context finetuning, reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, and preference alignment complete the released models. Thinking is a flag of the chat template rather than a separate model, and lifts mathematical reasoning by up to 20 points on the 8B model. The released models improve over their predecessors on nearly every benchmark; among fully open models of its class, the 8B leads on knowledge, instruction following, and cultural benchmarks, and its instruction following surpasses all compared models, including open-weight ones. On image and audio understanding, a first for the family, the models are competitive with fully open multimodal models, strongest on document understanding and long-form and lower-resource speech recognition, while specialized vision and audio models remain ahead on perception and transcription of English and other high-resource languages. As in Apertus 1.0, we train only on openly available data, respect crawler opt-outs retroactively, and exclude restrictively licensed material. We release the model weights, data preparation and training recipes, and evaluation suites under permissive licenses; openness extends to values, with the Apertus charter guiding alignment stages published alongside the models.

Training combines supervised and long-context finetuning, verifiable-reward reinforcement learning, and preference alignment; “thinking” is controlled by the chat template.
The models improve over Apertus 1.0 across nearly every benchmark; the 8B model leads comparable fully open models in knowledge, instruction following, and cultural benchmarks.
Image and audio capabilities are competitive among fully open multimodal models, especially for document understanding, long-form speech, and lower-resource speech recognition.
The project uses openly available data with crawler opt-outs and restrictive licenses excluded, and releases weights, recipes, evaluation suites, and alignment guidance permissively.
papers.selection_reason: Open multimodal LLM with image/audio understanding, long context, and RL-trained reasoning; fits multimodal and language foundation model interests.
papers.title: Apertus 1.5: From Open Text Models to Open Multimodal Reasoners
papers.tldr: Apertus 1.5 extends a fully open text-model family into multimodal reasoning with image/audio understanding, much longer context, and publicly released models, data practices, recipes, and evaluations.

papers.abstract: Chinese historical documents are invaluable cultural treasures, but their complexity poses significant comprehension challenges for non-specialists. Despite the success of Large Language Models (LLMs) and Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) in modern document tasks, their capabilities in Long (full-book) Historical Document understanding remain largely unexplored. To bridge this gap, we introduce LongHisDoc, the first benchmark tailored for long historical document understanding. LongHisDoc comprises 1,012 expert-annotated QA pairs derived from 101 PDF documents, with an average of 85.1 pages and 42,776.4 tokens per document. It spans 10 categories and features four QA types: single-page, cross-page, multi-hop, and unanswerable. Answering these questions requires integrating multimodal evidence from text, layout, and visual elements. Our evaluation reveals that the top-performing LVLM and LLM achieve only 62.9% and 69.9% accuracy, respectively, highlighting a substantial performance gap. Furthermore, we assess various modal retrievers and the end-to-end RAG performance to provide references for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems. We believe that LongHisDoc serves as a comprehensive benchmark to catalyze future research in full-book historical document understanding. The benchmark and evaluation code are available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/qweq12433454/LongHisDoc and https://github.com/SCUT-DLVCLab/LongHisDoc.
authors: Zeyu Shan, Yongxin Shi, Shihang Wu, Peirong Zhang, Yuanyuan Fang, Zhaopeng Wang, Lianwen Jin
bullets: Contains 1,012 expert-annotated QA pairs from 101 PDF documents averaging 85.1 pages and 42,776.4 tokens.
Covers 10 categories and four question types: single-page, cross-page, multi-hop, and unanswerable.
Questions require combining textual, layout, and visual evidence across long documents.
Top reported accuracies are 69.9% for LLMs and 62.9% for LVLMs, indicating substantial challenges.
Also evaluates modal retrievers and end-to-end RAG performance to support future system development.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces LongHisDoc, a benchmark for long historical document understanding, challenging long-context capabilities.
papers.title: LongHisDoc: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Chinese Long Historical Document Understanding
papers.tldr: LongHisDoc is a benchmark for evaluating LLMs and LVLMs on multimodal, full-book understanding of long Chinese historical documents.

papers.abstract: Long-context serving runs out of KV memory before the hardware reaches its useful throughput. HiSparse stores history in host memory and fetches only the selected entries, but it uses one cache budget at every load and does not handle draft-model speculative decoding such as DSpark and DFlash2. We present Adaptive DHiSparse, which supports speculative decoding over hierarchical sparse KV and adapts residency to load. It protects the required working set, retains additional history while GPU memory is spare, and recovers the rest through exact fused retrieval. DSpark and DFlash2 keep their proposal and acceptance rules: queries share missing-row retrieval, draft KV uses a window-bounded ring, and verification staging is reused across layer groups. At 100K context and concurrency 128, GLM-5.3 with DFlash2 delivers 793 output tokens/s per decode GPU, 1.45$\times$ HiSparse and 1.27$\times$ non-speculative adaptive serving. Held to the same latency bounds as HiSparse, it sustains up to 4$\times$ the concurrency and 2.3 to 3.7$\times$ the output, depending on the per-token bound. On DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash at 500K context and concurrency 512, Adaptive DHiSparse with DSpark delivers 1.85$\times$ the output of resident serving with DSpark. In a load step, optional residency reduces host fetches from 14.2% to 1.4% of selected rows at low load and releases memory under pressure.
bullets: Addresses KV-memory exhaustion and fixed cache budgets in long-context serving, including compatibility with DSpark and DFlash2.
Protects the required working set, uses spare GPU memory for extra history, and exactly retrieves missing entries from host memory under pressure.
Reuses speculative-decoding mechanisms such as shared missing-row retrieval, window-bounded draft-KV caching, and verification staging across layers.

At 100K context and concurrency 128, achieves 793 output tokens/s per GPU with GLM-5.3 and DFlash2; the abstract reports higher throughput and concurrency than HiSparse and non-speculative adaptive serving.
At low load, optional residency reduces host fetches from 14.2% to 1.4% of selected rows, while memory is released as load increases.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes load-adaptive hierarchical KV cache management with speculative decoding for long-context LLM serving, directly fitting efficiency and long-context topics.
papers.title: Adaptive DHiSparse: Speculative Decoding over a Load-Adaptive KV Hierarchy
papers.tldr: Adaptive DHiSparse combines load-adaptive hierarchical sparse KV caching with speculative decoding to improve long-context serving throughput while preserving latency bounds.

papers.abstract: LLM-as-a-Service has become a dominant paradigm for accessing large language models without requiring local deployment. However, the process raises severe privacy concerns when user queries may include sensitive or confidential contexts. Differential privacy (DP) provides a principled approach to protecting such inputs, but existing DP inference methods are primarily designed for short- or moderate-context settings and struggle with million-token-scale inputs due to limited context capacity and severe utility degradation under DP perturbation. In this paper, we propose DP-MIND, a memory-guided framework that scales differentially private inference to million-token contexts. DP-MIND enables private long-context inference by locally perturbing the input and processing it chunk by chunk with a compact memory that preserves task-relevant information across the sequence. To make this memory robust to DP noise, we optimize the memory construction policy directly on perturbed inputs using reinforcement learning, guided by both final answer correctness and memory consistency. We further recover perturbation-corrupted answer spans through a local denoising module without exposing the original context to the external model. We provide theoretical privacy analysis of DP-MIND and further conduct extensive empirical analysis across multiple long-context benchmarks with context lengths up to the million-token scale, demonstrating that DP-MIND consistently outperforms existing DP and long-context inference baselines in both scalability and utility.
authors: Zhihao Liu, Yitian Cheng, Shuang Liu, Rui Wen, Yuke Hu, Zhan Qin
bullets: Addresses privacy and utility challenges in LLM-as-a-Service for sensitive, million-token inputs.
Processes perturbed inputs chunk by chunk while a compact memory preserves task-relevant information across the sequence.
Uses reinforcement learning to make memory construction robust to differential privacy noise, optimizing correctness and memory consistency.
Applies local denoising to recover perturbation-corrupted answer spans without revealing the original context to the external model.
Theoretical and empirical analyses across long-context benchmarks show improved scalability and utility over existing DP and long-context inference baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Memory-guided differentially private inference for million-token contexts, fitting long-context and LLM memory.
papers.title: DP-MIND: Differentially private memory-guided Long context Inference
papers.tldr: DP-MIND enables differentially private inference over million-token contexts by combining input perturbation, chunk-wise memory, reinforcement-learned memory construction, and local answer denoising.

papers.abstract: Corpus-level long-context reasoning requires agents to acquire and integrate evidence across document collections that exceed their context windows. Existing agent harnesses enable incremental access to these corpora, but acquired evidence and evolving conclusions often remain entangled in a growing interaction history. This implicit state management can lead to two coupled failure modes: unbounded exploration, where retrieval expands the interaction history without resolving decision-relevant information gaps, and evidence-state drift, where previously acquired evidence or subsequent corrections fail to inform the current conclusion. We present LongHarness, a model-agnostic harness that makes the interaction between acquired evidence and evolving conclusions explicit. Its core mechanism, Evidence-Conclusion Coevolution, uses unresolved conclusions to guide exploration toward missing information, while newly acquired evidence strengthens or revises the conclusions that directed the search. LongHarness couples this process with Evidence Lifecycle Management, which keeps accumulated evidence current and traceable throughout the interaction. Together, these mechanisms focus retrieval on remaining information needs and keep conclusions aligned with current evidence. We evaluate LongHarness on OfficeQA Pro V1 and V2, AA-LCR, and LongBench v2 using GLM-5.3-Flash and Qwen3.8-Flash. Compared with direct reasoning using the same backbone, LongHarness improves GLM-5.3-Flash exact match on OfficeQA Pro from 15.8% to 60.2% on V1 and from 4.4% to 61.1% on V2. Against state-of-the-art agent harnesses, it surpasses Claude Code by 12.0 percentage points on V1 and Codex by 18.9 points on V2. With Qwen3.8-Flash, LongHarness reaches 61.7% on V1, outperforming Claude Code by 8.3 points and Codex by 12.0 points.
authors: Songtao Huang, Zhijie Zhong, Xiaohan He, Shuaiyu Zhang, Zhiyin Yu, Li Kang, Heng Zhou, Yutao Fan, Xiangchao Yan, Bo Zhang, Shiyang Feng
bullets: Targets unbounded exploration and evidence-state drift in corpus-level reasoning.
Uses Evidence–Conclusion Coevolution to direct retrieval toward unresolved information gaps and revise conclusions as evidence changes.
Adds Evidence Lifecycle Management to keep acquired evidence current and traceable.
Evaluated on OfficeQA Pro V1/V2, AA-LCR, and LongBench v2 with GLM-5.3-Flash and Qwen3.8-Flash.
On OfficeQA Pro, improves GLM-5.3-Flash exact match from 15.8% to 60.2% on V1 and 4.4% to 61.1% on V2; it also outperforms cited agent harnesses.
papers.selection_reason: Agentic harness for corpus-level long-context reasoning with explicit evidence-conclusion coevolution, directly relevant to long-context and memory management.
papers.title: LongHarness: Advancing Agentic Reasoning over 100M-Token Corpora via Stateful Evidence Management
papers.tldr: LongHarness improves agentic reasoning over 100M-token corpora by explicitly coevolving conclusions with traceable evidence, substantially boosting long-context QA performance.

papers.abstract: Processing a long sequence does not guarantee that distant information remains usable. As context grows, a fixed-size memory must retain many associations, connect information across positions, and preserve relevant structure without being overwhelmed by everything it observes. These are distinct requirements: a memory may store more information without representing the relationships needed for retrieval, and it may transport those relationships without preserving the ones that matter. Thus, the challenge is not simply extending context length, but constructing a memory that remains usable as context grows. We study this problem in large-chunk test-time training (TTT) and identify two basic failures: single-step writes accumulate interference, limiting capacity, while self-associative writes cannot form cross-position bindings. We introduce Double-Take (DT), which repairs these failures with multi-step unpinned updates and cross-position mixing, and adds bidirectional change-sensitive writes for selective retention. Capacity alone leaves end-to-end recall at the $0.10$ chance floor; adding binding raises it to $0.92$. Trained only on $32\,\mathrm{kb}$ genomic contexts, DT reaches $0.927$ AUROC at $131\,\mathrm{kb}$ and $0.856$ near $1\,\mathrm{Mb}$, while transferring zero-shot from human to mouse. Together, these results identify capacity, binding, and selectivity as three requirements for usable long-range memory.
authors: Vakul Raghavan, Utkarsh Grover, Mingyang Mao, Chengwen Wang, Xiaomin Lin
bullets: The work argues that extending context is insufficient: memory must retain information, bind distant positions, and selectively preserve relevant structure.
It identifies interference from single-step writes and the inability of self-associative writes to form cross-position bindings.
Double-Take addresses these issues with multi-step unpinned updates, cross-position mixing, and bidirectional change-sensitive writes.
Adding binding improves end-to-end recall from the 0.10 chance floor to 0.92, while models trained on 32 kb genomic contexts generalize to 131 kb and nearly 1 Mb.
The method also transfers zero-shot from human to mouse, supporting the role of capacity, binding, and selectivity in long-range memory.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a novel mechanism (Double-Take) for long-context memory that addresses capacity, binding, and selectivity. This is directly relevant to LLM Memory and Long-Context Models.
papers.title: Double-Take: Improving Capacity, Binding, and Selectivity In Long-Context Within Bidirectional Memory
papers.tldr: Double-Take makes long-context memory usable by combining capacity, cross-position binding, and selective retention in bidirectional test-time training.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) process long contexts, including long documents and lengthy conversations, but face token-level memory usage that increases proportionally to input length. Although model optimization and lossy prompt compression are widely used, these methods still fail to solve the long-context recall problem beyond pretrained and size-constrained context windows. This paper proposes a long-context recall method that maintains near-constant GPU memory usage as context length increases, without additional training. The main idea is to reconstruct facts using parameter activations in the LLM's feed-forward layers, which store residual vectors representing facts from the source document. Utilizing residual vectors allows the LLM to deterministically reconstruct query relevant facts without referencing the original document, preserving high fidelity and reducing memory usage without fine-tuning weights. Experimental results show that the proposed method enables answering single-fact questions in two-million-token story contexts where previous methods fail.
bullets: Targets long-context recall while avoiding memory growth proportional to input length.
Stores source-document facts in residual vectors from the LLM’s feed-forward layers.
Reconstructs query-relevant facts deterministically without rereading the original context or fine-tuning weights.
Answers single-fact questions in two-million-token story contexts, where prior methods fail.
Scope: demonstrated for single-fact question answering in long story contexts.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free long-context recall via residual vectors with near-constant memory; fits long-context and memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: Residual Vector-based Reconstruction as Long-Context Recall Regardless of Context Window Size
papers.tldr: A training-free method uses feed-forward residual vectors to recall facts from contexts far beyond standard context-window limits with near-constant GPU memory.

papers.abstract: Advanced large language models (LLMs) with long context windows can substantially reduce input truncation in document-level machine translation (DocMT). However, direct Doc2Doc translation remains prone to n-gram repetition and progressive quality degradation. A common remedy is to segment the document into finer-grained chunks. Nonetheless, conventional rule-based chunking approaches fail to handle the length distribution mismatch between training and inference. To address this, we introduce Fixed-Range Chunking (FRC), utilizing dynamic programming to partition documents into chunks within a predefined length interval. By consistently applying FRC during training and inference, the input documents of any length are mapped to the same length distribution, substantially reducing train-test length mismatch. Centered on FRC, we propose a lightweight dual-boundary matching algorithm for chunk alignment, alongside four distinct training strategies. Experimental results show that FRC-based fine-tuning substantially improves 7B LLMs over direct Doc2Doc fine-tuning and outperforms existing DocMT methods on IWSLT2017. We further construct GlobVDoc, a 10-language test set independent of mainstream DocMT training sources, and show that FRC improves out-of-distribution document translation.
bullets: Direct long-document translation can suffer from n-gram repetition and progressive quality loss.
Fixed-Range Chunking (FRC) uses dynamic programming to partition documents within a predefined length interval.
The same chunking distribution is applied during training and inference to reduce train–test mismatch.
The approach includes a lightweight dual-boundary chunk-alignment algorithm and four training strategies.
Experiments report gains for 7B LLMs on IWSLT2017 and improved out-of-distribution translation on the 10-language GlobVDoc test set.
papers.selection_reason: Fixed-range chunking for length-consistent document-level MT with LLMs; relevant to long-context processing.
papers.title: Doc2FRC: Length-Consistent Document-Level Machine Translation via Fixed-Range Chunking
papers.tldr: Doc2FRC improves document-level machine translation by consistently chunking documents into fixed-length ranges during training and inference, reducing length mismatch and translation degradation.

papers.abstract: Many key-value (KV) caches are compressed before anyone knows what will be asked of them: a document cached for retrieval, a prompt prefix shared across requests, the memory of a long conversation. The prevailing approach scores KV entries by rehearsal: the model rereads the context and keeps the entries it attends to, assuming that the more completely a cache rehearses its context, the better it remembers it. We show that under tight budgets this assumption backfires: rehearse everything, remember nothing. At a 3% keep ratio, rereading the whole context keeps 31.5 of 96.5 points on RULER, and on LongBench's natural-text tasks it falls below methods that rehearse nothing at all. The cause is that a cache keeps what it rehearses: rereading spreads the budget across the whole context, so the answer's own entries survive at little more than chance. Like a student before an exam, a cache remembers more by testing itself than by rereading. Two principles follow: rehearse what will be read, and rehearse as much as there is. We instantiate them as Attic-KV (Attic for short), a training-free rehearsal in which the model quizzes itself with question-answer pairs that quote the context, alongside anchor tokens in a content-adaptive amount. Changing only the rehearsal lifts three hosts that score it in three different ways: Attic alone is the best training-free method in all eight settings we test on RULER and LongBench's natural-text tasks, and plugged into the gradient-based KVgrad and the trained RestoreKV+, it raises them by up to 17.1 and 28.1 points. Its advantage grows as the budget shrinks, reaching 41.9 points over full rereading at a 3% keep ratio, and it compresses faster than rereading the whole context.
bullets: Full-context rereading spreads a tiny cache budget too broadly, causing important answer-related entries to be lost.
Attic-KV uses context-quoting question–answer pairs plus content-adaptive anchor tokens for training-free rehearsal.
Its benefit increases as the keep budget shrinks, including a reported 41.9-point gain over full rereading at a 3% keep ratio.
Attic is reported as the best training-free method across eight RULER and LongBench natural-text settings.
Adding Attic’s rehearsal to KVgrad and RestoreKV+ improves them by up to 17.1 and 28.1 points, respectively.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free KV cache compression method for LLM long-context tasks, directly relevant to memory-efficient inference and long-context processing.
papers.title: Rehearse Everything, Remember Nothing: Attic-KV Rehearses What Will Be Read
papers.tldr: Attic-KV improves ultra-low-budget KV-cache compression by rehearsing likely future reads with self-generated question–answer probes instead of rereading the entire context.

papers.abstract: The genome holds the blueprint that governs the biological properties of the cell. Consequently, advancing our knowledge of genomic function is crucial both for a broader understanding of biology and for continued biomedical advances. The success of large language models on natural language and protein sequences has motivated similar efforts on genomic data. However, standard genomic language models (gLMs) often require extremely large computational resources and still fall behind traditional methods on some downstream tasks. Recently, MSA-based pretraining has been proposed as an efficient alternative, but existing models are limited to short input contexts, restricting their use to short-range tasks, such as variant effect prediction. In this work, we present RAGenome, the first retrieval-based gLM that scales pretraining to longer contexts (100$\times$ longer than existing MSA-based gLMs), allowing it to capture both across-species evolutionary relationships and within-species longer-range interactions. Trained on whole-genome alignments from 100 vertebrates, RAGenome substantially improves the long-range capabilities of MSA-based gLMs, raising gene finding performance from 0.45 to 0.60, while remaining competitive on purely evolutionary-based tasks like prioritizing pathogenic variants. RAGenome provides competitive gLM performance at a fraction of the training cost, unifying evolutionary modeling and long-range capabilities within a single, flexible, scalable framework. Code is available at https://github.com/PanosAntoniadis/RAGenome.
authors: Frederikke Isa Marin, Panagiotis Antoniadis, Dionysia Danai Brilli, Andreas Bjerregaard, Rachael DeVries, Yan Li, Ole Winther, Wouter Boomsma
bullets: Addresses the short-context limitation and high computational cost of existing genomic language models, especially MSA-based models.
Introduces a retrieval-based gLM trained on whole-genome alignments from 100 vertebrates.
Scales context length to 100× that of prior MSA-based gLMs, capturing both cross-species evolution and within-species long-range interactions.
Improves gene-finding performance from 0.45 to 0.60 and remains competitive for pathogenic-variant prioritization.
Provides a single flexible framework for evolutionary and long-range genomic modeling at a fraction of the training cost.
papers.selection_reason: Retrieval-based genomic language model scaling to long contexts; relevant to long-context and retrieval-memory methods.
papers.title: RAGenome: Scaling Retrieval-Based Genomic Language Models to Long Contexts
papers.tldr: RAGenome uses retrieval-based pretraining on whole-genome alignments to extend genomic language models to much longer contexts while preserving evolutionary modeling capabilities.

papers.abstract: Current frontier LLMs can theoretically process long contexts with 1M tokens or more. But to what extent can they go beyond simple retrieval and perform deeper reasoning over such long contexts? We empirically investigate long-horizon reasoning capabilities of LLMs, focusing on deductive logic expressed in Prolog. We construct ProloNg, a synthetic testbed to probe Prolog Long Reasoning, which systematically varies the complexity (reasoning depth) of problems, where the hardest case has a reasoning depth of 22 and 62k context length. We study 8 reasoning models across 5 families of frontier LLMs, and find that performance degrades substantially as reasoning depth grows, with the majority of models approaching chance beyond depth 10.
authors: Hadeel Al-Negheimish, Jasna Ilieva, Yoon Kim
bullets: Evaluates whether long-context LLMs can perform multi-step deduction rather than simple retrieval.
Introduces ProloNg, a synthetic benchmark that systematically increases Prolog reasoning depth.
Tests 8 reasoning models spanning 5 frontier LLM families, including problems up to depth 22 and 62k-token contexts.
Finds substantial performance degradation as reasoning depth increases; most models approach chance beyond depth 10.
papers.selection_reason: Probes long-horizon deductive reasoning in LLMs, directly relevant to long-context models.
papers.title: Probing for Long-Horizon Deductive Reasoning Capabilities in Language Models with Prolog
papers.tldr: Frontier LLMs struggle with long-horizon deductive reasoning in Prolog, with most nearing chance performance beyond reasoning depth 10.

papers.abstract: AI research progress can be viewed as the interaction between two processes: benchmark creation and method discovery. Historically, both were driven by human intelligence. However, recent advances in AI have accelerated automated method discovery, while automated benchmark creation has received comparatively less attention. To enable self-advancing systems, we propose Generative Adversarial Loop (GAL), a generator-discriminator framework alternating between two agentic searches: (1) a discriminator that generates adversarial data to expose weaknesses in current systems, and (2) a generator that discovers algorithms to overcome them. We apply this framework to approximation algorithms for efficient inference. Unlike existing auto research systems, which primarily focus on algorithm discovery, GAL introduces a discriminator agent that automates goalpost setting by continually searching for weaknesses in the current algorithm. We demonstrate adversarial data generation across four tasks: KV compression, sparse video generation, sparse attention, and context extension, where the discriminator identifies weaknesses in state of the art techniques. We further show that GAL enables autonomous improvement, with newly discovered algorithms improving not only on adversarially generated data, but also on established benchmarks. Specifically, GAL improves CompactorPress on KV compression with Qwen3-4B at 4x, raising performance on the discriminator dataset from 0.35 to 0.97, while also outperforming RULER-HARD (+0.77 pts). For context extension, GAL boosts Dual Chunk Attention from 0.20 to 0.90 on the discriminator dataset, while yielding gains on standard benchmarks(ScienceFiction (+6 pts) and PG19 32K (-0.33 PPL)). GAL thus provides a path toward autonomous goalpost setting and algorithmic improvement, where AI systems continually discover their own weaknesses and develop methods to overcome them.
authors: Kislay Aditya Oj, Nidhi Jain, Sri Surya Varma Datla, Priyanka Jayaswal, Kumar Krishna Agrawal, Aditya Desai
bullets: Targets the imbalance between increasingly automated method discovery and comparatively limited automated benchmark creation.
Alternates a discriminator that generates adversarial data with a generator that discovers algorithms addressing the exposed weaknesses.
Applied to KV compression, sparse video generation, sparse attention, and context extension.
Demonstrated autonomous improvement on adversarial datasets and established benchmarks, including KV compression and context extension.
Scope is approximation algorithms for efficient inference; the framework depends on agentic searches that can generate meaningful weaknesses and solutions.
papers.selection_reason: Adversarial loop framework for automated algorithm discovery, demonstrated on KV compression, sparse attention, and context extension.
papers.title: Generative Adversarial Loops
papers.tldr: Generative Adversarial Loops automate both benchmark creation and algorithm discovery by having agents expose system weaknesses and develop methods to overcome them.

papers.abstract: A large language model can only use the text that fits in its context window, and it recomputes its internal key-value (KV) state for a prompt every time the prompt is sent. We test a memory layer, the public package galahad-kv, that saves the KV state of each block of about 16,000 tokens to encrypted local NVMe disk and loads it back later, byte-exact, without recomputing it. We ran it on 50,000,000 tokens of real public text, served through vLLM on one NVIDIA H100, with Gemma 4 12B and Gemma 4 31B. Every block we probed was loaded back from the encrypted store with no recompute (100 of 100, at depths from 0 to 50M tokens) on both models. Loading a block was 2.8x to 4.3x faster than recomputing it and used 8.8x to 12.3x less GPU energy, and GPU memory stayed flat over the whole 50M-token stream. Asked about facts planted millions of tokens earlier, the 12B model gave the right answer 82 times out of 100 and the 31B model 98 times out of 100. Neither model made up an answer. The limits are as follows. This is reuse of stored state, not a wider attention window: one block is loaded at a time, and how well a question is answered depends on the model. Writing the memory is a one-time cost, and the store takes terabytes of local NVMe disk. We describe the test protocol, which is built to resist common ways of gaming long-context benchmarks, and give a single-GPU reproduction that uses public software and a free licence for the package.
bullets: Motivation: standard long-context inference recomputes a prompt’s KV state and is constrained by GPU context capacity.
Method: galahad-kv stores roughly 16K-token KV blocks on encrypted local NVMe and reloads them byte-exactly through vLLM.
Evaluation: tested on 50M tokens of public text with Gemma 4 12B and 31B on one NVIDIA H100.
Results: all 100 probed blocks loaded without recomputation; loading was 2.8–4.3× faster and used 8.8–12.3× less GPU energy than recompute.
Scope: this reuses stored state rather than expanding attention; only one block is loaded at a time, with a one-time write cost and terabytes of disk storage required.
papers.selection_reason: Persistent KV-state memory layer for long-context LLM inference; directly relevant to KV cache/memory efficiency and LLM memory.
papers.title: Real Long-Term Memory for AI: A 50-Million-Token Window That Is Faster and Cheaper Than Recompute
papers.tldr: A disk-backed KV-cache memory layer enables exact reuse of context across up to 50M tokens, reducing retrieval latency and GPU energy versus recomputation while preserving flat GPU memory use.

papers.abstract: Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) offer linear-time scaling with sequence length while requiring only constant memory, yet they struggle to capture long-range dependencies due to vanishing gradients and limited receptive fields. To address these limitations, we introduce a second-order recurrent model in which the standard neuron-to-neuron communication is replaced by a spatially evolving field governed by (discretized) partial differential equations. Drawing inspiration from the role of cortical waves in brain computation, this mechanism allows structured spatiotemporal patterns to serve as an implicit, high-capacity memory. We show that the resulting model is equivalent to a structured infinite-order RNN in which the current state depends explicitly on its entire history of past states, yielding an effectively unbounded receptive field with a fixed number of parameters. We further derive constructive conditions to ensure marginal stability, constraining the gradient spectrum on the unit circle and thereby eliminating vanishing and exploding gradients. Empirically, the proposed architecture outperforms other recurrent models on long-horizon benchmarks while using substantially fewer parameters, demonstrating that spatial dynamics can effectively bridge the gap between efficient inference and long-term memory.
authors: Aleix Salvador-Pomarol, Arthur N. Montanari, Earl K. Miller, Adilson E. Motter, Jorge Cort\'es
bullets: Targets vanishing/exploding gradients and limited receptive fields in conventional RNNs.
Replaces neuron-to-neuron communication with a second-order spatial field governed by discretized partial differential equations.
Creates structured spatiotemporal patterns that act as high-capacity implicit memory.
Is equivalent to an infinite-order RNN whose state depends on its full history, with a fixed parameter count.
Outperforms other recurrent models on long-horizon benchmarks while using substantially fewer parameters.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a spatial neural computing approach to RNNs to achieve infinite context windows and unbounded receptive fields, directly addressing a core challenge in long-context LLMs.
papers.title: Learning infinite context windows in recurrent architectures via spatial neural computing
papers.tldr: A spatially evolving, PDE-based recurrent architecture provides fixed-parameter models with effectively infinite context and stable long-range memory.

papers.abstract: We study whether latent sequence compression of prompt prefixes preserves the capabilities that large language models rely on during inference. We introduce SemanticFold, a compression scheme that folds prefix hidden states at learned boundaries, and evaluate it across five model scales: Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-8B, SmolLM2-1.7B, Pythia-1.4B, and Pythia-6.9B. We use a fixed-target protocol: a frozen prefix is executed natively or compressed, and both arms teacher-force identical continuation tokens. This design rules out target-selection explanations for likelihood changes. We examine five endpoint families: fixed-target negative log-likelihood, finite-label reasoning accuracy, linear probe accessibility, open-ended generation, and systems-level memory and latency. We find that compression moves these endpoints non-monotonically and that they do not share a single compression threshold. On Qwen3-1.7B at compression ratio R=1.7, compressed-minus-native mean NLL decreases by 0.135 under paired bootstrap with 10000 draws. On SmolLM2 at R=1.2, the mean change is 0.013 higher than native. On both Pythia checkpoints, NLL is effectively unchanged. An NLL decomposition separating sequence shortening from the learned residual transform shows that the favorable Qwen likelihood is attributable primarily to residual adaptation rather than to shortening alone. MLP-only, which applies the transform without shortening, achieves 0.082 lower NLL than Full SemanticFold. Linear probe accuracy and macro AUC change by less than 0.03 in absolute value across conditions, with confidence intervals crossing zero. We conclude that preservation under latent compression has no single scalar certificate: language-model fit, decodability, and reasoning behavior answer different questions and can move in different directions under the same compression operation.
bullets: Introduces SemanticFold, which folds prefix hidden states at learned boundaries, and evaluates it across five language models.
Uses fixed-target teacher forcing to isolate compression effects on continuation likelihood from target-selection changes.
Compression effects are non-monotonic and model-dependent: likelihood improves on Qwen3-1.7B, slightly worsens on SmolLM2, and is effectively unchanged on Pythia.
Likelihood gains on Qwen3-1.7B mainly come from the learned residual transform rather than sequence shortening alone.
Linear-probe performance changes by less than 0.03 in absolute terms with confidence intervals crossing zero, while reasoning and generation endpoints need not track likelihood.
papers.selection_reason: Latent prefix compression for LLMs, relevant to long-context processing and token-reduction efficiency.
papers.title: SemanticFold: Latent Sequence Compression SeparatesLanguage Modeling, Decodability, and Reasoning
papers.tldr: SemanticFold shows that latent prefix compression affects language-model fit, decodability, and reasoning differently, with no single threshold or certificate of capability preservation.

papers.abstract: We introduce Hyperbolic Symplectic Positional Encoding (HySPE), grounding positional attention in non-compact symplectic transformations. While canonical Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) parameterizes the compact, elliptic branch of $\Sp(2,\R)$ via rotations, HySPE operationalizes its hyperbolic branch via a damped symmetric composition of dual shears, yielding a conformally symplectic contraction with two spectral decay rates per channel pair. To eliminate the exponential representation drift inherent to naive absolute factorizations, we diagonalize the operator in its invariant eigenbasis and introduce blockwise coordinate rebasing with adaptive centered execution. This guarantees length-independent numerical bounds while matching cached RoPE forward latency (7.21\,ms on an RTX 4090). On TinyShakespeare, HySPE-UltraLong maintains an invariant perplexity of 4.810 up to $16\times$ zero-shot extrapolation ($L=4096$), whereas RoPE degrades to 131.198. Scaled to a 51M-parameter subword Transformer on WikiText-103 ($L_{\text{train}}=512$), HySPE closely matches RoPE in-domain while robustly extrapolating to length 8192, reducing tail perplexity by 83.9\% over RoPE. While these controlled experiments establish HySPE's extrapolation robustness and numerical stability, evaluating its scaling behavior on large-scale foundation models remains an important direction for future investigation.
bullets: Uses damped dual shears to create a conformally symplectic positional encoding with two decay rates per channel pair.
Diagonalization and adaptive coordinate rebasing prevent exponential representation drift and provide length-independent numerical bounds.
Matches cached RoPE forward latency at 7.21 ms on an RTX 4090.
Maintains perplexity 4.810 through 16× zero-shot extrapolation on TinyShakespeare and reduces WikiText-103 tail perplexity by 83.9% at length 8192 versus RoPE.
Large-scale foundation-model scaling remains unevaluated.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a hyperbolic symplectic positional encoding (HySPE) that robustly extrapolates to 16x training length for LLMs, directly improving long-context capabilities.
papers.title: HySPE: Positional Encoding via Symplectic Dual Shears
papers.tldr: HySPE replaces RoPE’s rotations with stabilized hyperbolic symplectic transformations, enabling substantially more robust long-context extrapolation while retaining similar inference latency.

papers.abstract: Sparse attention mechanisms estimate attention over $n$ tokens using a small subset of keys. Many existing approaches use maximum inner product search (MIPS) to retrieve the heaviest keys, which motivates the following question: given black-box access to a MIPS oracle, how many keys must be retrieved to output an $\varepsilon$-accurate attention estimate? We answer this question by unifying prior approaches through the framework of priority sampling. With a single MIPS index, we show that $Θ(\sqrt{n}/\varepsilon)$ retrieved keys are both sufficient and necessary. With $Θ(\log n)$ indices, we give an algorithm that retrieves only $O(\log n+1/\varepsilon^2)$ keys and prove that this is near-optimal. More generally, we design algorithms that establish a smooth tradeoff between the number of MIPS indices and number of retrieved keys. We then show that if we allow augmentation of keys and queries, we can bypass the above lower bounds: there exists a simple priority-sampling estimator using a single MIPS index and $O(1/\varepsilon^2)$ retrieved keys. When integrated into LLM inference, our algorithms outperform top-$k$ and sampling approaches used in prior work and yield attention approximation that scales favorably to long contexts.
bullets: Single MIPS index: retrieving Θ(√n/ε) keys is both sufficient and necessary for ε-accurate attention estimation.
With Θ(log n) indices, retrieval falls to O(log n + 1/ε²), which is near-optimal.
A smooth tradeoff is established between the number of MIPS indices and retrieved keys.
Augmenting keys and queries bypasses the lower bound, achieving O(1/ε²) retrieved keys with one index.
In LLM inference, the proposed methods outperform prior top-k and sampling approaches and scale favorably to long contexts.
papers.selection_reason: Improves sparse attention via MIPS retrieval with optimality guarantees, directly relevant to efficient attention and long-context LLM inference.
papers.title: Attention via Black-Box Vector Search
papers.tldr: The paper characterizes how many keys black-box MIPS search must retrieve for accurate sparse attention and develops priority-sampling methods that reduce retrieval costs, especially with multiple indices or augmented keys and queries.

papers.abstract: The architectural design of Large Language Models (LLMs) is shifting from traditional full-attention-only models to hybrid models, which combine different attention modules to improve long-context efficiency and performance in length extrapolation and context extension. To explain why hybrid models work and how to design them better, we propose Mechanics of Long-Context Hybrid Models. As Part 1.1 of this series, we begin with hybrids of full attention and either sliding-window attention (SWA) or gated variants of linear attention (LA), represented by GLA and GDN. We first observe a Seesaw Effect in Context Extension: LA hybrids benefit more from long-context continual pretraining, whereas SWA hybrids perform better under length extrapolation. We attribute this behavior to differences in the positional inductive biases induced by these attention mechanisms. We find that SWA hybrids suffer from a Short-Context Learning Trap, Short-Window Weariness, and Long-Window Laziness, and require extended windows to enhance performance in continual long-context pretraining. For LA hybrids, we summarize the Matthew Effect of Hybrid Position Extrapolation and propose Sliding-Window Linear Attention, achieving 16$\times$ training-free length extrapolation while maintaining 100\% accuracy on NIAH-SK1 in 64k context length.
bullets: Studies hybrids combining full attention with sliding-window attention (SWA) or gated linear attention (GLA/GDN).
Finds a seesaw effect: linear-attention hybrids benefit more from continual long-context pretraining, while SWA hybrids favor length extrapolation.
Identifies SWA failure modes: short-context learning trap, short-window weariness, and long-window laziness.
Shows SWA hybrids need extended windows during continual long-context pretraining.
Proposes Sliding-Window Linear Attention to improve position extrapolation without additional training.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes hybrid attention mechanics for long-context and proposes novel Sliding-Window Linear Attention with 16x training-free length extrapolation.
papers.title: Mechanics of Long-Context Hybrid Models Part 1.1: From Hybrid Attention to Hybrid Position
papers.tldr: This work explains how positional biases shape long-context hybrid models and introduces Sliding-Window Linear Attention, enabling 16× training-free length extrapolation with perfect NIAH-SK1 accuracy at 64k context.

papers.abstract: We study long context language models. Instead of training long context natively, or designing a long context harness, we train a model over the simplest possible harness: a tool to call itself with any specified prompt and a tool to read tokens in a range from the input context. We finetune Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on a diverse synthetic dataset using this harness. With only 8,000 tokens of context, our small model is as strong as GPT-5.4 with 1M tokens of context on the OOLONG-synth benchmark when document length exceeds 40K tokens.
bullets: Targets long-context language modeling without native long-context training or a complex harness.
Trains Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on diverse synthetic data using self-calling and input token-range reading tools.
Uses agentic context management to selectively retrieve and process relevant document sections.
On OOLONG-synth documents longer than 40K tokens, matches GPT-5.4 with 1M-token context using only 8K tokens.
Scope: the reported result is limited to the OOLONG-synth benchmark and the stated document-length regime.
papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses long-context processing via a novel agentic harness, fitting long-context models.
papers.title: Trained Agentic Context Management
papers.tldr: A compact model trained to actively manage context through self-calls and token-range retrieval can handle very long documents effectively with only 8K tokens of context.

papers.abstract: Hybrid architectures combining linear sequence models with softmax attention provide an effective balance between efficient long-context modeling and precise token retrieval. Existing designs such as Native Hybrid Attention (NHA) combine compressed long-term states with sliding-window attention, but their exact attention is restricted to a fixed local window. In this work, we introduce Prefix-State Hybrid Block Attention (PHBA), which replaces local sliding-window attention with top-k block-sparse retrieval and couples each retrieved block with a compact prefix state summarizing its preceding context. The prefix states are constructed by a gated linear recurrence at block boundaries and retrieved together with the corresponding token blocks, allowing the model to combine precise long-range evidence with compressed historical context within a unified layer. We further develop a hardware-aware Triton implementation that streams routed token blocks and prefix states without materializing large intermediate tensors. Experiments show that PHBA improves long-context and retrieval performance over strong linear and hybrid baselines while retaining efficient training and inference.
bullets: Replaces fixed sliding-window attention with top-k retrieval of relevant token blocks.
Pairs each retrieved block with a gated recurrent prefix state summarizing its preceding context.
Unifies precise long-range evidence with compressed historical context in a hybrid attention layer.
Uses a hardware-aware Triton implementation that streams blocks and states without large intermediate tensors.
Experiments report improved long-context and retrieval performance while retaining efficient training and inference.
papers.selection_reason: Hybrid block-sparse attention with prefix states improves long-context retrieval and inference efficiency.
papers.title: PHBA: Prefix-State Hybrid Block Attention
papers.tldr: PHBA combines top-k block-sparse retrieval with compact prefix states to provide efficient, precise long-context modeling.

papers.abstract: Long-context inference and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) handle evidence selection at vastly different scales, from a single long prompt to an entire corpus. We ask whether a single model-internal mechanism can select evidence across this range. We introduce UNifying REtrieval And Long-Context with a Single Model (UNREAL), a model-native evidence selection framework to span corpus retrieval and long-context inference. UNREAL encodes chunks and derives retrieval queries directly from the frozen LLM's internal representations. It adds fewer than 500K trainable parameters and leaves the backbone unchanged. On a 3B-token, 21M-chunk Wikipedia index, all four dense and hybrid UNREAL backbones outperform state-of-the-art retriever-reranker systems. The best model raises recall from 49.1% to 73.2% on HotpotQA, from 31.7% to 60.1% on 2WikiMultiHopQA, and from 8.8% to 14.4% on MuSiQue. Applied to long-context tasks, the same selection mechanism removes distractors before generation, raising NoLiMa accuracy from 1.0% to 24.83% at its maximum context length of 128K tokens, and LV-Eval's F1 score from 49.97% to 54.66% at 256K. UNREAL also reduces FLOPs and time-to-first-token relative to full-context inference from roughly 32K tokens onward, with larger gains as context grows. Together, these results establish model-internal evidence selection as a common foundation for corpus retrieval and evidence-sparse long-context inference.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of selecting relevant evidence across both entire corpora and very long prompts.
Encodes document chunks and generates retrieval queries from the frozen LLM’s internal representations.
Adds fewer than 500K trainable parameters without changing the backbone.
Outperforms state-of-the-art retriever-reranker systems and substantially improves results on HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and MuSiQue.
Removes distractors in long-context tasks, improving NoLiMa and LV-Eval while reducing computation and time-to-first-token as context grows.
papers.selection_reason: Unifies retrieval and long-context evidence selection in a single LLM-native mechanism; directly relevant to long-context and LLM memory.
papers.title: UNREAL: Unifying Retrieval and Long-Context with a Single Model
papers.tldr: UNREAL uses a lightweight, model-internal evidence selector to unify corpus retrieval and long-context inference while keeping the LLM backbone frozen.

papers.abstract: Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) encodes token positions by rotating each two-dimensional channel of the query and key vectors at a channel-specific frequency, making the attention logits invariant to a common shift of positions. However, this rotation is periodic, and it leads to position aliasing where relative positions separated by a full rotation period become hard to tell apart. To address this, we propose WavePrune, which restricts each channel to its first rotation period. We show that it removes the distractions in attention maps created by position aliasing and improves overall long-context performance. Specifically, WavePrune raises the HELMET score on four of five models we test without any extra tuning (e.g., 35.7 -> 40.0 on Qwen3-8B). When pretraining models from scratch, WavePrune also achieves lower validation loss at extrapolated lengths than pretraining without it. Because WavePrune restricts each channel to a sliding window, it induces a fine-grained sparsity that our hardware-aligned CUDA kernels exploit for 1.15x prefill and 1.24x decoding speedups over FlashAttention-2 at 32K context. Together, these results show that RoPE's periodic structure, widely regarded as essential, is largely redundant beyond the first rotation period.
bullets: RoPE’s periodic rotations can make positions separated by a full period difficult to distinguish.
WavePrune restricts each channel to a sliding window covering only its first rotation period.
It improves HELMET scores on four of five tested models without extra tuning and lowers extrapolated-length validation loss during pretraining from scratch.
Hardware-aligned CUDA kernels achieve 1.15× faster prefilling and 1.24× faster decoding than FlashAttention-2 at 32K context.
The approach suggests RoPE information beyond the first rotation period is largely redundant; results are evaluated on five models and specific long-context settings.
papers.selection_reason: Improves RoPE long-context performance and yields attention sparsity speedups, directly relevant to long-context models and efficient attention.
papers.title: WavePrune: One period is often enough for RoPE
papers.tldr: WavePrune limits each RoPE channel to its first rotation period, reducing position aliasing while improving long-context quality and inference efficiency.

papers.abstract: Recurrent-attention hybrid language models (LMs), which interleave attention and recurrent layers, are increasingly used to combine the efficiency of the recurrent layers with the strong performance of attention layers. Prior work suggests that attention and recurrent layers offer complementary pathways to use past information: attention supports precise memory recall from earlier tokens, while recurrent layers support consolidation of disparate information over long contexts. However, we observe that simply having access to both pathways does not mean that hybrid LMs are effectively using them. We find that they rely substantially more on attention than on the recurrent state. Standard supervised fine-tuning improves overall performance but does not improve how the two memory pathways are coordinated: the model becomes more reliant on information propagated by attention layers, while its use of information propagated by recurrent layers remains limited. To encourage better coordination between the two memory pathways, we add an auxiliary loss that limits attention's access to earlier context while the recurrent state propagates through the full sequence. This objective encourages the model to retain and use information through the recurrent pathway alongside attention. It improves overall performance, with particularly strong gains on tasks involving longer contexts or requiring information aggregation, consistent with the strengths of recurrent layers observed in analysis. Crucially, this imbalance and the benefit of our auxiliary loss generalize: they apply to multiple recurrent-attention LMs in question-answering and agentic tasks, as well as to attention-based LMs that combine different forms of memory. Together, our findings show that simply providing multiple memory pathways does not ensure their effective use, and that targeted supervision is needed to better coordinate them.
authors: Hyunji Lee, Joykirat Singh, Zaid Khan, Justin Chih-Yao Chen, Elias Stengel-Eskin, Alessandro Sordoni, Arman Cohan, Mohit Bansal
bullets: Hybrid LMs combine attention for precise recall with recurrent states for long-range consolidation.
Despite access to both pathways, models rely substantially more on attention, and standard fine-tuning does not correct this imbalance.
An auxiliary loss limits attention’s access to earlier tokens while allowing recurrent information to propagate through the full sequence.
The resulting coordination improves overall performance, especially on longer-context and information-aggregation tasks.
The imbalance and intervention generalize across multiple hybrid LMs, question-answering and agentic tasks, and models with other memory forms.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes and improves memory pathway coordination in hybrid LMs; fits LLM memory and long-context topics.
papers.title: Balancing Memory Pathways: Analyzing and Improving Memory Utilization in Hybrid LMs
papers.tldr: Hybrid language models underuse recurrent memory, but restricting attention’s context during auxiliary training improves coordination and benefits long-context and information-aggregation tasks.

papers.abstract: Linear attention enables efficient long-context autoregressive decoding by compressing history into recurrent states, but this compression can make selective access to sparse and distant information difficult. Existing chunk-based extensions increase memory capacity, yet learned chunk-mixing coefficients may remain fixed with respect to input content and therefore cannot adapt historical access to each query. We introduce \emph{Hybrid Linear Attention} (HLA), a query-dependent chunk-level attention mechanism for Gated DeltaNet (GDN). HLA represents each completed chunk as an exact affine state transition and computes content-dependent routing gates from compact, self-attentively pooled representatives. Each gate interpolates the corresponding historical transition with the identity map, controlling both the chunk's additive memory and its transformation of earlier states. Effective-support regularization further encourages concentrated routing for sparse inference. We evaluate HLA under both pretrained adaptation and from-scratch training. Across Qwen3.5 models from 0.8B to 9B, HLA consistently improves over native GDN and fixed chunk mixing, with gains of up to 5.57 percentage points on LongBench-V2 and 3.97 points on RULER. In a controlled from-scratch 1.3B setting trained for 100B tokens with a 4K context, HLA also improves RULER performance from 4K to 32K, with gains increasing from 0.83 points at 4K to 4.22 points at 32K. These results demonstrate that query-dependent composition of recurrent memory improves long-context modeling and remains effective beyond the training context while using compact per-chunk affine summaries. Project page: https://caesarhhh.github.io/hla/
authors: Zhuokun Chen, Xi Lin, Xiyu Wu, Jiahao He, Jianfei Cai, Bohan Zhuang
bullets: Linear attention compresses history efficiently but can struggle to selectively access sparse, distant information.
HLA adds query-dependent chunk-level routing to Gated DeltaNet using compact, self-attentively pooled chunk representatives.
Each routing gate interpolates a chunk’s affine state transition with the identity, controlling both memory updates and state transformations.
Effective-support regularization encourages concentrated routing for sparse inference.
Across Qwen3.5 models, HLA improves long-context results over native GDN and fixed chunk mixing, including gains on LongBench-V2 and RULER; it also generalizes beyond the training context.
papers.selection_reason: Query-dependent chunk-level attention for linear attention improves long-context efficiency and recurrent memory composition.
papers.title: HLA: Expressive Hybrid Linear Attention via Chunk-Wise Dynamic Mixing
papers.tldr: HLA makes linear attention more expressive for long contexts by dynamically routing queries to relevant historical chunks.

papers.abstract: The next generation of multimodal research agents must reason over long-lived research histories rather than short model completions. During a single task, an agent may repeatedly search the web, inspect visual evidence, revisit earlier hypotheses, and accumulate tens of thousands of tokens of multimodal context. Despite this trend, online RL for multimodal research agents remains largely confined to shorter contexts and interaction horizons. We push online RL training to 128k context and 75+ tool-interaction turns. To our knowledge, this is the first online multimodal deep-research RL study trained at 128k context, and the first trained with a 75 tool-turn horizon. Scaling to this regime exposes several practical limitations of conventional RL training. Early in training, weak policies make poor use of large interaction budgets, causing expensive rollouts with little reward improvement. Later, policy entropy can collapse before performance has saturated, prematurely ending useful learning. We introduce Long-MDR, a three-component training recipe designed specifically for this setting: On-Policy Distillation Warmup, Progressive Horizon Expansion, and Entropy-Triggered Rescue. Together, these techniques improve both the learning efficiency and stability of long-horizon RL, enabling continued gains in a regime where direct training is slow and costly. At a 50-turn evaluation budget, our RL-trained Long-MDR-9B ranks first on five of six benchmarks among the compared 7B-9B agents.
bullets: Targets long-lived multimodal research tasks involving web search, visual evidence, and revisited hypotheses.
Introduces On-Policy Distillation Warmup, Progressive Horizon Expansion, and Entropy-Triggered Rescue.
Addresses inefficient early rollouts and premature entropy collapse during long-horizon RL training.
Trains at 128k context with horizons exceeding 75 tool turns, extending prior multimodal research-agent RL settings.
At a 50-turn evaluation budget, Long-MDR-9B ranks first on five of six benchmarks among compared 7B–9B agents.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses the challenge of long-context reinforcement learning for multimodal research agents, introducing techniques to handle 128k context and extended tool interaction horizons.
papers.title: Long-MDR: Long-Context Reinforcement Learning for Multimodal Deep-Research Agents
papers.tldr: Long-MDR enables stable and efficient online RL for multimodal research agents operating across 128k-token contexts and 75+ tool interactions.

papers.abstract: LLM agents for coding, search, and workplace tasks increasingly rely on long-context capabilities to effectively aggregate and reason over extended interaction histories. Recent work has incorporated agent trajectories into mid-training stage, drawing on their naturally long and interaction-rich structure. Yet how to organize the information within these trajectories into effective mid-training supervision remains underexplored. In this work, we investigate the relationship between long-context and agent atomic capabilities and introduce TrajLong, a novel framework that compiles trajectories into long-context training tasks with dense supervision, targeting three representative atomic capabilities: evidence grounding, cross-evidence aggregation, and temporal state maintenance. We mid-train Qwen3-14B-Base and Qwen3-30B-A3B-Base with data compiled by TrajLong, followed by supervised fine-tuning. Experiments on 6 long-context and 12 agent benchmarks demonstrate broad performance gains, with controlled ablations showing improvements over raw and masked trajectory baselines. Capability-level analyses further reveal task-dependent associations between long-context and agent atomic capabilities. These findings suggest that the shared capability demands of long-context reasoning and agent execution provide a principled basis for designing mid-training data to develop downstream agent capabilities.
authors: Miao Peng, Qintong Zhang, Nuo Chen, Yuhan Li, Guochen Yan, Xinran Gu, Hongqiu Wu, Hai Wang, Lydell Huang, Wentao Zhang, Jia Li
bullets: Targets evidence grounding, cross-evidence aggregation, and temporal state maintenance.
Compiles agent trajectories into long-context mid-training tasks with dense supervision.
Applies mid-training to Qwen3-14B-Base and Qwen3-30B-A3B-Base, followed by supervised fine-tuning.
Shows broad gains across 6 long-context and 12 agent benchmarks, outperforming raw and masked trajectory baselines in controlled ablations.
Finds task-dependent links between long-context reasoning and agent atomic capabilities.
papers.selection_reason: Long-context mid-training supervision for LLM agents directly fits long-context models.
papers.title: TrajLong: Co-Designing Agentic and Long-Context Supervision for Mid-Training
papers.tldr: TrajLong co-designs dense long-context supervision from agent trajectories to improve foundational capabilities for downstream LLM agents.

papers.abstract: Length generalization is the ability of sequential models to perform well on context lengths unseen during training. In this work, we show that the challenge of achieving length generalization is related not only to architectural choices such as positional encoding and the attention mechanism but also to the training procedure itself. We study how regularization affects length generalization and find that weight decay can hinder extrapolation. In contrast, dropout improves extrapolation when its placement within the architecture is reconsidered. In that regard, we show that the standard placement of dropout before layer normalization introduces a systematic distributional mismatch, and that applying dropout just before the linear projection resolves this issue. For example, a modified SmolLM3 with sliding window attention, continually pre-trained with dropout, can extrapolate perfectly to 64$\times$ on Needle-in-a-Haystack and far beyond the pre-training context size on RULER and HELMET. Mamba2 also benefits from dropout, suggesting an architecture-agnostic nature of the problem. We further propose Variance-Preserving Affine Dropout (VPAD), a new dropout strategy that substantially reduces the resulting pre-activation variance mismatch, leading to further extrapolation improvements in transformers.
authors: Pavlo Vasylenko, Matthias Lindemann, Andr\'e F. T. Martins, Marcos Treviso
bullets: Length generalization depends on training regularization as well as architecture and positional encoding.
Weight decay can impair extrapolation, whereas dropout can improve it when repositioned before the linear projection.
Standard dropout before layer normalization causes a distributional mismatch; the proposed placement alleviates it.
A modified SmolLM3 extrapolates 64× on Needle-in-a-Haystack and beyond its pre-training context on RULER and HELMET.
VPAD further reduces pre-activation variance mismatch, and dropout also benefits Mamba2, suggesting broad applicability.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates regularization for length generalization, directly relevant to long-context model capabilities.
papers.title: Length Generalization Needs Proper Regularization
papers.tldr: Properly placed dropout can substantially improve sequence-length extrapolation, while weight decay may hinder it.

papers.abstract: Long-context LLMs can now ingest entire online discussion threads, but understanding their social discourse requires more than reading a long document: models must track parent-reply relations, turning points, scoped subtrees, cross-branch contrasts, and participant trajectories. To test this structure-aware social reasoning, we introduce LongSocialBench, a benchmark of 1,462 verified human-authored multiple-choice items drawn from 94 complete Hacker News, Stack Exchange, and Reddit r/ChangeMyView episodes, with a median length of approximately 73K tokens. Each item pairs a complete serialized discussion and reply structure with a four-option question, requiring models to recover structured social evidence. Released items are verified for answerability, option uniqueness, and evidence grounding. Across 18 models and 29 evaluation settings, current long-context workflows remain far below human performance. The best individual result comes from Claude-Opus-4.7, which reaches 63.0% when prompted to eliminate incorrect options before answering, compared with 72.4% for independent human readers. Averaged across all 18 models, the full-context Baseline scores 43.9%. Supplying the gold evidence scope raises this to 55.0%, showing that substantial errors remain even after the relevant thread region is identified. LongSocialBench shows that the missing capability is not context access or prompting alone, but social understanding over structured reply trees.
authors: Xinyi Liu, Rinat Khaziev, Dilek Hakkani-T\"ur, Tarek F. Abdelzaher
bullets: Introduces 1,462 verified multiple-choice questions from 94 complete Hacker News, Stack Exchange, and Reddit r/ChangeMyView discussions, with median length of about 73K tokens.
Tests reasoning over parent-reply relations, turning points, subtrees, cross-branch contrasts, and participant trajectories.
Across 18 models and 29 settings, the best result is 63.0% for Claude-Opus-4.7 with option-elimination prompting, versus 72.4% for human readers.
The full-context baseline averages 43.9%; providing the gold evidence scope improves performance to 55.0%, but leaves substantial errors.
Finds that the central limitation is social understanding over structured reply trees, not merely context access or prompting.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a benchmark specifically probing long-context LLM understanding of structured social discourse, directly relevant to long-context model evaluation.
papers.title: LongSocialBench: Do Long-Context LLMs Understand Online Discussion Threads?
papers.tldr: LongSocialBench shows that long-context LLMs still struggle to understand the structured social dynamics of online discussion threads, despite being able to process their full length.

papers.abstract: A language model reads long text in one quadratic forward pass, stops at the context window, and loses accuracy with length before reaching it. We ask whether the read can be factorized when deciding over a finite set: which document is relevant, which option is supported, which passage is the evidence. Periscope, a training-free inference method, arranges the $N$ chunks of a text on a $K{\times}K$ grid with $K{=}\lceil\sqrt{N}\rceil$ and asks a frozen model the same question about $K$ local spans of consecutive chunks and $K$ strided spans that sample the whole text, reading the log-odds of every answer at one token. Each answer takes its best local and strided score, and scoring every chunk by its two spans gives an evidence map at no further cost, whose peak is the chunk behind the answer. Every probe is about $\sqrt{sc}$ tokens for a text of $s$ tokens and chunk size $c$, so a window of $W$ tokens reaches $W^{2}/c$ tokens at $s^{1.5}$ cost. The map replaces the long read. On LongBench v2, reading only the $K$ chunks the map ranks highest, 9k tokens, matches the same model's best window read across windows from 32k to 1M tokens, and on InfiniteBench, where the median context is 150k tokens, it leads the best window read by 5 points. The same map ranks BRIGHT's long-document corpora with the best NDCG@10 of six methods. Each call caches only one probe, so a 27B model reads 4.5M-token contexts on one 80GB GPU, where a single pass would need 296GB of cache. A long read then needs a GPU that holds the model, not one that holds the text.
authors: Mohamed Eltahir, Anas Obayd, Raed Rashid, Abdulrahman Alghamdi, Abdulrahman Mousa, Abdallah Ahmed, Tanveer Hussain, Naeemullah Khan
bullets: Addresses context-window limits, accuracy degradation, and quadratic cost in long-document reading.
Arranges text chunks on a grid and queries local consecutive spans plus strided spans covering the whole text.
Combines answer log-odds to rank chunks and identify the evidence behind an answer.
On LongBench v2, 9k selected tokens match the model’s best window read across 32k–1M-token contexts; on InfiniteBench, Periscope leads by 5 points.
Handles 4.5M-token contexts for a 27B model on one 80GB GPU, while a single-pass read would require 296GB of cache.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free context-window extension with cache-efficient long-context inference, directly relevant to long-context and memory efficiency.
papers.title: Periscope: Extending Frozen Language Models Beyond Their Context Window
papers.tldr: Periscope extends frozen language models to million-token texts by using training-free local and strided probes to map evidence without reading the entire document at once.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) shows promise for enterprise knowledge work, yet it often underperforms in high-stakes decision settings that require deep synthesis, strict traceability, and recovery from underspecified prompts. One-pass retrieval-and-write pipelines frequently yield shallow summaries, inconsistent grounding, and weak mechanisms for completeness verification. We introduce ADORE (Adaptive Deep Orchestration for Research in Enterprise), an agentic framework that replaces linear retrieval with iterative, user-steered investigation coordinated by a central orchestrator and a set of specialized agents. ADORE's key insight is that a structured Memory Bank (a curated evidence store with explicit claim-evidence linkage and section-level admissible evidence) enables traceable report generation and systematic checks for evidence completeness.
